en: Preface to the *Sifen jieben* (The Four-Part Code of Precepts) by Way of Meaning:
In the year of Gengchen, while I was at Zhenji Monastery in Hangzhou, I wished to emulate Guifeng by extracting the essentials of the Vinaya to instruct those of later learning.
However, my efforts were ultimately thwarted by illness. This spring, having come from Gushan to Baoshan, I have declined all visitors.

"I request only that you propagate and chant the *Vinaya*. Since others have requested a commentary on the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* as a manual for novice monks (*śrāmaṇera*), I said, 'This is my long-standing aspiration,' and thus granted my consent.
I began writing during the first decade of the middle autumn month and finished at the end of the first decade of the early winter month.
It took exactly three months, completing after three drafts were set aside. Regarding both the facts and the principles therein, all—
I have compiled this from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-piṭaka*. All matters concerning what is permitted and what is prohibited are strictly based on the Buddha’s original precepts;
I do not dare to arbitrarily judge them according to my own whims. Alas!

That such a work as this should be completed on this very day—amidst this era when heaven and earth undergo a total transformation, during this autumn when the world is yet unsettled in its nascent state, when white blades pierce the air and corpses lie strewn across the fields, and the inhabitants flee in terror.
Fleeing into mountain valleys, they risk their lives day and night; yet why do I labor against my illness to compose this?
It is because people know that the changes in the course of worldly fortune bring great suffering, but they do not realize that the changes in the course of the Dharma bring even greater suffering.
The suffering of a change in worldly fortune lasts but a moment, whereas the suffering of a change in the course of the Dharma lasts for ten thousand kalpas. A moment...
The calamity of suffering here ends with the destruction of one’s own body; the calamity of suffering for ten thousand kalpas reaches its limit in the three miserable realms.
Comparing this with that, how could the former ever equal even a hundred-thousand-millionth part of the latter?

Yet, because people see only what has already occurred and cannot perceive what is yet to come, they are struck with panic and lose their composure regarding the former, while remaining complacent and seeking mere security regarding the latter. I lament that since the beginning of the Heavenly Mandate...
The elders of venerable virtue have withered and passed away, while those of late standing daily decline toward the abyss, like a mad torrent that cannot be turned back.
Furthermore, they recklessly display their empty views and treat the precepts as mere hair ornaments; if there is no defense against this, where will it end?

This is why I have applied myself with such diligence and urgency to complete this work, not daring to let worldly difficulties obstruct me. I simply consider how to put this book into practice in the present.
In such an age, it would be fortunate indeed if one were not treated with contempt or derision while playing the zither at the gate of the King of Qi;
how much less could one dare hope for him to rely upon and practice it? Nevertheless, this is like the sacrificial sheep offered at the beginning of the month:
whether it is preserved or discarded depends on the benevolent man.
On the first day of the month of the first yang in winter of the Bingxu year, the śramaṇa Yuanxian, successor to the orthodox lineage of Cao-Dong,
inscribed this at Baoshan Monastery in Jianzhin.
Table of Contents for the *Jiyi* (Summary of Meanings) of the Four-Part Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
Volume One:
Preface to the Precept Sūtra; Four Pārājika Dharmas;
Thirteen Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharmas; Two Aniyata Dharmas.
Volume Two:
Thirty *Niḥsargika-pāyattika* Dharmas; Volume Three: Ninety *Pāyattika* Dharmas.
The remainder of the ninety *pāyattika* rules; the four *pratideśanīya* dharmas, Volume Four;
the *śaikṣa* dharmas; the seven methods for settling disputes.
Catalogue of the Verses of the Seven Buddhas and the Dedication Hymns (End).
Fascicle One of the *Sifen jieben yueyi* (The Four-Part Prātimokṣa Sūtra with Explanations of Meaning).
Composed by the monk Yuánxián, a successor to the ancestral lineage at Gǔshān in Fúzhōu.
The *Sifen* [Vinaya] consists of four parts: first, the precepts for bhikṣus; second, the precepts for bhikṣuṇīs, along with the procedures for receiving and reciting the precepts;

third, the rules for the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) and the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*); and fourth, the regulations for monastic dwellings and the miscellaneous *khandakas*. It is therefore called the "Four Parts" (*caturvarga*). *Khandaka* means...

"Dharmaguptaka" means "Collection of the Dharma," which refers to its divisional meaning. The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* (Precepts Text) is the portion at the beginning of the Bhikṣu-prātimokṣa, consisting of the words by which the Buddha established the precepts;
it is that which the assembly recites together every half-month. Its source originates from the Dharmaguptaka school.
"Dharmaguptaka" translates here as "Dharma-secrecy" (*Dharmagupta*); this is the title of the founder of the school. Previously, thirty years after the Buddha attained enlightenment...
In the eighth year, [the Buddha] attended a royal feast in Rājagṛha. When the feast was over, Rāhula dropped his bowl to the ground while washing it;
it shattered into five pieces. The Buddha said, "This portends that after my parinirvāṇa, various wicked bhikṣus will divide my Vinaya into five schools.
One hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was the Venerable Upagupta.
These disciples were five in number, each adhering to their own views; consequently, they divided the Vinaya into five schools:
first, the Dharmaguptaka school; second, the Sarvāstivāda school; third, the Kāśyapīya school; fourth, the Mahīśāsaka school;
and fifth, the Vātsīputrīya school. As for the ancient Vinaya, it was the Mahāsāṃghika. This original transmission reached the Tang dynasty, where in total there were...
There are four versions of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*. That which Master Daoxuan followed was the version translated by Dharmayaśas during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Because this version differs slightly from the Vinaya [of other recensions], the monk Huaisu of Xitaiyuan Monastery in Tang China later extracted the essential points from it;

this is popularly known as the "New Vinaya. Regarding these two versions—the Old and the New—none dare to disparage one over the other; they have been submitted for imperial decree and are held in reverence.
The two versions were established in parallel; these are the two texts currently found in the canon.

Having examined them in detail, I find that while their meaning is in fact without discrepancy, there are slight differences in the wording. I have now collated and finalized both versions together, not daring to arbitrarily add or subtract anything.
I prostrate and pay homage to all Buddhas, As well as the Dharma and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus.

Now, in order to expound the Vinaya rules so that the True Dharma may long endure, I shall recite the Sūtra on Precepts. First, I recite this verse; this constitutes the introduction to the recitation of the precepts. The full text remains in the Vinaya.
It is extensive. It is suspected that this was spoken by the patriarch Dharmagupta. Now, having examined the prolixity and extracted the essentials, it is unknown by whom these deletions were made.
The first two lines pay homage to the Triple Gem to seek their hidden protection. The next two lines clarify the fundamental intent of reciting the precepts and proclaim their exposition.
*Vinaya* is here translated as "Law" (*lü*) and also as "Excellent Discipline" (*shànzhì*). Therefore—

The Vinaya governs offenses. Regarding the phrase "causing the True Dharma to abide for a long time": the precepts serve as the grand foundation for meditative concentration and wisdom, and the essential path to liberation.
If one does not attain the precepts, then even if one possesses meditative concentration and wisdom, they will all become demonic and heterodox.
If the precepts are recited, the True Dharma will abide for a long time; if they are not recited, the True Dharma will not abide for long.
The precepts are like a boundless ocean; like jewels, one never tires of seeking them. Desiring to protect the wealth of the Noble Dharma, all you who have gathered, listen as I speak.
This praises the virtue of the precepts to encourage one to listen. The dharma of the precepts is vast and expansive, like the great ocean with no boundaries;
it is worthy of being esteemed as precious as rare jewels. One should seek it diligently and never give rise to weariness.
The noble wealth of the Dharma is itself a treasure. If one wishes to guard these precepts so as not to lose them, one must constantly listen.
By means of this precept, may you constantly exert yourselves so that the precepts may be protected.
Desiring to eliminate the four *pārājika* offenses and to extinguish the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, I shall speak before the assembled community regarding the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules.

This statement that the precepts can extinguish transgressions is intended to encourage one to listen. If the precepts have been violated, one should constantly listen to the recitation of the precepts and openly confess;
thus, the transgression may be extinguished. "Obstruction" (āvaraṇa) means to prevent or ward off;

it refers to being able to prevent oneself from falling into [lower realms]. There are five categories of precepts (*pañca-varga*), but here only three are mentioned, citing the most serious cases to encompass the rest.
"Listen attentively.
Vipassī, Sikhi, Vessabhū, Kakusandha, Konāgamana, Kassapa, and Śākyamuni—
these World-Honored Ones of great virtue have spoken of this matter for my sake."
I now wish to explain this well; may all you worthy ones listen together to these words.
These precepts were established by the seven Buddhas in common; they were not arbitrarily devised by later persons. Therefore, you should all listen together.
Just as a person whose feet are injured is unable to travel anywhere,
so too one who has violated the precepts cannot be reborn among gods or humans. If you wish to be reborn in the heavens or among human beings,
you must always protect the feet of the precepts and ensure they are not damaged, just as a charioteer enters a perilous path with care.
The loss of the linchpin and the breaking of the axle are causes for anxiety; so too is the destruction of the precepts. At the time of death, one harbors fear and dread.

This is established as a metaphor to demonstrate the harm of violating the precepts. Just as a person whose feet are destroyed cannot walk, one who violates the precepts cannot be reborn among gods or humans.
If one wishes to be reborn among gods or humans, one must necessarily guard the precepts; how much more so when it concerns entering the Noble Path!

Furthermore, it is like a charioteer entering a perilous road who, having lost the linchpin and broken the axle, cannot emerge from that danger. Likewise, one who destroys the precepts cannot escape the evil realms.
At the moment of death, malevolent signs appear before them, and they will inevitably fall into the three miserable paths; they can do nothing but harbor deep fear.
Thus, one knows that the precepts must never be violated. (The "linchpin" [轄] refers to the iron pin at the head of the chariot axle.)
Just as when a person looks into a mirror, Joy or sorrow arises according to whether they are handsome or ugly, So it is with the recitation of the precepts:
Complete integrity or violation gives rise to joy or grief. Just as when two armies engage in battle, The brave advance while the cowardly retreat, So it is with the recitation of the precepts:
Purity and defilement give rise to peace or fear.
This is an analogy established to demonstrate the benefits of reciting the *Prātimokṣa*. It is like a person looking into a mirror and seeing their own beauty or ugliness;
they rejoice in what is beautiful and feel sorrow over what is ugly. Likewise, when the *Prātimokṣa* is recited, one sees for oneself whether one’s conduct is complete or impaired;

one rejoices in its completeness and feels concern over its impairment. Furthermore, it is like two armies engaged in battle: the brave advance while the cowardly retreat. So too with the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*...
The pure find peace, while the defiled feel dread. Joy and peace bring about the intent for further progress;
sorrow and dread provide the opportunity for repentance and reform. Such are the benefits of reciting the precepts.
Among those in the world, the king is supreme; Among all streams, the ocean is supreme; Among all stars, the moon is supreme;
Among all holy ones, the Buddha is supreme. Among all the various codes of discipline, The Sūtra of Precepts is the highest and most supreme.
The Tathāgata established these prohibitions and precepts, To be recited every half-month.
The preceding series of repeated exhortations is now concluded. This section, however, evaluates its superior merit to serve as a summary of the foregoing text.
It is stated thus because, within the Vinaya of the Hīnayāna, the Bhikṣu precepts are considered supreme; it is precisely because these precepts are supreme that [this evaluation is made].
The Tathāgata established these prohibitions and precepts so that they must be recited every half-month;
this is to admonish those who are muddled and indolent, and to eliminate transgressions and faults.
The harmonious Saṃgha assembles (responding: "The Saṃgha has assembled in harmony"). Those who have not received full ordination are excluded (if present, they are sent away, responding:

"Those who have not received full ordination have already been excluded"; if none are present, responding: "There are no who have not received full ordination"). The bhikṣus who did not attend state their *chanda* and purity (if present, they state it according to the Dharma;

if none are present, responding: "There are none who state their *chanda* and purity"). Who sent a bhikṣuṇī to request instruction? (If present, they respond fully according to the request; if none are present, responding: "There is no bhikṣuṇī here who has come to request instruction"). The Saṃgha...
What is being performed now by this assembly? (Answer: The *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the precepts.

Venerable Saṃgha, listen! Today is the fifteenth day of the waxing moon; the community of monks is to recite the precepts. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen:
we shall recite the precepts in harmony. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
This is the ritual procedure for the *karmavācanā*. Regarding "harmony" (*saṃgha-sāmagrī*): the Vinaya states that those who ought to come must come;
those who ought to give their consent (*chanda*) must give their consent and come; and those present must not voice objections when they have the right to do so—this is called harmony.
The opposite is called lack of harmony. Regarding "assembling": the Vinaya states that one should spread out seats, strike the *gandī* three times, and the entire assembly must gather together.

Assembled in one place. Regarding those who have not yet received the lower [ordination]: according to the Vinaya, neither laypeople nor śrāmaṇeras are permitted to listen to the confession of precepts (poṣadha) for the great assembly of monks;
those who do so incur immeasurable offenses, and therefore they are sent away. Regarding those who do not come:

the Vinaya states that if a bhikṣu has business concerning the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha, or if he is ill or tending to the sick, he is permitted to give his consent (*chanda*). As for giving consent, it means permitting him...

One may convey the *chanda* (consent) to others; however, one must exclude cases involving the establishment of boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*) and base matters (*kutsita-karma*). To convey [the consent] in such instances constitutes an offense.

The person conveying the *chanda* shall, while within the assembly, adjust their deportment and say: "Venerable sirs, please attend with one-pointed mind. Now, the bhikṣu named so-and-so declares himself pure and free from all obstructing conditions.
Due to the cause and condition of illness, he is unable to attend the formal act of the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma."
The formal expression of consent and purity (*chandapariśuddhi*) is concluded with a single recitation. [The Buddha asked: "Who has sent this nun down?
Because the community of nuns was ignorant and lacked the habit of visiting [the monks], the Buddha permitted them to go among the monks once every half-month to request an instructor (*avavādaka*).
The person receiving the commission should, within the assembly, adjust their deportment and say: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! The harmonious bhikṣuṇīs of such-and-such a place have appointed..."
"Venerable Saṃgha, the bhikṣuṇī [Name] has for half a month prostrated at the feet of the harmonious Saṃgha and requested instruction.
Having said this three times, the Saṃgha should select an instructor from among its members and formally appoint him by means of a *jñapti-karman*.

If there is no one capable, the Elder should perform the abbreviated method of instruction and address the person who is to inform her, saying: 'Tomorrow the bhikṣuṇīs will come to request instruction; is it not the proper time? He should reply:"

Last night, when the nuns went on their rounds of invitation, they found that no one was available. However, there was a decree from the Elder (Upādhyāya) instructing the assembly of nuns to practice the Path with diligence, to be prudent, and not to be negligent.
Those who received this charge informed the arriving nuns in accordance with the Dharma. When the nuns returned and assembled, the Elder’s decree was proclaimed;
they should then listen with palms joined and respond, saying: "We receive it upon our heads and shall carry it out," and then perform prostrations.
Having prostrated, they withdraw. If a bhikṣuṇī does not request a teacher for instruction from the *saṃgha* during the half-month, she commits an offense of transgression (*pāyattika*).

*Karmavācanā* (here translated as "performing the ritual to accomplish the matter") refers to performing the ritual by announcing it to the assembly. The passage beginning with "Venerable Sirs" (*bhadanta*) constitutes the formal words of the *karmavācanā*.
Regarding "the bright fortnight" (*śuklapakṣa*) and "the dark fortnight" (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*): the first half of the month is the bright fortnight, and the second half of the month is the dark fortnight.

"The time has come for the Sangha," meaning that it is the moment when the ritual procedure (*dharmakarma*) is to be performed. "Listen with patience" means to grant permission to hear the performance of the *karmavācanā*.
"Venerable sirs, I now wish to recite the Prātimokṣa. Venerable sirs, listen attentively and reflect well upon it."
If you know for yourself that you have committed an offense, you should immediately confess it; if you have not committed one, remain silent.
By remaining silent, the Venerable Ones know that you are pure. If you are questioned by another, you should answer truthfully.
Thus, O Bhikṣus, if within the great assembly, after being asked up to three times, a monk remembers having a transgression and does not confess it, he incurs the offense of intentional lying.

Regarding verbal offenses: The Buddha has declared that intentional lying is a dharma that obstructs the Path. If a bhikṣu remembers having committed an offense and desires to seek purity, he should confess it.
Through confession, one attains peace and happiness; through non-confession, the offense becomes increasingly grave.
This causes one to recollect one's transgressions and to perform repentance.
*Prātimokṣa* is translated here as "Guarantee of Liberation," meaning that by upholding these precepts, one guarantees the attainment of liberation.

It is also called "Individual Liberation," meaning that through the three types of action and seven branches, one attains liberation individually by using the precepts to prevent wrongdoing. If someone asks about this: [it refers to] this.
Beyond the three questions, if there is another matter that must be examined before the assembly, one should likewise answer according to the facts.
One incurs the offense of intentional lying by knowingly concealing a transgression while being aware that one has committed it.
Although there has been no speech, it is likewise a case of declaring one who is guilty to be innocent; this is a false and unreal matter that obstructs the Path.
It constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Venerable sirs, I have now recited the introduction to the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*. I now ask the venerable sirs: Are you pure in this regard? (Ask three times.)
Venerable sirs, herein we are pure, for we remain silent; thus let this matter be so held.
The above is the general title of the Preface to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra; what follows is the detailed exposition of the precepts.
Venerable sirs, these four *pārājika* dharmas are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
*Pārājika* here means "abandonment"; it signifies that one who commits this offense is forever abandoned outside the shores of the Buddha’s ocean.

If a bhikṣu, who shares the same precepts as other bhikṣus, does not relinquish the precepts and does not confess his weakness in observing them, yet commits an act of unchastity—even with an animal—this bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense; he is no longer to live in communion.
The Venerable Sudinna, during a year of famine, led his assembly to his native village to beg for food.

His mother repeatedly urged the Venerable to abandon the path and return to lay life. The Venerable refused her three times. His mother said, "Since you will not return, you may serve as seed so that your lineage shall not be severed.
At that time, the Buddha had not yet established the precepts, and the Venerable did not know [the prohibition].
[He] transgressed. He then consented to his mother’s command and, together with his wife, Cheng, committed that act. Later, the Buddha, knowing the reason, established a precept.
"Sharing the same precepts as the bhikṣus" means sharing the full ordination (upasaṃpadā) received together with all the bhikṣus. Regarding "not abandoning the precepts," the Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu does not delight in pure conduct, he is permitted to abandon the precepts and return home. When abandoning them, one must do so before the Three Jewels, as follows:

The Dharma [requires] three proclamations to constitute relinquishment. If one does so with a deranged mind, or in the presence of a deranged person, or even before devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, or those who do not understand such speech, in all these cases it does not constitute relinquishment.

If the speech is indistinct, it likewise does not constitute relinquishment. "One whose precepts are weak" means one who frequently violates the precepts. When one frequently violates the precepts, they shall then...

Through courageous repentance, the essence of the precepts was restored. Now, if you cannot repent, your evil will increase day by day until you inevitably commit impure conduct—that is, sexual misconduct—even to the point of engaging with a female monkey while living alone in the forest like a certain bhikṣu.

Later, due to this, that bhikṣu... [the other bhikṣus... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a Vinaya commentary or narrative concerning the restoration of the *śīla-skandha* through repentance (*pāpadeśanā*), followed by a warning regarding the consequences of failing to do so, specifically citing the case of a monk who committed sexual misconduct with a female monkey.)
The Venerable Kāśyapa observed this and informed the Buddha; therefore, [the Buddha] established a comprehensive prohibition.

For any bhikṣu who violates [this rule] with respect to any male, female, or non-human being—whether it be the path or not the path, whether there is an obstruction or no obstruction—if he first enters even as much as a hair’s breadth, he incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If he employs the means but does not enter, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If an enemy forcibly seizes the bhikṣu...
If one engages in unchaste conduct, there is no offense for one who does not experience pleasure; there is an offense for one who experiences pleasure.

If a bhikṣu instructs another bhikṣu to engage in unchaste conduct, if that [instructed] bhikṣu carries out the instruction, it is a sthūlātyaya; if he does not carry out the instruction, it is a duṣkṛta.
For a bhikṣuṇī who commits this, it is a pārājika. For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī...

Māni. [If one commits] *duṣkṛta*, there is the penalty of *pravāsanīya* (banishment). If one is asleep and lacks awareness, or does not experience pleasure, and has no intention of sexual desire at all, there is no offense.
Regarding "one who has committed a *pārājika* and is not to live in communion":

this means that the offender may not share the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* or perform *karmavācanā* together with the pure assembly. Indeed, such is the case for those who have committed this [offense].
He shall immediately be expelled. If there is one who has committed an offense but does not conceal it, he shall be demoted to a position after the bhikṣus and before the śrāmaṇeras;
he shall not participate in any affairs common to all bhikṣus.
He must not confer the precepts upon others, nor may he maintain a śrāmaṇera, nor receive dependence from another, nor instruct bhikṣuṇīs. He must humble himself and undergo discipline.
One must subdue the mind and conduct; throughout one's life, one must not depart from them. Only upon realizing the fruit of Arhatship does one transcend into the rank of the Great Sangha.
If a bhikṣu, whether in a village or in a secluded place, takes what is not given with a thieving mind, it constitutes theft according to the value of the object.
Taking the Dharma: If one is a king and is seized by the king’s ministers, or is killed, or bound, or driven out of the country, saying, "You are a thief!
You are deluded! You know nothing!"—this bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and is no longer to live in communion.
The Venerable Dhanika built a house for himself and privately took timber belonging to King Samaṇḍaka.

When the matter was discovered and he was arrested, according to the laws of the land, one who steals five *kārsāpaṇas* should be sentenced to death. However, because he was a bhikṣu, the king merely rebuked him and sent him away.

The Buddha, knowing this, established the precept: one must only take things that have been given by another; if another has not given them, yet one takes them with a thieving mind, it is indeed theft.
"According to the law of taking what is not given" means that the offense is determined based on the laws regarding taking what is not given as enacted by the king.
In all cases of stealing property, if the value reaches five *kārsāpaṇas* and the object is moved from its original place, [it constitutes the full offense].

A *śa* constitutes the offense of abandonment (*pārājika*). Five *kārsāpaṇas*—which in this land is equivalent to one silver *māṣaka*—constitute the limit. If it is less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one intends to take [the property] but has not yet taken it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If one employs means to destroy another's property; or if one takes it by relying on intimacy or force;
or if one takes it through verbal deception; or if one uses incantations and the like.
If one takes [the goods] by force, one commits a *pārājika* offense upon obtaining five *māṣakas*; if one obtains less than five *māṣakas*, or if one has not yet obtained them, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one employs various expedients to steal for another person by evading customs duties, it is in all cases a *sthūlātyaya*. If one employs expedients and succeeds in obtaining five *māṣakas*, one commits a *pārājika*;
if one does not obtain them, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If one employs expedients and succeeds in obtaining less than five *māṣakas*, [it is likewise a *sthūlātyaya*].
It is a *sthūlātyaya*; it is not a *duṣkṛta*. If one instructs another to seek five *kārsāpaṇas* and they obtain five *kārsāpaṇas*, both commit a *pārājika*.
If they do not obtain them, both commit a *sthūlātyaya*. If one instructs another to seek less than five *kārsāpaṇas* and they obtain less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, both commit a *sthūlātyaya*.
If they do not obtain them, both commit a *duṣkṛta*. If one instructs a person to seek...
[If] five *kārsāpaṇas* [are the object], and the one who receives the instruction obtains less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, both commit a *sthūlātyaya*.

If, by means of an expedient, one instructs another to seek less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, and the one who receives the instruction obtains five *kārsāpaṇas*, the one who receives the instruction commits a *pārājika*, while the instructor commits a *sthūlātyaya*.
If, by means of an expedient, one instructs another to seek five *kārsāpaṇas*, and the one who receives the instruction takes other items worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, [the same applies].
The one who commits the offense incurs *pārājika*; the instructor incurs *sthūlātyaya*.

If one instructs another through expedient means to seek five coins, and the person so instructed, believing they are merely being sent to fetch goods, takes the five coins without the intent to steal, the instructor incurs *pārājika* while the person so instructed incurs no offense.
If one instructs another to take goods, and the person so instructed, believing the instruction was to steal them, obtains five coins, the person so instructed... [incurs the offense].

If one takes five coins from an object belonging to another where there is doubt that it belongs to another, or from an ownerless object where there is doubt that it belongs to another, or from an ownerless object where there is no doubt that it is ownerless, the offense is a *sthūlātyaya*. If one takes less than five coins from an object belonging to another where there is doubt that it belongs to another, or from an ownerless object where there is doubt that it belongs to another, or from an ownerless object where there is no doubt that it is ownerless, the offense is a *duṣkṛta*.

One who instructs [another] to do so is not guilty of an offense. If one takes five coins from an object belonging to another where there is doubt that it belongs to another, or from an ownerless object where there is doubt that it belongs to another, or from an ownerless object where there is no doubt that it is ownerless, both [the taker and the instructor] commit a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one takes less than five coins from an object belonging to another where there is doubt that it belongs to another, or from an ownerless object where there is doubt that it belongs to another, or from an ownerless object where there is no doubt that it is ownerless, both commit a *duṣkṛta*.
It is a *duṣkṛta*. For a bhikṣuṇī who commits this offense, it is a *pārājika*. For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *sātisāra* (transgression) leading to expulsion.

There is no offense if one takes [the object] with the perception that it belongs to another; or if one takes it with the perception that it is one's own property; or if one takes it with the perception that it is refuse;
or if one takes it with the perception that it is being taken temporarily; or if one takes it with the intention of a close friend.
If a bhikṣu, with his own hand, takes the life of a human being; or provides a person with a weapon; or praises death; or encourages death, saying, "Ho, man!

What is the use of this wretched life? It is better to die than to live"; or if, with such thoughts, he uses various means to praise death and encourage death—this bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and shall not dwell in communion.
The bhikṣus at the Pārileyyaka Garden practiced the meditation on impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) and became so deeply repulsed by their physical bodies that they sought to take their own lives.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Mukilinda, who was of non-Buddhist lineage; he entered the garden carrying a blade.

The bhikṣus entreated him to end their lives, promising to reward him with their robes and alms bowls. Consequently, deaths occurred one after another. When the lay devotees saw this, they reviled [the monks].
[The Buddha] disapproved. Because he knew [the circumstances], he established this precept. Regarding "one who takes human life": this excludes killing those who are not human.
Regarding "giving a knife to another": knowing that another intends to commit suicide, one gives them a knife; or, one provides a knife to another person, commanding them to carry out the killing.
Regarding "praising death": extolling the excellence and joy of dying. Regarding "urging death": exhorting them to die quickly. *Duḥ*! (A cry of reproach.)

"Manzi xia" (The Man's Lower Part) is a passage of earnest exhortation. "Holding a blade and giving it to another" refers to cases where one does not kill with their own hand, yet the intent is truly to kill.

Generally speaking, if a bhikṣu kills themselves, instructs another to kill, causes a bird or beast to kill, uses poison to kill, or employs expedients such as pits and traps, even using water, fire, wood, stone, or other means to sever life, all such acts constitute [killing].

If one commits the offense of abandonment (*pārājika*), but the victim does not die through the means employed, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If one kills a deva, nāga, yakṣa, or animal capable of changing its form, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if the victim does not die through the means employed, it is a *duṣkṛta*. Killing an ordinary animal is a *pāyattika*.

If one kills with the intent [of killing] a non-human, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If a person is suspected of being a non-human; or if one perceives a person as a non-human; or if one perceives a non-human as a person;
or if a non-human is suspected of being a person—if one kills them in any of these cases, it is all a *sthūlātyaya*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, it is a *pārājika*. For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is all a *duṣkṛta* leading to expulsion.
Expulsion. If one throws a sword, staff, tile, stone, or the like, and kills by mistake, there is no offense for all those who die while being entirely free of harmful intent.
If a bhikṣu, knowing nothing at all, says, "I have attained the state of a superior person; I have already entered the noble wisdom of excellence," [he commits an offense].
“Dharma. I know this; I see this. Later, whether questioned or not, desiring to be pure, he speaks thus:
“In truth, I did not know and I did not see, yet I said I knew and I saw; it was a false and deceptive lie.
With the exception of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), this bhikṣu has committed a *pārājika* offense and shall not live in communion.

Due to a famine, alms were difficult to obtain. The Buddha therefore commanded that monks should observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*) wherever they were. At that time, the monks of the Pārileyyaka Garden devised a stratagem, hoping to make it easier for them to obtain food.
They went to the houses of lay devotees and claimed, "We have attained the state of a superior person" (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*).

"The state of a superior person" is also called the "state beyond the human" (*uttari-manussa-dhamma*); it refers to the sublime Dharma of noble wisdom, namely the four fruits of the śrāvaka and the four [stages of realization].
"Knowledge is the Dharma. This refers to the supreme Dharma of noble wisdom, stating: "I know; I see this. The passage beginning with "At another time...

consists of words spoken to others in confession. Even if one is able to confess, it still constitutes the offense of abandonment (*pārājika*), with the exception of those who suffer from overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
This was because a certain bhikṣu, out of shame for not having attained the Path, falsely claimed he had already attained it, and later, through diligence...

Because he had progressed [in the path], he realized the fruit of Arhatship. He then confessed that his previous false speech constituted a *pārājika* offense. He reported this to the Buddha, who granted him absolution.
This was said because he acted out of a mind of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), and it should not be compared to those who speak falsely for the sake of seeking gain and offerings.
Generally, if a bhikṣu says to another person that he has attained the "superior man's dharma" (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) and the other person understands him, it is a *pārājika*.

*Pārājika*. If the other person does not understand, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If one uses hand gestures, or writes a letter, or sends a messenger, or makes signs, and the other understands, it is a *pārājika*;
if they do not understand, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If one has truly attained the Path and speaks of it to someone who is not in agreement, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, it is a *pārājika*. [The Vinaya of the] Śivaka...
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense resulting in expulsion.
If one has truly attained [realization] and speaks of it to a person of like mind, or if one speaks of various dharmas to others without claiming "I have attained it," there is no offense.
Venerable sirs, I have finished reciting the four *pārājika* rules.
If a bhikṣu commits any one of these *pārājika* rules, he may not dwell together with the bhikṣus, as it was before, so it is after.
A bhikṣu who has committed a *pārājika* rule should not dwell in common with them.
"As before" means that those who commit an offense during the preceding half-month are all guilty of a *pārājika* and are not to live in communion.
"Afterward is also like this" means that those who commit an offense after this half-month are likewise subject to the same formal determination of the offense.
Now I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter? (This is asked three times.
Venerable ones, you are pure in this matter, because of your silence. Thus it shall be held.
Venerable sirs, these thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
*Saṃgha* here means "the community"; *avaśeṣa* here means "remainder. One who commits such an offense has already abandoned [the path] to a certain extent.
It is as if a person were being struck by another, yet the throat has not been severed; life remains merely as a lingering spark. One should quickly provide rescue.
If a bhikṣu intentionally manipulates his own organ to emit semen, except in a dream, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Kāḷudāyin’s lustful mind was so intense that he stimulated his organ and emitted semen. The Buddha, knowing this, established the precept.
Later, there was a bhikṣu who emitted semen in a dream; suspecting he had violated this precept, he informed the Buddha. The Buddha cleared him of the offense.
Generally, for one who stimulates the organ but does not emit semen, it is a sthūlātyaya. If a bhikṣu instructs another to cause emission of semen, the instructor commits a sthūlātyaya.
It is prohibited. If one does not lose [the semen], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one instructs another person, whether the other loses it or not, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, it is a *pāyattika* offense. For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense in all cases.
If there is no manipulation and one loses it spontaneously, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu, with a lustful mind, makes physical contact with a woman— whether by grasping her hand, grasping her hair,
or touching any part of her body— it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Kāḷudāyin waited outside the door of his cell for women to arrive; he then led them inside to view the room and proceeded to make physical contact with their bodies.
The Buddha, knowing this, established the rule: if one takes hold of a hand, it constitutes physical contact.

To make physical contact with the body of any woman—even a single touch—constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. This applies even if the contact is made through clothing or other garments against her body.
[If it is] a portion, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If one touches clothing with clothing, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one touches a female deity, a female asura, a female ghost or spirit, a female nāga, or a female animal capable of changing form, in all such cases it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If it is a female animal incapable of changing form, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one [touches] a male...
To touch [a woman] is a *duṣkṛta*. If one touches someone with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one perceives a human female as a non-human female, or perceives a non-human female as a human female, or has doubt regarding a non-human female being a human female, in all these cases it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this offense, it is a *pāyattika*. For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is in all cases a *duṣkṛta*.
If they touch one another by mistake and there is no intention of sexual desire, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of sexual desire, utters coarse and lewd words of sexual desire to a woman, for every such coarse and lewd word of sexual desire [uttered], [he commits an offense].
Saṃghāvaśeṣa. Kālodāyin, because the Buddha had prohibited physical contact, led a woman into his room and spoke coarse and lewd words of sexual desire to her.
The Buddha, knowing this, established the rule: according to the number of words spoken, provided they were clearly understood.
For each single utterance, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If the speech is indistinct, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If the words are outside the two [sexual] organs and are not particularly coarse or evil, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one speaks such coarse and evil words toward a female deity, an asura woman, a female spirit, a female nāga, a female animal capable of transformation, or a hermaphrodite or eunuch, it is likewise [a *sthūlātyaya*]. Regarding her...
If one knows [the recipient understands], it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if one does not know, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one uses hand gestures, writes a letter, sends a messenger, or manifests signs, and the other knows [the meaning], it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if the other does not know, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
To speak harsh words to an animal that cannot transform its form is a *duṣkṛta*. To speak harsh words to a man... [is a *sthūlātyaya*].

[If one] speaks [of it], it is a *duṣkṛta*. If there is doubt as to whether she is a human woman or a non-human woman; if one perceives a human woman as a non-human woman; if one perceives a non-human woman as a human woman;
or if there is doubt as to whether a non-human woman is a human woman—in all these cases, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this offense, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is in all cases a *duṣkṛta*. If...
If one speaks to a woman, saying that the female body is impure and so forth, there is no offense.

However, if a bhikṣu, with a lustful mind, in the presence of a woman, praises his own person, saying: "Sister, I practice the holy life, maintain the precepts, am diligent, and cultivate wholesome dharmas;
you may offer me the dharma of sexual intercourse as a form of worship," and if he says such things as this... [offense].
The first [offense]. Regarding such speech: it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Because of the Buddha’s prohibition that Kālodāyin must not speak coarse and lewd words of sexual desire to women, he nevertheless praised his own physical virtues to various women and solicited their offerings. The Buddha, knowing this, established the rule.
If one addresses a woman with words praising her body and soliciting sexual desire, if these are clearly understood, there is one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for each such utterance;

if they are not clearly understood, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If one praises her body and solicits offerings, but does not solicit sexual desire—provided that the request is for some form of service other than the two [sexual] paths—it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one uses hand gestures, writes a letter, or sends a messenger...
If one sends a messenger or displays signs, and the other understands, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if they do not understand, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If it is a celestial maiden, an asura maiden, or even a female animal capable of transforming her shape, and she speaks to him clearly, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if she does not speak clearly, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If it is by means of hand gestures and so forth, and the other understands, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if [they do not understand]... [text ends].
If one knows [the recipient is a human] and praises their body, it is a *duṣkṛta*. To praise the body of an animal that cannot transform its form, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
To praise the body of a male, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one regards a human female as a non-human female; or if one perceives a human female as a non-human female;
or if one perceives a non-human female as a human female; or if one suspects a non-human female to be a human female—in all these cases, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
It is a *pārājika* offense for a nun; it is a *sthūlātyaya* for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*.

It is a *duṣkṛta* offense for all of them if a *bhikṣu* acts as a go-between, traveling back and forth between the two parties, conveying the man’s intentions to the woman and the woman’s intentions to the man. If...
If one acts as a matchmaker for the sake of establishing a marriage, or for the sake of a private liaison—even for a mere moment—it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
In the city of Rājagṛha, there was a bhikṣu named Kāla who was well-versed in worldly customs; he frequently acted as a go-between for marriages.
The laypeople of the city then remarked, "The sons of the Śākya are skilled at acting as matchmakers. The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha established this precept on their account.

If a bhikṣu personally receives a message, goes in person to deliver it, and returns to report it, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense. If he goes in person to deliver it but does not return to report it, it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
If he hears a message, goes in person to speak it, and returns to report it, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense; if he does not return to report it, it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
If he sends a letter, dispatches a messenger, uses a signet ring, or employs gestures to communicate back and forth, the offenses are all the same.
If one speaks with [the woman] but she does not accept [the proposal], and one goes to her [family] to speak of it and then returns to report [the refusal], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one accepts the proposal but does not go to speak to her nor return to report, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one does not accept the proposal but goes to speak of it and does not return to report, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding the report upon returning: if one says, "She has already been married to another," or if one says, "She has gone elsewhere," or if one says...
If he says she is dead; or if he says she has been carried off by bandits; or if he says she does not exist—all these are *sthūlātyaya*.
If he says she has leprosy (*kuṣṭha*); or if he says she has an abscess (*piḍaka*); or if he says she has white leprosy, consumption, or insanity;

or if he says there is a sore in her anus from which pus flows incessantly—all these are *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If a bhikṣu acts as a matchmaker for a woman once, it is *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. This applies accordingly.
Regarding matchmaking: if one has explained the matter clearly and it is finalized, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for each instance.
If it is not finalized, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. Matchmaking with animals is a *duṣkṛta*; matchmaking between men is also a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu carries a letter for another and does not read it, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If he performs other errands for a layperson (*avadātavasana*), it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The offense for bhikṣuṇīs is the same. For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta.
There is no offense if it is for the sake of reconciling a separated husband and wife; or if it is for the sake of a parent’s illness; or if one is imprisoned and carries a letter to deliver;
or if it is for the sake of a lay devotee who is ill; or if one is imprisoned and carries a letter to deliver.
If it is for the sake of the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha, or for the sake of a sick bhikṣu, there is no offense in reading a document and carrying it there.
If a bhikṣu himself solicits materials to build a house, without an owner and for his own use, he must build it according to the prescribed measurements. Regarding these measurements:
It shall be twelve spans long and seven spans wide internally. A monk should take other monks with him to inspect the site;
those monks should then indicate whether the site is free from difficulties and free from obstructions.

If a monk, for himself and without a patron, begs materials to build a hut on a site that has difficulties or obstructions, and does not take other monks with him to inspect the site, [he commits an offense].
If one constructs it in excess of the prescribed measure, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

While the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain, he permitted the bhikṣus to build their own dwellings. There was a certain bhikṣu who built a house on a grand scale, which caused him to exhaust the offerings of the faithful;
consequently, the donors criticized and avoided him. Furthermore, another bhikṣu, while building his own house, used his hands to hack [at the wood].
"Great Tree! That tree deity thought: 'The tree has been cut down; my descendants will have no refuge. She wished to strike the bhikṣu, yet she feared incurring sin.
She came to inform the Buddha, who sighed and said, 'Excellent! If one strikes a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts, the sin incurred shall be immeasurable.
Now, by the side of the Ganges there is a great tree named Śāla. Its deity has just passed away. You may [go there]..."
"Go quickly and take up residence there. The Buddha then established the precept: "If a site has no owner, one must request it from others.
Since it is for oneself and not for the great assembly, how could one extensively solicit wealth and materials to build a house of excessive size?

A *zhai* (span) is the distance between the tips of the fingers when the hands are spread apart. One *zhai* of the Buddha’s hand corresponds to one chi and six cun according to the current standard measure. [The remainder...]
"A bhikṣu" refers to one who knows the Dharma; that bhikṣu is indeed a knower of the Dharma.

"Difficult places" refers to locations such as those inhabited by lions, tigers, wolves, thieves, and bandits; or evil territories and evil kings; or even places where there are many insects and ants.
"Obstructed places" refers to locations that present hindrances, such as fields, gardens, houses, dwellings, roads, and mounds.
These include cemeteries and the like, as well as nunneries, taverns, and places where kings, ministers, and non-Buddhists come and go for recreation; these are the locations [forbidden].
If a bhikṣu, without having another bhikṣu accompany him, indicates a site for building a house, this constitutes one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If one constructs [a dwelling] in excess of the prescribed measure, there is one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; if it is in a place that is difficult or obstructed, there are two *duṣkṛta* offenses.

If it has been constructed but not yet completed, there are two *sthūlātyaya* offenses and two *duṣkṛta* offenses. If one instructs another to complete the construction, there are two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and two *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If one instructs another to construct it but it is not yet completed, there are two *sthūlātyaya* offenses and two *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If one causes another to construct [a building], there are two *sthūlātyaya* offenses and two *duṣkṛta* offenses. If it is constructed but not yet finished, there are four *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If a *bhikṣuṇī* commits this offense, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; for a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
If one constructs a Buddha hall, a lecture hall, or for the sake of a great assembly, and it exceeds the prescribed dimensions, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu wishes to build a large dwelling for himself that has a patron, he should take other bhikṣus to inspect the site.
Those bhikṣus should point out a site that is free from difficulties and free from obstructions.
If a bhikṣu builds a large dwelling for himself that has a patron on a site with difficulties or obstructions, and does not take other bhikṣus to inspect the site...
This constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Because the Venerable Cunda was on friendly terms with King Udayana, the king wished to have a large dwelling built for him near the city of Kauśāmbī.
There was a *nyagrodha* deity-tree there where travelers, carriages, and horses would all stop to rest.
[The Buddha said: "No. Venerable sir, you went to build a house, and everyone criticized and disparaged you. The Buddha, knowing this, established a rule:

when building a large dwelling, one may exceed the standard size if it is for the sake of a donor's intention; there is no offense. However, one must request the Saṃgha to designate the site, provided there are no difficulties or obstructions.
If there is no designation by the Saṃgha in this case, it constitutes one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. If there are difficulties or obstructions, it constitutes two [offenses]."
Dustāpatti (duṣkṛta). If it is made but not yet completed: one sthūlātyaya and one dustāpatti. If one instructs another to complete it:
one saṃghāvaśeṣa and two dustāpattis. If it is not yet completed: one sthūlātyaya and two dustāpattis.
If one acts on behalf of another: one sthūlātyaya and two dustāpattis. If it is made but not yet completed: three [dustāpattis].
It is a *duṣkṛta*. If a *bhikṣuṇī* commits it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
If the king performs the action himself, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu, being overcome by anger, slanders a bhikṣu who is not guilty of a pārājika offense with a groundless pārājika charge,
desiring to ruin that person’s pure conduct; and if at a later time, whether questioned or unasked,
he knows that this matter was spoken without basis and says, "I spoke these words because of anger," if a bhikṣu makes such a statement, the Saṃgha...
Pācittiya. The Venerable Trapusa was appointed by the community to oversee bedding, dwellings, and utensils, as well as to assign monks to their meals in order.
A bhikṣu named Maitrībala came and took the lowest seat; consequently, he received a poor room and poor bedding.

[The account] is complete. On the following day, she was assigned to receive food. Upon receiving poor-quality food again, she became angry and resentful, claiming that the Venerable One harbored feelings of favoritism and aversion.
She then used her sister, the Bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyaṇī, as a pretext to slander him with a groundless *pārājika* offense.

The Buddha dispatched the Saṃgha to investigate the facts, and based on this, he established the precept. "Groundless" means lacking the root of seeing, lacking the root of hearing, and lacking the root of suspicion. These are the three.
Neither [of these] exists. Yet, one falsely accuses another with a *pārājika* offense. If the statement is clear and distinct, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if it is not clear and distinct, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If one uses hand gestures, writing, letters, messengers, or signs, and the other understands, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one does so unknowingly, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. Excluding the four grave offenses (*pārājika*), the determination of the offense is the same for one who slanders with what is not the Dharma.
If one slanders a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if one slanders a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is in all cases a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this offense, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is in all cases... [a *duṣkṛta*].
It is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu, out of anger, takes a portion from a different category and slanders a bhikṣu who is not guilty of a *pārājika* offense by means of a groundless *pārājika* charge,
desiring to destroy that person’s pure conduct, and if at a later time he is questioned or...
[The Buddha] did not question him. [The monk] knew that this was taking a portion from among the discordant matters. That bhikṣu himself said, "I spoke these words out of anger.
For one who speaks such words, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
This refers to the previous incident concerning the bhikṣu Maitrībala. The Saṃgha had previously punished him for a groundless charge.
Later, while at the foot of Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, he saw two sheep mating.

He declared that the ram was Upavāna and the ewe was the bhikṣuṇī Maitrī, and thus slandered them again, saying, "I have personally witnessed this; it is not groundless. The Buddha investigated the facts of the matter.
Regarding the formulation of the precept: "Different portion" (*anyabhāga*) is synonymous with "another's portion," meaning it is not one's own kin.

Generally, those who share the same surname, name, or appearance but are not actually related are all termed "different portions. "Taking even a small part" means taking a slight portion from among those different portions to give rise to slander.
The determination of the offense is the same as above.

If a bhikṣu desires to cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha, employs means to adopt the practices that cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha, and persists in them without relinquishing them, other bhikṣus should admonish that bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir, do not cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha; do not employ means to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha;
do not adopt the practices that cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha and persist in them without relinquishing them. Venerable sir, you should be in harmony with the Saṃgha."

They shall live in harmony, with joy and without contention, studying under the same teacher like water and milk blending together; thus they shall increase their welfare and dwell in peace within the Buddha’s Dharma.
When a bhikṣu, being thus admonished, persists in his refusal to relinquish [the matter], that bhikṣu should admonish him up to three times.
If [the offender] relinquishes [the act] after up to three admonitions, it is well; if they do not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Devadatta, wishing to kill the Buddha but being unable to do so, then devised a method for schism in the Saṃgha in order to entice the assembly to follow him.

The Buddha consequently established this precept. The first phrase, "wishing to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha," expresses his original intent. This refers to the preparatory effort (*upakrama*).
"Accepting the method for destroying the harmony of the Saṃgha" refers to accepting the expedient means for destroying the harmony of the Saṃgha.
Devadatta had five such practices: first, begging for food for as long as one lives; second, wearing rag-robes for as long as one lives;
third, sitting in the open air for as long as one lives; fourth, not consuming butter or salt for as long as one lives; fifth, not eating meat for as long as one lives.
Fish and meat—these five things appear to be wholesome, yet if the mind remains intent on destroying the harmony of the Saṃgha, they are merely deceitful pretenses.

Furthermore, to declare what is Dharma as non-Dharma, what is non-Dharma as Dharma, what is Vinaya as non-Vinaya, and what is non-Vinaya as Vinaya, or even to devise various causes and conditions to cause the division and dispersal of the Saṃgha—all such acts constitute the destruction of the harmony of the Saṃgha. [If one does not desist] after being admonished three times...

If one renounces [the offense], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, because the desire to destroy [the precept] has arisen, though it has not yet been fulfilled. If the fruit is actually destroyed, the offense is equal to the seven *ānantarya* transgressions;
it does not stop at this alone. Nevertheless, it must still undergo the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. If one renounces it after the formal motion (*jñapti*) is completed, it is one *sthūlātyaya*.
If one relinquishes [the offense] after the first *karmavācanā*, it is two *sthūlātyaya*s; if one relinquishes it after the second *karmavācanā*, it is three *sthūlātyaya*s;
if one relinquishes it after the third *karmavācanā* is completed, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If one relinquishes it before the initial motion (*jñapti*) is finished, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

In all cases prior to the motion, such as when one employs means with the intent to disrupt the harmony of the Saṃgha and so forth, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This applies even if the Saṃgha proceeds to perform the *karmavācanā* for him.

At that time, if a bhikṣu instructs [others] not to relinquish [the object], it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If he instructs them not to relinquish it before the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) has been performed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For the other four classes of persons who so instruct, it is all *duṣkṛta*. If a bhikṣuṇī commits this offense, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is all *duṣkṛta*. If one breaks what is non-Dharma or non-Vinaya...
This is not an offense regarding all evil associates.
If a bhikṣu has other companions—whether one, two, three, or even innumerable—and that bhikṣu says to those bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs, do not admonish this bhikṣu; this bhikṣu speaks according to the Dharma and speaks according to the Vinaya."
"We delight in what this bhikṣu says; we approve of it. That bhikṣu should admonish them, saying:
"Venerable sirs, do not say this: 'This bhikṣu speaks according to the Dharma and according to the Vinaya;
we delight in what he says; we approve of it. Why is that? This bhikṣu does not speak according to the Dharma..."
The Vinaya formula: "Venerable sirs, do not seek to cause a schism in the Saṃgha. You should desire harmony with the Saṃgha.
Venerable sirs, be in harmony with the Saṃgha, rejoicing and without dispute, studying under the same teacher, like water and milk mixed together, within the Buddha-Dharma."
There is an increase in dwelling in happiness. When a bhikṣu is thus admonished and persists in his refusal to relinquish [the matter], that bhikṣu should be admonished up to three times.
If he relinquishes it by the third admonition, it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
There were four remaining followers of Deva: first, Trivardhana; second, Khaṇḍadravya; third, Kubera;
and fourth, Kālatiṣya. These were the leaders among his faction.
The number [of those involved] should also be many. Previously, when Devadatta sought to cause a schism in the Saṃgha, the pure assembly repeatedly admonished him;

however, this faction of the heterodox assisted in his destruction and, conversely, admonished the pure assembly, saying, "Do not rebuke Devadatta. Because the Buddha heard this, he established the rule.
The passage beginning with "This bhikṣu" refers to the words used by the faction of the heterodox to admonish the pure assembly; here, "this bhikṣu" points to Devadatta.
[This is] so. "That bhikṣu should be admonished" refers to the members of the pure assembly turning to admonish the faction;
the meaning is: "Do not seek to destroy the harmony of the Saṃgha. "You [plural]," etc., is the exhortation for them to achieve harmony. "That bhikṣu," etc. [is the following].

The offense is established. Whether it is relinquished through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) or not, the establishment of the offense is as stated above. The establishment of other offenses is also as stated above.
If a bhikṣu dwells in dependence upon a village or a town and commits evil conduct that defiles families, and this is both seen and heard.
The monks should say to that monk: "Venerable sir, you have committed evil deeds, defiled families, and this has been both seen and heard.
You should now depart from this village; you need not remain here. That monk will then say to those monks:
"Venerable sir, at present there are bhikṣus who possess attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion. Among bhikṣus who have committed such identical offenses, some are expelled while others are not.

The bhikṣus admonish [you], saying: 'Venerable sir, do not speak these words, claiming that among the bhikṣus there are those with attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion, such that among those who have committed identical offenses, some are expelled and others are not.'"

There are those who do not drive [the offender] away. Yet the bhikṣus, being without attachment, hatred, fear, or delusion, both see and hear that this person of great virtue has committed evil deeds and defiled the families of others.
When these bhikṣus thus admonish him, he stubbornly persists and does not relinquish his conduct.
That bhikṣu should be admonished three times. If he relinquishes [the course] after being admonished up to three times, it is well. If he does not relinquish it, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
This originated with the two bhikṣus Aśvajit and Punarvasu, who were staying at the Karṇa village dwelling and acting...
They engage in evil conduct that defiles the families of others. They plant flowers and trees themselves, irrigate them, pluck the blossoms to make garlands, and present them to others;

they instruct others to do the same. Furthermore, they sit, eat, and drink together with women, and even in their moments of play, laughter, song, dance, and movement, they are entirely devoid of dignified decorum (*īryāpatha*).
While the laity all take delight in this, there are pure bhikṣus who possess such dignity...
As for the formal procedure (*vidhi*): when they went there to beg for alms and failed to receive any food, they returned and informed the Buddha.

The Buddha then dispatched Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra to lead the assembly and perform the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) against them. The two bhikṣus said, "The Saṃgha possesses favoritism and malice."

The two Venerables returned and informed the Buddha. The Buddha again rebuked them from afar and established a restrictive precept: "Committing evil deeds" refers to such acts as planting flowers and trees upon others' land.

There are four ways of defiling another's household: first, defiling a household by relying on that household; this means that when a bhikṣu receives goods from a person's house, he gives them to one family and not to another;
the one to whom they are given rejoices, while the one to whom they are not given becomes resentful. Second, [defiling by] relying on material gain...
1. Corrupting families: This refers to a bhikṣu who, regarding gains obtained in accordance with the Dharma, gives them to one family and not to another;
those to whom he gives are pleased, while those to whom he does not give become angry. 2. Corrupting families through reliance on relatives and friends:

This refers to a bhikṣu who is friendly with kings and ministers; he protects one family and does not protect another; those he protects are pleased, while those he does not protect become angry. 3. Corrupting families through reliance on monasteries: [The text continues: ...reliance on monasteries.
"Defiling the family" refers to a bhikṣu who takes monastic property and gives it to one family while withholding it from another;
those to whom it is given rejoice, while those from whom it is withheld become angry. The other bhikṣus should speak to him below—that is, they should admonish him and expel him.

The phrase "this bhikṣu below" is a self-defensive expression used by the transgressor of the precepts. Because of attachment, they do not expel him; because of hatred, they forcibly expel him; [and] because of fear...

Therefore, one does not dare to drive [the animal away]. Because of delusion, one does not know whether it is appropriate to drive it away or not. Thus, while the commission of the offense is the same, there is a distinction between driving it away and not driving it away.
When the various bhikṣus offer their admonition, it serves as proof for the entry into that offense. The phrase "this bhikṣu" below concludes the definition of the offense.

Regarding the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations), whether the transgression is relinquished or not, the conclusion of the offense is the same as above. The remaining points are concluded.
The offense is the same as above. However, there is no offense if one plants flowers or trees for the sake of the Three Jewels’ perpetual endurance, or performs offerings and the like.
If a bhikṣu is of evil disposition and does not accept admonition, and the other bhikṣus have already admonished him in accordance with the Dharma regarding the rules of training...
He himself does not accept words of admonition, saying: "Venerable sirs, do not speak to me of what is good or bad;
nor shall I speak to you venerable sirs of what is good or bad. Venerable sirs, please desist; do not admonish me. Other monks should admonish that monk, saying:
"Do not yourself refuse to accept words of admonition; Venerable sir, you yourself ought to accept admonition."
[The Buddha] said: "Venerable ones, you should admonish the bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma; the bhikṣus should likewise admonish you in accordance with the Dharma.
In this way, the community of the Buddha’s disciples prospers, admonishing one another, instructing one another, and confessing to one another.
When a bhikṣu is thus being admonished, if he persists and does not relinquish [his position], that bhikṣu should be admonished up to three times. Up to three times.
If he relinquishes [this behavior], it is well. If he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
This originated from the Venerable Channa’s malicious nature and refusal to accept instruction. When anyone would admonish him, he would say, "Venerable sirs, do not admonish me;
I should instruct you instead," and further claimed, "I am the Holy Lord who has attained Perfect Enlightenment. The Buddha knew this.
Therefore, it is prescribed: from the words "Venerable sirs" onwards is the formal refusal to accept the admonition; from "that bhikṣu" onwards is the formal admonition by the bhikṣus;

and from "this bhikṣu" onwards is the determination of the offense. The formal procedure (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) regarding whether he relinquishes [the position] or not, and the determination of the offense, are the same as above.
The determination of other offenses is also the same as above. If he says, "It is not the Dharma, it is not the Vinaya," then...
There is no offense for one who does not accept admonition.
Venerable sirs, I have now recited the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas: nine offenses are committed at the first instance, while the remainder require up to three admonitions.
If a bhikṣu commits any one of these dharmas and knowingly conceals it, he must be compelled to undergo *parivāsa*.
When the *parivāsa* has been completed, one should grant him six nights of *mānatva*. When the *mānatva* has been completed, he should be granted absolution from the offense (*ābṛhaṇa*).
This monk’s offense must be cleared within an assembly of twenty monks. If there is even one person less, such that the assembly does not number twenty, this monk’s offense cannot be removed;
furthermore, the monks may be censured. This is the proper time.
This summarizes the aforementioned offenses. Regarding the first nine precepts, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting of the community) upon the very first transgression.
Regarding the latter four precepts, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* only after three admonitions have been issued and the offense is not relinquished.

*Pārivāsa*—which is translated as "separate dwelling"—means that various bhikṣus shall not participate with him in communal monastic affairs, nor share in the same rising and sitting. If the offender conceals the offense, he must [undergo penance] accordingly.

According to the number of days the offense was concealed, he was strictly penalized by being made to undergo the *parivāsa* (probation). Once the *parivāsa* was completed, he was granted a six-night *mānatva*.
*Mānatva* is translated as "joy of mind" (*yi-xi*); this means that as the offense is about to be cleared upon the completion of the *parivāsa*, one performs this practice with joy.
It is also called the "extremely arduous and humble practice," meaning that at dawn, one must sweep and clean for the Buddha.
The stupa and the monastic quarters; the places where monks wash themselves or relieve themselves. Furthermore, one must not give one’s consent (*chanda*), nor accept the consent of others.
One must not walk before or behind a *bhikṣu*. One must not receive prostrations from anyone.
One must not preach the Dharma or engage in formal debate with others. One should carry worn-out robes and an alms bowl. One should perform prostrations. Thus says the Great Sangha.
"Venerable [Name], you have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. I hope that the Venerable Ones will grant [Name] purification from this offense.
Having completed the six-night penance (*mānatva*), he should be granted purification within an assembly of twenty monks.

If there is even one monk fewer, the offense cannot be cleared, and the Saṃgha may also be censured. If the offense was committed but not concealed, he should be granted the six-night *mānatva* directly."

Now I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter? (This is asked three times.
Since the venerable ones are silent, they are pure in this matter. Thus shall it be held.
Venerable sirs, these two indeterminate rules (aniyata-dharmas) are recited every half-month from within the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
"Indeterminate" means that the disciplinary measure is not fixed among the three categories of offenses; one must examine the facts to determine the nature of the transgression.
If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded place, a concealed place, or a place suitable for sexual intercourse,
and speaks improper words, and a faithful upāsikā states one of three matters—
whether it be a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyattika* offense— and that seated bhikṣu himself says, "I have committed this offense," [he is to be dealt with accordingly].

Among these three categories of offenses, one should be dealt with according to each specific rule—whether it be a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyattika*—just as described by a trustworthy female lay follower (*upāsikā*).
One should deal with that bhikṣu according to the law; this is called an indeterminate rule (*aniyata-dharma*).
Kāḷudāyin, before he had gone forth, had committed adultery with the wife of a friend who was a lay follower (upāsikā).
Even after he had gone forth, he continued to associate with her. One day, he went to her house and sat together with her in a secluded place, speaking improper words.

There was a laywoman (*upāsikā*) established in faith who, having observed [the situation], reported it to the Buddha; therefore, he established this rule. "A secluded place" (*rahaḥ-sthāna*) means a place where no people are present.

"A concealed place" (*praticchanna-sthāna*) means a place that is not exposed to view. A place that is both devoid of people and not exposed to view is a place suitable for committing sexual misconduct.
"Established in faith" means abiding in truthful faith and not speaking falsely. "If" (*yadi*) is an indefinite term. Regarding the three...

Within the Dharma, those who abide in faith according to their capacity shall truthfully state the specific characteristics of the offense committed, awaiting one who knows the Vinaya to determine the legal penalty.
Among these, one who commits sexual misconduct incurs a *pārājika* (defeat); one who utters improper speech incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting of the Saṃgha).

However, one who merely sits together with such a person, without committing either of the two aforementioned acts, incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation). This "sitting" refers to a position lower than that of a regular bhikṣu; it is the terminology used when an offender confesses their transgression.
If a bhikṣu confesses each instance individually, he should be dealt with according to his confession.
If a bhikṣu does not confess each instance individually, he should be dealt with by means of the *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya-vinaya* (the rule for investigating the nature of the offense).

If a bhikṣu is already sitting in a secluded place and a woman comes to pay her respects and bow to him, there is no offense; however, he must quickly dismiss her. If they sit together, it is likewise an offense.
[The offense of] falling [into defeat]. If a bhikṣu sits with a woman in an exposed place that is not suitable for sexual intercourse and speaks coarse and wicked words,
and a faithful upāsikā declares one of two dharmas against him— either a saṃghāvaśeṣa or [another offense]— [he is guilty].
If it is a *pāyattika*, the monk who was sitting there confesses himself, saying, "I have committed this offense.
He is to be dealt with according to one of the two rules: either a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*, as stated by the trustworthy laywoman (*upāsikā*).
This bhikṣu should be dealt with according to the Dharma; this is called an *aniyata-dharma*.

Regarding the offense of this rule, both the one who commits it and the one who reports it are the same as in the preceding cases; however, it is distinguished because it occurs in a place where sexual intercourse is not possible.
There is no *pārājika*. It is settled according to two rules.
Venerable sirs, I have now recited the two *aniyata* dharmas. I now ask the venerable sirs: Are you pure in this matter?
(Ask three times.)
Venerable sirs, since there is silence, you are pure in this matter. Thus shall this be upheld.

Venerable sirs, these thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
In the Sanskrit language, *niḥsargika* means "to be relinquished" (*śe*), and *pāyattika* means "falling" (*duo*). These thirty matters are all...
One commits an offense regarding clothing. One shall fall into the Avīci, Saṃvṛta, Tapana, and Pratāpana hells. Now, a regulation is established to penalize such clothing:
if one relinquishes it before the Saṅgha, one is exempt from falling [into those hells]. This applies to the monks within the boundary (sīmā), whether they be many or a single individual.
