Both may be relinquished; however, one must not relinquish it before a separate group (*pṛthaggaṇa*). A "separate group" refers to four or more persons who have privately gone outside the boundary and formed a distinct assembly for themselves.
If one relinquishes [the robe] before such a separate group, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Once the robe has been relinquished, one should request confession within the community (*saṃgha*). Having made the request, one should invite a single person to serve as the presiding master of the confession. As for that...
The person must be a pure bhikṣu; furthermore, one must not accept the confession immediately. One must first inform the assembly, and only after having informed them may the confession be accepted.
Once the confession has been accepted, the robe should be returned to this bhikṣu from within the assembly.
There are two methods for returning the robe: the first is to pass it back and forth among those present at that very seat; the second is to return it directly. Regarding its...
Regarding the offenses committed: these may include keeping an extra robe for ten days; keeping an out-of-season robe for more than one month;
keeping an urgent gift robe for more than ten days; keeping an extra alms bowl for more than ten days; or keeping medicine for more than seven days.
These five matters must be transferred to another person on the spot. Furthermore, it may be that a person has business and wishes to travel far, and is thus unable [to keep them].
If it is postponed until the following day, one may ask within the Saṃgha: "To whom is this robe relinquished?

If he replies, "It is relinquished to such-and-such a bhikṣu," the Saṃgha shall immediately give that robe to him, and thereafter perform the formal procedure of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the motion and one proclamation).
Return this robe to the bhikṣu. If it does not involve any of the five aforementioned matters, one should use the method of direct entrustment:
perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* within the Saṃgha and return the robe directly to him.

If it involves any of the five aforementioned matters, but the person has no reason for a long journey and the matter can be deferred until the following day, one may likewise use the method of direct entrustment and return it; however, this applies only to robes made of wild silkworm cotton.
Bedding and seating (śayanāsana) may not be returned; it should be cut into pieces and used for plastering walls or earthen platforms. All other items must be returned.
If one abandons a robe and does not return it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If someone says, "Do not return it," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one transfers it to another person, uses it for a different garment, or causes it to be damaged, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu, having finished his robes and having had the kaṭhina robe suspended, keeps an extra robe for ten days without having performed the formal act of "pure distribution," he may keep it;
if it exceeds ten days, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense.

The Buddha ordained that a bhikṣu’s three robes must not be excessive in length. Regarding "excessive robes": a robe is considered excessive if it is eight finger-breadths long and four finger-breadths wide according to the measurements of the Tathāgata.
At that time, there were six groups of bhikṣus seated beneath the Buddha, one of whom was named Nanda.
The second was named Upananda; the third, Kālodāyin; the fourth, Channa; the fifth, Aśvajit;
and the sixth, Punarvasu. These six companions all kept extra robes, changing them morning and evening as an ornament for themselves.
The Buddha, knowing this, established the rule. "When the robes are finished" means the three robes are complete.

*Kathina* (translated as "garment of celebration" or "garment of merit") is so called because the merit of the ninety-day summer retreat is preeminent; thus, donors present new garments to celebrate it.
This robe has five strips and ten sections. It is removed on the sixteenth day of the seventh month, marking the end of the retreat.

[The robe] is received later. One who receives this robe is permitted to stay overnight separated from it, to keep an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*), and to accept individual invitations (*pṛthag-āmantraṇa*).

By the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, one should distribute it according to one's share to novices and others; therefore, it is said to have been "taken out. Once this robe has been relinquished, one must again receive the three robes (*tricīvara*).
One is not permitted to stay overnight separated from them, nor is one permitted to keep an extra robe; these must be formally dedicated through the ritual of *viśuddhi-dāna* (pure giving). If...
Regarding impure giving: if one exchanges [the item] and gives it to another, there is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense plus a *duṣkṛta*.

Regarding the rule that one may keep [an extra robe] for ten days: Ānanda obtained a costly robe and wished to offer it to Kāśyapa. While Kāśyapa had not yet returned, Ānanda wished to keep it himself, fearing he might commit this offense.

He therefore went to inform the Buddha. The Buddha asked how long it would be until Kāśyapa’s return, and [Ānanda] replied: [...]* *Note: The source text provides the narrative context for the rules regarding "impure giving" (*aśuddha-dāna*) and the ten-day limit on keeping extra robes, specifically citing the case of Ānanda and Kāśyapa.*
Ten days. The Buddha then permitted that one may keep [extra robes] for ten days.

If one obtains a robe on the first day, and obtains another on the second day, and so on up to the tenth day, and keeps them until the appearance of the dawn light on the eleventh day, all constitute the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The same applies to the offense for a *bhikṣuṇī*. For a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is all a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu, having finished his robes and having had the kaṭhina robe suspended, should stay overnight apart from any one of his three robes in a different location—
unless by formal authorization of the Saṃgha— he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika).
The group of six bhikṣus went traveling among the people and entrusted their three robes to a bhikṣu who was a relative or friend.
That bhikṣu washed and dried them for them. Another bhikṣu saw this and reported it to the Buddha, who consequently established this rule:

if one stays overnight in a different location separated from any one of the three robes, one commits an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense involving forfeiture), provided it is not due to a formal authorization (*saṃgha-kamma*) by the Saṃgha. This is the reason for the rule.
A certain sick bhikṣu had business to attend to and wished to go among the people. Because his refuse-rag robes were heavy and he could not carry them, he informed the Buddha.

The Buddha, for his sake, performed the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement) to establish the rule of "not losing the robes. Thus, there is no offense.

If one is separated from any robe other than the three principal robes, it is a *duṣkṛta* (an offense of wrong-doing). For a bhikṣuṇī who commits this, the offense is the same; for a śikṣamāṇā, it is likewise.

...and so forth; all constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense. However, there is no offense if, before the appearance of the dawn light, one takes hold of the robe with the hand, or is constrained by difficult circumstances, or if the robe is within reach of a thrown stone.
If a bhikṣu, having finished his robes and having had the kaṭhina cloth suspended, obtains an out-of-season robe and wishes to accept it, he may accept it;
having accepted it, he should quickly have it made up. If it is sufficient, that is well; if it is not sufficient, he may keep it for one month in order to complete it.
If he keeps it longer than that, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

The Buddha established the rule that one may keep extra robes for no more than ten days. There was a bhikṣu whose great robe (saṃghāṭī) was worn out, yet he could not complete a new one within ten days;
thus, he could not immediately discard his old one. He then informed the Buddha, who permitted him to keep it for one month in order to fulfill the requirements for making a robe.

Regarding "out-of-season robes" (akālacīvara), this refers to robes given at a time other than the prescribed season for giving robes. The "season for giving robes" refers to the period following the *pravāraṇā*.
Afterwards, there is one month without the *kaṭhina* robe, and five months with the *kaṭhina* robe.
For a bhikṣuṇī who commits this offense, the penalty is the same. For a śikṣamāṇā and others, it is all a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu takes a robe from a nun who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā saw a certain bhikṣu wearing a tattered robe; moved by compassion, she took off the expensive robe she was wearing herself, exchanged it for his, and put it on.
She came to visit the Buddha, and the Buddha asked her, "Why are you wearing such a tattered robe?"
"Is it a robe? The nun answered truthfully. The Buddha said, "If your robes are sufficient and you have a surplus, I permit you to give them away. Why?
Because even when women wear fine upper garments, they still feel dissatisfied; how much more so with tattered ones? Therefore, I establish this precept.
Later, because the bhikṣus did not dare to accept robes from nuns who were their relatives, the Buddha added the words "who is not a relative."
Except for those involved in trade. Because two groups within the Jeta Grove received gifts of robes and divided them among themselves, there were some that did not fit the bodies [of the nuns].
A nun brought one such robe to exchange it with a bhikṣu, but the bhikṣu did not dare to exchange it. He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha granted an exemption for it.
If a bhikṣuṇī or a śikṣamāṇā commits this offense, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣu has a nun who is not a relative wash, dye, or beat an old robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This was established because of Kālodayin, who exchanged glances with the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā and departed.
The five robes, both clean and soiled, were washed by the bhikṣuṇīs. Because the task of washing was extremely vulgar and debasing, the bhikṣuṇīs took offense and informed the Buddha;

thus, he established this rule. Subsequently, the bhikṣus did not dare to have their relatives—the bhikṣuṇīs—wash or dye [their robes]. The Buddha further added the words "non-relative" [to the rule].

In this context, to cause [a bhikṣuṇī] to wash, dye, or beat [the robes] constitutes three *naiḥsargika-pāyattikas*; if one causes [her] to do so but she has not yet washed, dyed, or beaten them, [it is likewise an offense].
...three *duṣkṛta* offenses. If one [item] is reduced by one or two, it may be inferred accordingly.
If one causes a non-relative nun (*bhikṣuṇī*) to wash, dye, or beat a new garment, there are three *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If one causes a non-relative *śikṣamāṇā* or *śrāmaṇerī* to wash, dye, or [beat] an old garment, this is likewise a *duṣkṛta*. [The same applies for] a *bhikṣuṇī* and...
If a śikṣamāṇā or others commits [these offenses], it is a duṣkṛta in all cases.
If she is ill and has no *niḥsargika* (related) nun, and she has a non-*niḥsargika* nun wash, dye, or beat [the robes]; or if she borrows another's robe to wash, dye, or beat—it is not an offense.
If a bhikṣu requests a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, except at the appropriate time, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The "appropriate time" refers to when a bhikṣu has had his robes taken away, lost, burned, or carried away by water;
this is called the appropriate time.
In the city of Śrāvastī there was an elder who was a close friend of Upananda.
One day he went to Jetavana to visit him, and the Venerable One preached the Dharma for him. He was greatly delighted and wished to make an offering, but the Venerable One declined it.
The elder pressed him insistently, asking, "What do you require? The Venerable One said, "I require only the garment you are currently wearing. The elder replied, "Wait..."
"Come to my house tomorrow; I shall give it to you. "But since we must not lack outer garments upon entering the city today," the Venerable One said, "Stop!
I have no further need of it. Being left with no other choice, he took off his robe and departed separately. When he entered the city, a gatekeeper asked, "Why do you have no outer garment?
He falsely replied, "It was stolen by bandits outside the gates of Jeta’s Grove. Those who heard this mocked him.

[The Buddha] disapproved. Having heard of this, he established a rule. Subsequently, because the bhikṣus did not dare to solicit robes from kinsmen who were householders, he added the phrase "from those who are not kinsmen.
Regarding the exception for "other times": there was a bhikṣu who, having completed his summer retreat, came to see the Buddha.
It was hot by day, and traveling at night, he was robbed of his robes by bandits. Entering the city naked, he borrowed a robe from another bhikṣu.
Because of seeing the Buddha, the Buddha permitted [the acquisition of] robes at times such as when one's robe has been snatched away, lost, burnt, or carried off by water.
For a bhikṣuṇī who commits this offense, the penalty is the same. For śikṣamāṇās and others, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
In this region, if one requests a robe from a householder and does not take it by force, there is no offense. If the householder gives it of their own accord, there is likewise no offense.
If a bhikṣu has had his robes taken away, lost, burned, or carried off by water, and a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative invites him at will and offers him many robes,
that bhikṣu should accept them with moderation. If he accepts more than that, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
At that time, there were many bhikṣus whose robes had been stolen; they arrived at Jetavana naked.
When the lay devotees heard of this, they brought many robes to offer as alms. Another bhikṣu took them by stealth and gave them to the group of six bhikṣus (Ṣaḍvargika).

The Buddha, having heard of this, established a rule: regarding "those who invite freely," these are those who have themselves resolved to ask with a sincere heart; regarding "those who give many robes."
One should wish for many robes to be bestowed; there is no limit to taking one or two. If one robe is lost, one should not take another.
If two robes are lost, if the remaining robe is double, triple, or quadruple thickness, it should be torn down.
If all three robes are lost, one should accept them with contentment, receiving whatever robes the layperson provides. If the robes are thin...
If it is thin and not durable, one may take it and make it double, triple, or quadruple layers. It should be positioned upon the shoulder;

a border should be attached, or it should be reinforced against dirt and grease, or provided with hooks and buttons. To accept [a robe] that exceeds these [prescribed] limits constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, the offense is the same. For a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu, when householders or a householder’s wife have prepared the price for robes to purchase such robes for a bhikṣu and intend to give them to a specific bhikṣu,
should go to that householder’s home before having been invited by him to accept such an offer, and say: "It would be well, householder,
if you were to provide me with the price for such robes for my sake, so that I may obtain fine ones"— if he should obtain the robes [he has committed an offense].
[If a monk] should [act thus], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

When Baddhananda heard a certain householder and his wife privately discussing the procurement of the price for a robe, Baddhananda, out of greed for fine things, went immediately to their home and urged them to procure an expensive robe. The householder complained, saying, "I am currently [engaged in] private..."
[The monks] deliberated: "In the future, one may request as much as one desires; why then did he so hastily make such a statement? When the Buddha heard this, he established a rule:
if one obtains the robe, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; if one does not obtain the robe, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, the offense is the same.
For *śikṣamāṇās* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu, when two householders or a householder’s wife have prepared the price for a robe to purchase such a robe and give it to a certain bhikṣu, goes to the homes of those two householders before having first accepted an invitation, and speaks thus:
"Excellent, householders! Prepare such a price for a robe and make a single robe for me, so that it may be fine."
If he obtains the robe-cloth, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

When Ba-nan-da heard that two lay families were each preparing the price for a robe, out of greed for something fine, he went immediately to both houses and requested that they work together to produce a single robe.
Their intention was that by working together on a single robe, the two [families]...
"The family need not increase the price, yet I shall obtain fine robes and may also avoid my previous offense.
Both lay devotees resented this. Upon hearing of it, the Buddha established a rule: to receive the robe constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; to fail to receive the robe constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, the offense is the same; for a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is all a *duṣkṛta*.
If a monk, or a king, or a royal minister, or a brahmin, or a householder, or a householder’s wife, sends a messenger to deliver the price for a robe to a monk;
when the messenger arrives at the monk's location, he says: "Venerable sir, this is now for your sake."
"This price for robes is being sent; you may accept it. That bhikṣu should say to that messenger: "I should not accept this price for robes.
If I require robes, I shall accept them when they are appropriate and pure. That messenger should say to the bhikṣu: "Venerable sir, do you have an attendant?
The bhikṣu who requires robes should say: "There is. [Whether it be] a monastery attendant or a lay follower...
"Upāsaka, this is the monk's steward. That messenger shall go to the steward, give him the price for the robe, and return to the monk, saying:
'Venerable Sir, I have already given the price for the robe to the steward named so-and-so whom you indicated.
Venerable Sir, please go there at the proper time; you shall obtain the robe. The monk who requires a robe should then go to the steward."
If, after being reminded two or three times, he says, "I need a robe," it is well if he obtains a robe;
if he does not obtain a robe, he should stand silently before him for four, five, or six times to cause him to remember.
It is well if he obtains a robe; if he does not obtain a robe and yet seeks to obtain one beyond that limit, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. If...
He shall not accept the robe. He should go to the place where the price for the robe was obtained—either going himself or sending a messenger—and say:
"Previously you sent a messenger with the price for a robe to be given to a certain bhikṣu; that bhikṣu did not ultimately receive the robe. You should take it back."
"Do not let it be lost; this is the proper time.
Venerable Upananda was on friendly terms with a high minister. The minister sent a messenger to deliver the price for a robe to the Venerable One.
The Venerable One immediately dispatched a messenger to have a certain householder take charge of it. At another time, the minister asked:
The messenger said, "Regarding the price for robes sent previously, have you made the robes yet? The messenger replied, "Not yet. The minister sent the messenger again to inquire about the reason.
When the Venerable One learned of this, he went quickly to the householder's home and took the price to make the robes.
Just then, the householder had some business and was leaving the door; hearing that the robe-price had been taken, he said, "Wait a moment until I return. I have a prior engagement now. If...
"If you depart late, you shall be fined five hundred pieces of gold. The Venerable One firmly refused. Having no other choice, the householder took the price for the robes and gave it to him;
only then did he depart. Because of the delay, he was fined five hundred pieces of gold. The assembly all criticized and disparaged him.
The Buddha, knowing this, established a rule: "I should not accept [gold]. This was because the Buddha had ordained that bhikṣus were not permitted to receive gold or silver with their own hands.
[This refers to] money and so forth. When it is appropriate and pure, one should accept it, as stated in the following passage: "It is good for one who obtains clothing.
To seek beyond what is permitted and thereby obtain [it] constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; if not obtained, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, the offense is the same.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is a *duṣkṛta* in all cases.
If a bhikṣu makes a bedding using wild silkworm cotton, it is an *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
When the group of six bhikṣus made bedding using wild silkworm cotton, they went to a silkworm-raising household to purchase it. The silkworm-raiser said, "The cocoons are not yet mature;
wait a little. That bhikṣu waited by their side day after day. Because the silkworm-raiser was in a hurry, he exposed the silkworm cocoons to the sun each day.

Silkworm pupae cause distressing heat and make noise. When a layperson saw this, they criticized and disparaged it. The Buddha heard of this and established a rule: if [the object] is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense;

if not yet completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. It is the same for one who instructs another to make it. If one makes it for another person, whether it is completed or not, it is both a *duṣkṛta* offense.
When relinquishing it within the Saṃgha, one should chop it into pieces with an axe, mix it with mud, and apply it to walls.
[The penalty for] the mound. A bhikṣuṇī who commits this offense incurs the same guilt. For śikṣamāṇās and others, it is all a duṣkṛta.
If she obtains one that is already completed, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu makes a bedding out of new, pure black sheep’s wool, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
In the city of Vaiśālī, there were many youths who were prone to sexual misconduct and excessive desire; they made felt rugs out of pure black sheep’s wool.

He wore a garment for traveling at night so that people would not see him. The group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) monks imitated him, also making bedding out of pure black wool from horned sheep (*urabhraka*).
When the young monks saw this, they disparaged it, saying, "Because we are fond of lust, he acts in this way;

is this monk also fond of lust? The Buddha heard of this and therefore established a rule. "Horned sheep" refers to the wild sheep of the Hu. [The rules concerning] whether the material is finished or unfinished, and so forth, are hereby concluded.
The offense is the same as above. If a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, or others commit this, it is all a duṣkṛta.
If she obtains one that is already completed, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding, he should use two parts of pure black wool, three parts white, and four parts variegated.
If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding without using two parts black, three parts white, and four parts variegated, [he commits an offense].
Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*:
the group of six bhikṣus made a new bedding out of pure white sheep’s wool. When a householder saw this, he criticized and disparaged them.

This refers to cases such as those involving kings or high ministers. Because the Buddha heard of this, he established the precept. The character *māṅ* (pronounced *máng*) means a cow of variegated black and white colors;
the common edition uses the character *páng*, which is incorrect. I have now corrected it according to the Tibetan edition. Whether the act is completed or not, the offense is the same as above.
For bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and others who commit this, it is all a *duṣkṛta* offense. If [the animal] has already been obtained...
If it is completed, there is no offense.

If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding or mat, he should use it for six years. If he uses it for less than six years and, without relinquishing the old one, makes another new one—except by formal authorization from the Saṃgha—he commits a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The group of six bhikṣus kept many bedding materials; because they did not discard the old ones, they constantly prepared new ones.

The Buddha, knowing this, established a prohibition. "Except by formal monastic authorization (*saṃgha-karman*). At that time, there was a sick bhikṣu who wished to travel somewhere, but because his old bedding was heavy and difficult to carry, he informed the Buddha.
The Buddha performed a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for him, permitting the making of a second set. [Regarding] whether the formation [of the offense] is complete or incomplete, it constitutes an offense.
The same applies above. For bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and others who commit [this offense], it is equally a duṣkṛta.
If one obtains what has already been completed, or if one abandons the previous [attempt] and performs it again, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat, he must take a piece from an old one measuring one span in length and breadth and sew it onto the new one for the purpose of discoloring it.
If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat and does not take a piece from an old one measuring one span in length and breadth, [he commits an offense].
If one uses new cloth for a seat-cover while using dyed (discolored) cloth on top, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

One day, the Buddha did not accept an invitation himself but dispatched the bhikṣus to accept it. It was the Buddha’s constant practice that after the bhikṣus had accepted an invitation, they would search through all the rooms;
seeing that old sitting-mats were scattered and strewn everywhere, he then established this rule regarding the use of dyed cloth.
This means that if one takes an old garment whose color has faded and places it over a new one, one may then alter the color of the new garment while the old one remains available for use.
Whether the alteration is successful or not, the offense is the same as mentioned above.
For bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and others who commit this offense, it is all *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if the item was already completed by another person.
There is no offense if one lacks the necessary equipment.
If a bhikṣu obtains wool while traveling on a road, he may take it if he requires it. If there is no one to carry it, he may carry it himself for a distance of three yojanas.
If there is no one to carry it and he carries it himself beyond three yojanas, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

While traveling on the road, Bāṇanda obtained a great deal of wool and carried it by threading it onto the end of a staff. When laypeople saw this, they mocked and disparaged him, saying he was like a wool merchant.
The Buddha, knowing of this, established the rule: one may carry [wool] oneself for a distance of one *yojana* (forty *li*).

If there is no one to carry it, one may carry it oneself; if one exceeds three *yojanas*, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. However, if there is someone to carry it, the bhikṣu may travel within that interval.
One must not assist in carrying [the wool]. To assist in carrying it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one causes a bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī to carry it beyond three *yojanas*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. This excludes wool; to carry another person's belongings beyond three *yojanas* is likewise a *duṣkṛta* offense.
As for the offenses committed by bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and others: [they are the same as those of a bhikṣu].
In both cases, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one carries clothing, hats, leather sandals, or similar items.
If a bhikṣu has a nun who is not a relative wash, dye, or card wool, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The group of six bhikṣus had the bhikṣuṇī Gautamī wash, dye, and card wool.
While on their way to visit the Buddha, the Buddha saw that her hands were black and asked for the reason. The bhikṣuṇī answered truthfully. Consequently, he established a rule:

while there was already a prohibition against having a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash or dye wool, he now added a further prohibition against carding it. "Carding" means to separate, sort, and process the fibers.

If one causes [a robe] to be washed, dyed, or carded, one commits three *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses. If two [of these actions] are committed, then two *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses; if one is committed, then one *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If one causes [the work] to be done but has not yet had it washed, dyed, or carded, there are three *dukkaṭa* offenses.

The rest may be understood accordingly. If one causes a non-relative *śikṣamāṇā* or *śrāmaṇerī* to do so, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense for both. [The same applies to] a *bhikṣuṇī* and a *śikṣamāṇā*...
Regarding those who commit the offense of *mānāpya* (probation): it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for both. It is not an offense if it is for the sake of a sick person or for the sake of the Saṃgha.

If a bhikṣu takes gold, silver, or money with his own hand, or instructs another to take it, or receives it by placing it on the ground, or accepts it verbally, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
When Upananda went to a householder’s home, the householder purchased food with money and gave it to him. Upananda did not wish to eat it;
instead, he took the money by hand and deposited it at a marketplace stall. This led to the reproach and suspicion of the laity. The Buddha, knowing this, established the precept.
Regarding receiving by placing on the ground: because one does not receive with the hand, one is instead made to receive by placing it on the ground.

Regarding receiving by mouth: although one has not yet received it with the hand, one verbally declares, "I receive. In general, gold, silver, money, and the like should not be received with the hand;
they should be delivered to a park-keeper (*ārāmika*) or a lay follower (*upāsaka*), which is called "purifying" (*viśuddhi*). Once that person has taken them, he returns them [to the donor].
The bhikṣu should accept it and instruct a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) to take charge of it. If that person does not return it, he should have another bhikṣu say to him:
"The Buddha has given this to you for the sake of purification; you should return this object to that bhikṣu.
If the other bhikṣu still does not speak [to the owner], he should go there himself and say: "The Buddha has given this to you for the sake of purification; you should return this object to me."
Now, it may be given to the Saṃgha, to a stūpa, to one’s upādhyāya, or to one’s ācārya.
If they do not permit it, one may inform the original owner and have it taken back; do not lose that gift of faith. If one acts in this manner, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu does not inform the person concerned, yet knows that the person is looking after it, it is a duṣkṛta. For a bhikṣuṇī who commits this, [the same applies].
The offense is the same. For *śikṣamāṇās* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.

If one seeks timber for building a house, or carries gold, silver, and so forth for the sake of provisions on a journey, or causes a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) to carry them, in all such cases there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of buying and selling of gold, silver, or precious objects, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
When Baddhananda went to the marketplace and exchanged money for money, the laypeople saw him and criticized him, saying, "The sons of the Śākya exchange money for money;

they are truly skilled at trading. The Buddha, knowing this, established the rule: that which is completed through exchange constitutes a forfeiture offense (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*); otherwise, it does not.
If it is completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, the offense is the same. For a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
If one exchanges money for goods for the sake of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of buying and selling, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
When Baddhananda was traveling on the road, he did not beg for alms; instead, he exchanged ginger for food and departed.
Later, Śāriputra came to beg for alms at that house, but they demanded the price of the rice. Śāriputra said, "I am a bhikṣu; I do not exchange food. They replied, [as follows].
"Previously, the Venerable Upananda came and exchanged ginger for food. Why, O Virtuous One, do you say that it is not improper to exchange food?
Furthermore, a certain non-Buddhist ascetic obtained a garment of great value and thought to himself, 'What use have I for this expensive garment?
I shall trade it for something else. He then went to Jetavana, where he happened upon Upananda beating and dyeing old clothes until they looked as good as new."
He exchanged it with him. Later, realizing it was his own garment, he returned to Baddhālaka to demand his original clothes back.
Baddhālaka refused, and they quarreled over the matter. When the Buddha heard of this, he established a rule:

whereas the previous provision had only prohibited gold, silver, and precious objects, this provision additionally prohibits all miscellaneous items. In general, when taking goods out to trade with laypeople, [it is forbidden].
If one incurs this offense, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture) if the item is easily completed; it is a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) if it is not easily completed.
If one trades with the five classes of renunciants or causes a *kappiyakāraka* (pure person) to trade on one's behalf, there is no offense. If there is regret, one should return the item;
if one does not return it, it is likewise a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this offense, the penalty is the same. For a *śikṣamāṇā*, [the penalty is the same].
In all such cases, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

If a bhikṣu keeps an extra bowl without having performed the formal act of "pure giving" (*viśuddha-dāna*), he may do so for up to ten days; if he exceeds this period, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Bhadrananda kept many alms bowls. When a lay devotee saw this, he criticized and disparaged him. Having heard of this, the Buddha established a prohibition.

Later, Ānanda obtained an expensive bowl which he wished to offer to Mahākāśyapa. However, Kāśyapa had gone out on a journey and had not yet returned; fearing that keeping the bowl might constitute an offense, Ānanda went to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha asked how long it would be before his return, and he replied, "Ten days. The Buddha then permitted a period of ten days. If...
On the first day one obtains a bowl; on the second and third days one again obtains bowls; continuing in this manner until the tenth day, one obtains a bowl.

If one keeps it until the eleventh day, when the dawn has fully appeared, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. This is because the calculation is based solely on the period from the first day up to the tenth day.
If one does not relinquish this extra bowl but instead exchanges it for another bowl, there is one *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense and one *dukkaṭa* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī who commits this, the offense is the same. For śikṣamāṇās and others, it is all *dukkaṭa*. If one accepts a bowl as a deposit, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu possesses an alms-bowl that has fewer than five mends and is not leaking, yet seeks a new bowl for the sake of its excellence, and obtains one, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
That bhikṣu should go before the Saṃgha and relinquish it; the Saṃgha shall take the lowest-ranking bowl from among them and give it to him to keep, which he must maintain until it breaks.
Bhadanta Pāṭaliputra’s bowl broke. He entered the city and went to a householder’s home to beg for a bowl; the householder purchased one and gave it to him.
He subsequently visited many other householders to beg and obtained bowls from them as well.

Later, on a certain day, the householders gathered in one place and happened to discuss this matter, each saying that they had purchased a bowl and given it to Bhadanta Pāṭaliputra. The householders all felt resentment toward him. The Buddha heard of this.
The Regulation: "To 'patch' means to mend. If it has five patches and does not leak, it may still be used and maintained. If it leaks, one should seek another bowl separately.
If it has fewer than five patches and does not leak, yet one seeks a new one, one commits an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
If it has five full patches and does not leak, yet one seeks a new one, it is a transgression (dukkaṭa). Regarding patching: for an iron bowl, use iron filings as an abrasive."
Moisten it with oil, place it inside an iron bowl, and grind it thoroughly with an iron hammer before using it to seal the hole.
Then, burn it over a low fire to make it hard. If it is coarse or rough, apply oil and fumigate it according to the prescribed method.
For earthenware bowls, use powdered stone in the same manner as described above. Furthermore, for iron or earthenware bowls that have leaks, use granulated sugar.
Fill the holes with mud and dry them thoroughly by heating over a fire until they are solid; then they will not leak. A bhikṣuṇī who commits this offense incurs the same guilt.
For śikṣamāṇās and others, it is all duṣkṛta. If another person gives [the materials] as a gift, or if one purchases them at their own price, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu personally begs for thread and has a weaver who is not a relative weave it into a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
When Baddhananda wished to sew a saṃghāṭī, he entered the city to beg for thread; he begged from various places until he had obtained a great quantity of thread.

Therefore, he had the three robes woven; he personally supervised the spinning and the weaving. When a lay devotee saw this, he criticized and disparaged him. Upon hearing of this, the Buddha established a rule:
if the weaver is a relative and the one who provides the thread is also a relative, there is no offense.

If the weaver is not a relative but the one who provides the thread is a relative, there is an offense. If the weaver is a relative but the one who provides the thread is not a relative, [there is an offense].
It is likewise an offense. If a bhikṣu personally supervises the weaving, weaves himself, or makes the skeins himself, it is all a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If a bhikṣuṇī commits this, the offense is the same. For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.

If a bhikṣu, when a householder or a householder’s wife has employed a weaver to weave a robe for that bhikṣu, should go to the weaver’s place before having been invited to do so and say: "Weave this robe for me;
weave it very well, making it wide, large, and firm. I shall give you a certain amount as payment. If that bhikṣu gives such payment, [he commits an offense].
Even for the value of a single meal, if one obtains a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
A certain householder provided thread to a weaver to have a robe woven for Bānaṃda; having delivered the thread, he departed immediately.
Bānaṃda went to the weaver’s place and ordered him to weave it well. The weaver said that the thread was insufficient, whereupon Bānaṃda...
He went to the householder’s home and asked for more thread; he said the price was too low, and then added that he would increase the price for him.

When the householder returned and questioned him about these matters, his wife reported everything as it had occurred. Because the householder took offense at this, the Buddha heard of it and established the rule.
If one obtains the robe, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; if one does not obtain the robe, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this offense, the punishment is the same.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu first gives a robe to another bhikṣu and later, out of anger, either seizes it himself or causes another to seize it, saying, "Give me back my robe;
I will not give it to you," that bhikṣu must return the robe; [otherwise] it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
Bhadananda had a disciple who was skilled at exhorting and converting others. Bhadananda took pleasure in him and agreed to travel with him, subsequently giving him a robe.
Another bhikṣu privately told the disciple that Bhadananda’s conduct was contrary to the Dharma and the Vinaya, and that he should not follow him.
Consequently, the disciple withdrew from him. Bhadananda, becoming enraged, snatched back the robe he had given him. The disciple [stood] tall...
He cried out, "Do not! Do not! When the Buddha heard this, he established the rule: to take away a robe from its original place constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense;
if it has not been removed from its original place, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, the offense is the same. For *śikṣamāṇās* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
If one borrows another's robe and takes it back without returning it, there is no offense. If that person has broken the precepts or holds wrong views...
If one performs various unlawful acts and seizes what should be expelled, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu keeps ghee, fresh butter, honey, or rock honey, he may consume them for up to seven days;
if he exceeds this period, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
A bhikṣu suffered from wind-disorders (*vāta-roga*) and skin ailments such as scabies during the autumn months. The Buddha permitted him to keep five kinds of medicinal substances.
Previously, it had been prohibited to take them outside of the prescribed time (*akāla-bhaiṣajya*), but because his illness did not subside, the Buddha then allowed their use at improper times.

Furthermore, while the Buddha was traveling with the assembly through the kingdom of Magadha, Piṅgalavatsa lived for a long time in this city; he had many acquaintances and acquired a great deal [of requisites].
Regarding offerings: if ghee, oil, and so forth accumulate until they fill large jars and become foul and messy, householders will see them and criticize them.

Because the Buddha heard of this, he established a rule: if one receives medicinal requisites on the first day, receives them again on the second day, and continues to receive them up to the seventh day, all must be formally dedicated through a pure gift (*śuddha-dāna*).
If it reaches the eighth day and the light of dawn appears, one commits the offense of forfeiture and transgression (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
If one exchanges medicine for other medicine, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense plus one *dukkaṭa*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, the offense is the same. For *śikṣamāṇās* and others, it is all *dukkaṭa*.

If, by the seventh day, one relinquishes it to another *bhikṣu* to eat, or if the seven days have not yet expired, it must be returned; that *bhikṣu* may then use it to anoint his feet or to anoint the door.
If the lamp has burned out, one should, after seven days have passed, smear the door, the lintel, and the threshold with ghee and oil, and give honey and stone sugar to the park keeper.
If a bhikṣu has one month remaining in the spring season, he should seek a rain-bath robe; for half a month he should use it for bathing. If a bhikṣu...
If one seeks a bathing robe more than one month in advance, or uses it for bathing more than half a month in advance, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
When Visākhā, the Mother, prepared a meal offering for the Buddha and the Saṃgha, she sent her maidservant to announce that the time had arrived. At that time, the sky...
It was raining heavily. The Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to bathe in the rain; they all bathed naked in the downpour.

A maidservant saw them and returned to tell her mother, "There are no bhikṣus in Jeta’s Grove; they are all naked heretics. The mother understood the reason for this and sent her to invite [the Buddha] again.
The Buddha immediately accepted the invitation. When the meal was finished, Mother Viśākhā requested that he accept gifts of rain-bathing robes. The Buddha then—
The Buddha granted permission. Later, the group of six bhikṣus constantly sought rain-bathing robes during the spring, summer, and winter, using them for other purposes and still bathing naked.

Knowing this, the Buddha established a regulation: when one month of spring remains—corresponding to the sixteenth day of the third month in this land—one may use the robe for bathing for half a month, which corresponds to the first day of the fourth month in this land.
If one seeks it at an improper time or uses it at an improper time, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If one should use it but does not, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. For bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and others who commit this, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one gives up the rain-bath robe and subsequently uses it for another purpose, there is no offense. If one has no rain-bath robe, one need not wear it.
However, one who bathes does not commit an offense.
If a bhikṣu has less than ten days remaining of the three-month summer retreat, he may accept an urgent gift of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*).
Having accepted it, he may keep it until the end of the robe season. If he keeps it beyond that time, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
At that time, there was a rebellion among the people of Śrāvastī. The King dispatched a high minister to suppress it.
The minister wished to provide offerings and robes before departing, but as ten days of the summer retreat (varṣā) still remained until its completion, the bhikṣus did not dare accept the robes.

They then informed the Buddha of the situation, whereupon he established a rule: regarding "robes for urgent giving" (ātyayika-cīvara), when there is an urgent matter and one gives as an offering, one cannot wait until the end of the retreat.

One may keep [the robe] for the duration of the entire *varṣā* (rainy season retreat). This means that one may keep it until the day the robe is formally received, because the Buddha ordained that one may receive the robe only after the *varṣā* has concluded.
To keep it beyond that period constitutes an "extra robe" (*atirekacīvara*), and thus one commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The same offense applies to a *bhikṣuṇī*. For a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is all a *duṣkṛta* offense. If...

If there is a danger of thieves or circumstances such as the loss of robes, it is not an offense to keep them beyond the aforementioned period. Or, if one has accepted a robe as a loan and keeps it after the time limit has passed, it is not an offense.
If a bhikṣu has completed the three-month summer retreat and the full fifteen days of the eighth month have elapsed, [regarding] the āraṇyaka...
In a remote place that is subject to doubt, fear, terror, or difficulty,
if a bhikṣu dwells in such a location and leaves even one of his three robes behind in a village dwelling, or if he has a reason to stay apart from his robes for up to six nights,
should he exceed this limit, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
After the *varṣā* retreat, the bhikṣus each went to dwell in forest hermitages (*āraṇya*). There, they were plundered of their robes and belongings by bandits and were even beaten.

Because they all subsequently came to dwell within the Jeta Grove, the Buddha established a rule permitting them to leave one robe each behind in a village dwelling while staying apart from their robes.
Later, the group of six bhikṣus (Ṣaḍvargika) then deposited their three robes with the families of their relatives.

Having traveled for a long time without returning, the Buddha heard of this and further established a rule of six nights. If one exceeds six nights until the appearance of the dawn light, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding those who have completed the three-month summer retreat: the summer retreat begins on the sixteenth day of the fourth month and concludes on the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
"Completing [the retreat] on the fifteenth day of the eighth month" refers to the division of the year into three periods in the Western Regions.
At that time, since each season lasts four months, the summer retreat concludes on the fifteenth day of the eighth month.

For bhikṣuṇīs and śikṣamāṇās, any violation [of this rule] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. However, if one is detained or obstructed by unavoidable circumstances, there is no offense even if the six-night limit is exceeded.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that it is property belonging to the Saṃgha, diverts it for his own personal use, he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika).
A certain householder wished to provide a meal offering for the Buddha and the Saṃgha, as well as gifts of robes.

When Baddhālī heard of this, he went to the man's house and said: "The community of monks is already wealthy; there is no need to offer robes. It will suffice simply to offer food. [He spoke thus regarding the robes.]
"You may give it to me. The householder believed him. When the next day arrived for the community of monks to receive offerings, they were fully endowed with dignified deportment.

Seeing this, the householder cried out in a loud voice, "Alas! I should not have given the robes to the community of monks! When the monks asked why, he replied, "It was because of Nanda. Knowing the reason, the Buddha established this rule:
regarding any property belonging to the Sangha, whether light or heavy, large or small, if one diverts it into one's own possession, it must be forfeited.

[If one] diverts [the property]: if an object permitted for the Saṃgha is diverted to the stūpa; permitted for the stūpa is diverted to the Saṃgha; permitted for the present [Saṃgha] is diverted to the ten directions;
permitted for the ten directions is diverted to the present; permitted for the monks is diverted to the nuns; permitted for the nuns is diverted to the monks—in all these cases, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If it has already been permitted but one suspects it was not; if it has not been permitted but one perceives it as permitted; or if it has not been permitted but one suspects it was.

Regarding those who have already consented, both [the giver and the receiver] commit a *duṣkṛta* offense. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, the offense is the same. For a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, both commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one knows that she has consented to a small amount but encourages her to give more; or if she has consented to giving to a few people but encourages her to give to many;
or if she has consented to give to an inferior person but encourages her to give to a virtuous person—there is no offense. If one does not know her consent, there is no offense.
Venerable sirs, I have already recited the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas. Now I ask the venerable sirs:
Are you pure in this regard? (Ask three times.)
Venerable sirs, because you are silent, it is understood that you are pure in this matter; thus shall this be held.
Venerable sirs, these ninety *pāyattika* rules are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
*Pāyattika* (波逸提) is translated here as "falling" (*patati*). The first thirty rules all involve committing an offense regarding robes or bowls;

therefore, one is required to relinquish the offending object in order to seek confession, which is termed "relinquishment and falling" (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). These current ninety rules, however, involve committing offenses only through speech or conduct;
since there is no object to be relinquished, they are simply called "falling."
If a bhikṣu speaks falsely knowing it to be so, it is a pāyattika offense.
Because of the bhikṣu Hastibala, when he debated with certain brahmins, if he was not successful, he would contradict his own previous words;
likewise, when questioned by the Saṃgha, he again contradicted his previous words and was rebuked by the assembly. The Buddha knew this.

Therefore, it is established: to speak falsely while knowing the truth means to say one has seen when one has not seen; to say one has not seen when one has seen; to say one has heard when one has not heard;

to say one has not heard when one has heard; to say one has touched when one has not touched; to say one has not touched when one has touched; to say one knows when one does not know; to say one does not know when one knows;
and even to say one doubts when one does not doubt, or to say one does not doubt when one does doubt. To speak such words clearly within an assembly constitutes [a transgression].
If it is understood, it is a *pāyattika*; if not understood, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

When the precepts are being recited, if one remembers having committed an offense yet does not confess it after being asked three times, it is a *dukkaṭa*. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, the offense is the same.
For *śikṣamāṇās* and others, it is likewise a *dukkaṭa*. However, if there is a skillful means employed for the sake of providing benefit, speaking in such a manner is not an offense.
No offense.
If a bhikṣu mocks another bhikṣu by calling him "skull-seeder," it is a pāyattika.
This was on account of the group of six who, while settling a dispute, insulted the bhikṣus as "skull-seeders," causing the bhikṣus to feel ashamed and forgetful.
If one speaks after having previously failed to do so, the Buddha, having heard of this, established the rule. Regarding those who disparage by mentioning their lineage or skull:
this may refer to the lowliness of their clan, the vulgarity of their craft, or their abundance of sinful offenses.
If the speech is intelligible, it is a *pāyattika*; if it is unintelligible, it is a *dukkaṭa*. [This applies to] bhikṣuṇīs.
Those who commit [the offense] incur the same guilt. For śikṣamāṇās and others, it is equally a duṣkṛta.

However, there is no offense in cases where one speaks inadvertently, or speaks for the sake of a close friend, or speaks for the purpose of instruction, or speaks for the sake of the Dharma and the Vinaya.
If a bhikṣu speaks with double-tongued speech, it is a pāyattika offense. For example,
because the group of six transmitted words spoken in private here to those there, and again transmitted words spoken in private there back here,
strife arose among the community where none had existed before, and strife that already existed could not be settled.

[The Buddha] eradicated [this fault]. Because the Buddha heard of it, he established this precept: If a bhikṣu engages in double-tongued speech to cause strife and discord among all assemblies, whether householders or those who have left the home life, and speaks so as to be clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika* offense; if not clearly understood, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a bhikṣuṇī who commits this, the offense is the same. For śikṣamāṇās and others, it is likewise a *dukkaṭa*. If, however, one breaks [the bonds of] evil associates...
There is no offense for those who belong to a faction of evil companions, those who destroy the means [of harmony] and cause schism in the Saṃgha,
or those who perform illegal and non-disciplinary *karmavācanās*. If a bhikṣu sleeps in the same room as a woman, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
The Venerable Aniruddha, having traveled a great distance to a place where no monks resided, entered a village seeking lodging.
There was only one courtesan’s house that regularly accommodated guests; the Venerable went there to request a night's stay. The courtesan directed him to a room at the entrance of the gate.
Shortly thereafter, an elder also came seeking lodging. That elder had many servants and attendants, who crowded close around the Venerable. The courtesan—
The woman then had him enter her chamber to stay the night. Once the Venerable One had entered the room, he spread out his bedding and sat cross-legged.

At the beginning of the first watch of the night, the woman’s lustful mind arose; she approached the Venerable One and sought to consummate their marriage. The Venerable One remained silent and did not respond.
It was the same during the latter part of the night. The woman then removed her clothes and drew near him, but the Venerable One caused his body to surge into the air.
The woman felt ashamed and apologized; the Venerable One returned to his original seat and preached the Dharma for her. The woman requested the precepts of taking refuge.

The next day, he returned and informed the Buddha of this incident, which led to the formal rule: "If a woman stays overnight in the same room [as a monk], for every side of her body that touches the ground, it is a *pāyattika* offense."
If one turns over or shifts position [while the woman is present], it is a *pāyattika*. If a woman stands during the day while a bhikṣu lies down, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The offense for a bhikṣuṇī is the same. For śikṣamāṇās and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
If a woman arrives before or after the bhikṣu and he is entirely unaware of her presence, there is no offense. Or if he is lying ill and unable to rise, or...
There is no offense in cases where it is difficult to avoid.
If a bhikṣu stays overnight with a person who has not received the full ordination, and exceeds two nights until dawn on the third night,
it is a pāyattika.
One of the group of six monks was staying overnight with several elders in a lecture hall. He fell into a deep, unrestrained sleep and rolled over so that his body was exposed.
A neighboring bhikṣu covered him with his robe; after a short while, he was exposed again, and the neighboring bhikṣu covered him once more.
Immediately thereafter, he rolled over again and his body rose up. The elders burst into loud laughter and mocked him. At that time, the...
The bhikṣus were all filled with shame. When the Buddha heard of this, he established a rule. At that time, Rāhula had not yet received full ordination;

when the assembly sent him out, there was no place for him to stay, so he went to sleep in the latrine. The Buddha, knowing he was in the latrine, led him back to his own room and stayed with him for one night.
He then further established a rule: if they stay together for two nights, and upon reaching the third night before the break of dawn, [one must depart].
One must avoid it. If one does not avoid it, it is a *pāyattika*. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, the offense is the same.

For *śikṣamāṇās* and others, it is all *duṣkṛta*. If a person who has not yet received the full ordination arrives before or after the *bhikṣu*, and neither party is aware of the other, there is no offense.
Whether walking or standing, sitting or lying down due to illness, or if constrained by difficult circumstances...
One who is restrained does not commit an offense.
If a bhikṣu recites the Buddha’s sūtras together with a person who has not received full ordination, it is a pāyattika.
The group of six bhikṣus was reciting the Buddha’s sūtras together with various elders in the lecture hall; their voices were loud and high-pitched, like those of [householders].
The sound of the Brahmins reciting their books was a disturbance. Because those practicing meditation informed the Buddha of this, he established a rule:
regarding "reciting together," it means two people reciting a single phrase together. If they do so neither before nor after [the other], one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī who commits this, the offense is the same. For śikṣamāṇās and others, it is all *duṣkṛta*. In all cases of recitation, one person must necessarily speak first.
If one person finishes speaking first, and the teacher does not instruct them by saying, "I have finished; you may speak now," the teacher incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
However, if two people share the same practice and recite together, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense, speaks of it to one who has not received full ordination,
except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.
At that time, there were bhikṣus undergoing *parivāsa* and *mānatva* who sat among those of lower standing.
The group of six bhikṣus asked the laypeople, "Do you know who these people are sitting among those of lower standing? The laypeople replied, "We do not know.
The group of six said, "These individuals have committed such-and-such an offense and such-and-such an offense; therefore, the Saṃgha..."
The Sangha’s penalty was that he was made to sit in the lower seats. When the bhikṣus heard this, they felt shame and remorse and reported it to the Buddha, who therefore established this rule:
regarding grave offenses (*sthūlātyaya*), those that are clearly articulated are *pārājika* or *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, while those that are not clearly articulated are *pāyattika*;
those that are not clearly articulated are *duṣkṛta*. Excluding grave offenses, if one [accuses] another who has not yet received full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) of any other offense...

To speak of it to others constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. To confess a grave or coarse offense (*sthūlātyaya*) to one who has not received the full ordination (*upasampadā*) constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense, except when authorized by a formal monastic act (*saṃghakarma*).

At that time, Śāriputra performed a formal act for the sake of the assembly, appointing [himself] to go among the king’s retinue, the ministers, and the common people to proclaim the faults and evils of Devadatta.
Having heard the Buddha’s formulation of the precepts, he became doubtful that he had committed an offense.
Because of this offense, the Buddha established [this rule] to eliminate it. A bhikṣuṇī who commits it incurs the same offense. For śikṣamāṇās and others, it is equally a duṣkṛta.
If a layperson has already publicly heard of this grave and wicked offense, there is no offense [for the bhikṣuṇī].
If a bhikṣu speaks of a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma) to a person who has not received full ordination, saying, "I know this;
I have seen this," and claiming that his knowledge and vision are real, it is a pāyattika offense.
The bhikṣus of the Bālakalpa Garden spoke to others of having attained superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*).
The Buddha said, "If one has truly attained them, one still must not speak of it to others; how much more so if one has not? Thus, I shall establish a precept.

Regarding "superhuman states," this refers to those states that transcend the five aggregates (*skandha*), the six sense bases (*āyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*); namely, the dharmas of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and liberation (*vimukti*).
"Knowing and seeing reality" means knowing and seeing it as it truly is, not falsely or deceptively. To speak clearly [of such matters] constitutes a *pāyattika*;
to speak unclearly constitutes a *dukkaṭa*. This applies whether one uses hand gestures, writes a letter, or makes signs.

If one tells this to someone who knows [the facts], it is a *pāyattika*. If they do not know, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If one speaks to a person who has received the full ordination (*upasampadā*) but is not a consenting party, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this offense, the penalty is the same. For *śikṣamāṇās* and others, it is likewise a *dukkaṭa*.
If it is done out of overweening pride (*abhimāna*), or if one actually possesses [the qualities] and speaks to a consenting *bhikṣu*, or...
If one merely speaks of superhuman states (*uttari-manuṣya-dharma*) without saying "I have attained them," there is no offense for either party.
However, if a bhikṣu teaches the Dharma to a woman and exceeds five or six words, except when a man capable of understanding is present, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
Kāḷodāyin went to the house of a certain elder and whispered in the ear of the wife in front of her mother-in-law. The mother-in-law, feeling suspicious, asked what was happening.
The wife replied, "He is preaching the Dharma to me. The mother-in-law said, "If he is preaching the Dharma, you should preach it aloud so that we may hear it."

"Why do you speak only to yourself in your ear? Because the Buddha heard this, he established a precept: if one speaks more than five or six words while teaching the Dharma, it constitutes an offense.

Five words refers to the five aggregates being non-self; six words refers to the six sense bases being impermanent. If a wise man is present nearby, then even if one exceeds this limit, there is no offense.
If the speech exceeds the limit and is clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation); if it is not clearly understood, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
It is a *duṣkṛta*. For a bhikṣuṇī who commits this offense, the penalty is the same. For *śikṣamāṇās* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.

If one explains the five precepts, the eightfold fast (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*), the Eightfold Noble Path, the ten paths of wholesome action, or the ten paths of unwholesome action, as well as answering questions on doubtful points—even if the man has no knowledge—one may explain them for him.
If he does not understand, one may provide a detailed exposition; in both cases, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu digs the earth with his own hands or instructs another to dig the earth, it is a pāyattika offense.
While the group of six bhikṣus were repairing a lecture hall for the Buddha, they dug the earth with their own hands and instructed others to dig, saying, "Dig here;
place it there. When an elder saw this, he criticized and disparaged them. The Buddha, knowing this, established the rule: digging the earth means merely moving the soil.
It is a *pāyattika*. If one drives a stake into the ground, or if one lights a fire upon the ground, it is in both cases a *pāyattika*.
If one employs a *kappiya-kāraka* (a "pure person") to dig the earth, one should say, "Know this; look at this. Failing to give such instruction constitutes a *dukkaṭa*.

For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this offense, the penalty is the same. For *śikṣamāṇās* and others, it is likewise a *dukkaṭa*. If one drags bamboo or wood and thereby disturbs the soil, [the same applies].
If one takes cow dung; or takes soil from a collapsed riverbank or molehills; or removes soil from a walking path (caṅkrama);
or removes soil from within a house; or strikes the ground with a staff; or digs unintentionally—in all such cases, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu destroys a village of spirits, it is a pāyattika.
When a bhikṣu in the wilderness was repairing a dwelling and cut down trees with his own hands, the Buddha heard of this and established the rule.
"Village of spirits" refers to all grasses and trees; they are called a "village" because grasses and trees are the dwellings where spirits reside. If...
If one cuts [them], it destroys the village and leaves no place for shelter. Regarding all grasses and trees:

if they are living and one perceives them as living, whether one cuts them oneself, instructs another to cut them, drives stakes into the tree, or even burns them with fire, it is an *pāyattika* offense in every case.
If one cuts more than half of a living grass or tree, it is an *pāyattika*. If they are living but one perceives them as not living, or if they are not...

If one perceives what is living as living, or suspects it is living, or suspects it is not living, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). If it is half-living and half-dry, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one causes a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to perform allowable acts) to cut [wood], yet does not instruct him to recognize or observe whether it is [living], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
A bhikṣuṇī who commits this offense incurs the same guilt. For śikṣamāṇās and others, it is equally a duṣkṛta.
There is no offense if one cuts withered grass or wood, or drags bamboo, wood, or similar objects across grass or wood.
If a bhikṣu speaks falsely or uses evasive speech to annoy others, it is a pāyattika offense.
The bhikṣu Chanda was guilty of an offense; when the other bhikṣus questioned him, he answered with evasive words, saying:
"To whom did you speak? About what matter did you speak? On what principle were you debating? Was it spoken to me, or was it spoken to others? Who [was it]?"

He committed an offense. From what did the offense arise? "I do not see the offense. The Buddha, knowing this, ordered that a *jñapti-karman* (formal act consisting of a motion) be performed against him;
this was termed "speaking otherwise" (*anyathā-vāda*). Subsequently, because the Buddha had established the rule that one must not speak otherwise, Chanda began to harass the Saṃgha:
when summoned he would not come, and when not summoned he would come; when he should rise he would not rise, and when he should not rise he would rise; when he should speak...
He does not speak; he speaks when he ought not to speak. The Buddha, knowing this, further performs the *jñapti-karman* (formal motion) for him, which is termed "causing provocation.

If one commits the offense before the formal motion has been made, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). If one commits the offense after the formal motion has been made, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).
The same applies to offenses committed by *bhikṣuṇīs*. For *śikṣamāṇās* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*. If one is so deeply distracted that they do not understand, there is no offense.
There is no offense in cases such as when the person previously mentioned speaks in a low voice or speaks too rapidly so that they are not understood; or when they perform improper acts;
or even in various circumstances where they are difficult to summon and do not come.
If a bhikṣu reviles another in anger, it is a pāyattika offense.

When the bhikṣu Trapusa-māra was appointed by the Saṃgha to oversee bedding and to assign monks their meals, the bhikṣu Maitrībala criticized him in a private place, saying he harbored feelings of favoritism and animosity.
When the assembly admonished him, he replied, "I did not say so face-to-face."
[He] said, "I was merely censuring him in private. The Buddha, knowing this, established a rule. After being censured and reproached, [the monk] continued to find fault with him without ceasing.
The community again admonished him, to which he replied, "I did not censure him; I was merely reviling him. Therefore, the Buddha further established a rule against both censuring and reviling.
If one speaks [the rebuke] clearly, it is a *pāyattika*; if not clearly, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If the one being rebuked receives the instruction, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this offense, the guilt is the same. For *śikṣamāṇās* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
If a *bhikṣu* actually possesses such evil qualities and, having confessed them according to the Dharma, causes the other to repent, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu takes a monastic rope bed, wooden bed, bedding, or sitting mat and spreads it out in the open air, or instructs another to spread it out,
and then departs without putting it away himself or instructing another to put it away, it is a pāyattika offense.
The group of seventeen bhikṣus took the sitting mats belonging to the Saṃgha and spread them out to sit upon in the open air.
When the time for the meal arrived, they did not collect the mats and went directly to the feast. Consequently, the sitting mats were defiled by wind-blown dust, soil, insects, and birds.

Knowing this, the Buddha established the rule. As for the term "belonging to the Saṃgha" (saṃghika): any object that has already been relinquished and entered into the Saṃgha is called "Saṃgha property. This refers to [the great...]

These are items belonging to the community that remain in permanent use. If one takes a monastic rope-bench or similar item and spreads it out on an open space, one must lift it up when departing, either handing it over to the administrative official (*karmadāna*) or to other bhikṣus, or placing it in a location where it will not be damaged.
If one departs without having lifted it, it is a *pāyattika* offense. If one has stepped with one foot inside the door and one foot outside the door, one has not yet departed.
[If one does so], it is a *duṣkṛta*. If two persons sit together on a single rope-couch (*śayanāsana*), the junior person should collect [the bedding].

If the junior person intends for the senior person to collect it, and the senior person likewise intends for the junior person to collect it, yet in the end neither collects it, both commit a *pāyattika*.

For the junior person, because it was not in accordance with proper decorum (*anīryāpatha*), there is an additional *duṣkṛta*. If a *bhikṣuṇī* commits this offense, the penalty is the same. This is the rule (*śikṣāpada*).
For śikṣamāṇās and others, it is equally a duṣkṛta offense. If there are difficulties or obstacles such that one is unable to collect [the items], there is no offense.
As for the group of seventeen: in Rājagṛha, there were several youths between the ages of twelve and seventeen who came together to leave the household life and formed a single group.
If a bhikṣu, within a monastic dwelling, spreads out bedding— whether spreading it himself or instructing another to spread it— and then sits or lies upon it,
yet when departing does not himself remove it nor instruct another to remove it, it is a pāyattika offense.
A visiting bhikṣu came and stayed overnight, spreading bedding in a peripheral room. When he later departed, he neither removed it nor informed the resident bhikṣus.
Consequently, the bedding became completely rotted and ruined. The Buddha heard of this and established a rule: whenever a visitor departs, they must inform the person in charge of affairs.

If there is no one available to be notified, they should place the items in a place where they will not be damaged. If one finally leaves without removing them, they shall be considered to have exited the boundary [of the monastery].
This is an external *pāyattika*. If one foot is inside the boundary and one foot is outside the boundary, it is a *duṣkṛta* as long as one has not yet departed.

If there is an urgent matter and one departs without immediately returning, and stays outside the boundary for two nights, then upon the dawning of the light on the third night, one must personally go back to the room and put away [the bedding], or send someone to inform the person in charge to do so.
One must take charge of it. If one does not do so, it is a *pāyattika*. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this offense, the penalty is the same.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one is constrained by difficult circumstances, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu already occupies a dwelling, later comes and forcibly spreads out bedding within it to stay the night,
thinking: "If he finds it cramped, he will naturally move away from me," and acts with this as his sole motive and for no other reason—
this is improper conduct and constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
The group of six and the group of seventeen were traveling together.

Upon arriving at a place where no monks resided, the group of seventeen said to the group of six, "Venerable elders, you should seek out a dwelling first. The group of six replied, "Go ahead yourself;
what business is it of ours? Thereupon, the group of seventeen went on ahead to seek a dwelling and prepared the bedding. The group of six arrived later.
When [monks] arrived, they vied for their seating order based on seniority. The group of seventeen refused to comply, so the group of six subsequently spread out their bedding in the middle.
The group of seventeen called out loudly, "Venerable sirs, do not do this! Venerable sirs, do not do this! Because the Buddha heard of it, he established this rule:
a bhikṣuṇī who violates it commits the same offense; śikṣamāṇās and others likewise commit a duṣkṛta.
If one did not know beforehand; if it was spacious and there was no obstruction; if one had fallen to the ground due to illness;
or if one was constrained by difficult circumstances—there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu, out of anger toward another bhikṣu and being displeased with him, personally drags him out of the monastic dwelling, or instructs another to do so.
[They] were led out; [this constitutes] a *pāyattika*.

The group of six and the group of seventeen were traveling together on the same road. Upon reaching a small dwelling place, the group of seventeen spoke to the group of six as they had done previously, but the group of six paid them no heed.
The group of seventeen went ahead to sprinkle and sweep the rooms and spread out fine [mats].
Regarding bedding and requisites: the group of six, having learned of this, entered at dusk and vied for their positions, forcing the group of seventeen to move out.
When the group of seventeen refused to move, they became angry and forcibly dragged them out of the room. The Buddha, having heard of this, established a rule:
for every person dragged out and for every door passed through, it is a *pāyattika* offense. If many people are dragged out through many doors, there are many [offenses].

If one person carries [an object] out through one door, or many people carry it out through many doors, in all cases there is a *pāyattika* offense. If one person drags [an object] out through one door, there is one *pāyattika* offense.
If one takes another's property and places it outside the door, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If one shuts another inside and leaves them outside the door, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, the offense is the same. For *śikṣamāṇās* and others, it is likewise.
It is a *dukkaṭa*. If one stays overnight with a person who has not received the full ordination (*upasampadā*), and at the time before the dawn light appears on the third night, one leads them out;

or if one leads out someone who has broken the precepts, broken their views, or broken their decorum, or who has been formally accused by others or expelled by others—there is no offense in either case.
Likewise, there is no offense if one leads out a person known to be a eunuch or a hermaphrodite.
If a bhikṣu, in a room or on an upper story of a multi-storied building, sits or lies down upon a rope bed or a wooden bed with detachable legs, it is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu stays on an upper story and sits on a bed with detachable legs, he lacks composure; if the legs of the bed detach and strike [someone], it is an offense.

"Venerable Bhikṣu, [this rule was established] because it caused blood to flow from his body; the Buddha heard of this and therefore enacted the prohibition. Regarding 'a bed with detachable legs': this refers to a bed whose legs can be removed.
