If a Bhikṣuṇī commits this offense, the penalty is the same. For Śikṣamāṇās and others, it is equally a Duṣkṛta.
If one sits on a bed that does not have detachable legs, there is no offense."
If a bhikṣu, knowing that water contains living beings, pours it over mud or grass himself, or instructs another to pour it, he commits a pāyattika offense.
When the bhikṣu Chanda constructed a large dwelling, he poured water containing living beings over the mud; the householders, [finding this] lacking in compassion...
The monks disparaged this as being harmful to life. When the Buddha heard of it, he established a rule: if there are insects in water and one perceives them as such, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If there are insects in water but one suspects they are not, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense. If there are no insects in water but one perceives them as such, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If there are no insects in water but one suspects they are present, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense. This applies equally to whey, wine, vinegar, or malt-water, should they contain insects.
If one uses it to pour over mud or grass, or if one instructs another to do so, it is a *pāyattika* offense. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, the offense is the same.
For *śikṣamāṇās* and others, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If the water contains insects, one should use a fine cloth to make a filter;
having strained it through, there is no offense in using it. If there are still insects even after straining with a three-layered filter, the Saṃgha [should not use it] at that place.
One should abide [in restraint], for the destruction of life is a grave matter.
If a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling, he must direct the work regarding the doors, windows, and other decorative fittings, as well as the roofing and thatching.
[The roof] shall be leveled at two or three layers.

If it exceeds this, it is an *pāyattika*. The bhikṣu Chanda constructed a large dwelling; after covering it once, there was still grass remaining, so he covered it again. Because the roof was thus double-layered, it eventually collapsed.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and disparaged him. The Buddha heard of this and established the precept: for any roofing of a house...
When the third section has not yet been concluded, one must immediately go to a place where [the recitation] is neither seen nor heard. If one does not go, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one leaves a place where it is seen to go to a place where it is heard, or leaves a place where it is heard to go to a place where it is seen, in both cases it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, the offense is the same. For *śikṣamāṇās* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*. If...
There is no offense if one is detained by some difficulty and is unable to reach a place where it would not be seen or heard.
If a bhikṣu teaches bhikṣuṇīs without having been appointed by the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.
The group of six bhikṣus instructed the bhikṣuṇīs; they did not speak the True Dharma, but spoke only of worldly matters and trivialities.
The bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī came and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Now, within the Saṃgha, one must select a capable bhikṣu to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
A formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* shall be performed to appoint him to go and instruct the bhikṣuṇīs. The group of six was not appointed.
They then went outside the boundary and appointed one another to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs. Mahāprajāpatī returned once more and informed the Buddha. The Buddha then established the precept:
"When the Saṃgha appoints someone, they should make the following formal announcement: 'Venerable Saṃgha, please listen.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let it appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs. This is the announcement. Venerable One.
The Saṃgha listens. This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
Which elders among you approve of the Saṃgha appointing this bhikṣu, so-and-so, to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs? Those who approve remain silent; those who do not approve speak.
The Saṃgha has approved the appointment of this bhikṣu, so-and-so, to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs. Because the Saṃgha approves and remains silent, this matter is settled.
It is to be held thus:
If a bhikṣu, having been appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, continues until sunset, it is a pāyattika offense.
Venerable Nanda was appointed by the assembly to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs; the venerable one preached the Dharma with a beautiful voice.
The sound was pleasant for the community of nuns to hear, and so it continued until sunset. At that time, the nuns left Jetavana and headed for Śrāvastī.
The city gates were already closed, and they were unable to enter. They consequently stayed overnight outside the gate within the city moat. When the gates opened at dawn, they entered the city.
When the elders saw them, they all said, "The nuns stayed overnight in Jetavana; the Buddha heard of this and has therefore established a prohibition."
In all cases of instructing nuns, one should cease before sunset; if one continues until sunset, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one recites or receives the scriptures from other women, or discusses other matters with them, and continues until sunset, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If it is already sunset but one perceives it as not yet being sunset, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If one is in another location and preaches the Dharma for the sake of the assembly, [there is no offense].
If a nun comes to listen, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu: "The bhikṣu teaches the bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of food and drink," it is a pāyattika.
The group of six bhikṣus was not permitted to appoint a bhikṣu to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs;

they consequently became jealous and slandered those who did instruct them, claiming they lacked sincerity and acted only for the sake of food and drink. When the Buddha heard this, he established a precept:
if one speaks clearly and intelligibly [with such intent], it is a pāyattika; if one speaks without being clear or intelligible, it is a dukkaṭa. This applies to bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and śikṣamāṇās.
In such cases, those who commit the offense are all guilty of a *duṣkṛta*. If the matter is indeed as stated, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange for trade, it is a *pāyattika*.
There was a bhikṣu who went for alms, fully endowed with dignified deportment. When a bhikṣuṇī saw him, she felt deep respect and repeatedly invited him [to accept robes].
He did not accept her invitations. One day, at the distribution of robes in Jetavana, the bhikṣu received a robe and was leaving the gate when the bhikṣuṇī arrived.
The bhikṣu gave the robe to her, his intention being to repay her previous act of respect; he anticipated that the bhikṣuṇī would certainly not accept it, yet she ultimately accepted it.
The bhikṣus repeatedly informed others, reproaching this nun for being improper in accepting their robes. When the Buddha heard of this, he established a regulation.
Consequently, the bhikṣus thereafter did not dare to give robes to nuns who were relatives. Therefore, the Buddha added the qualification "non-relative.

Furthermore, when the Jeta Grove obtained robes, they were shared equally between the two assemblies; or when a nun obtained a robe from the Saṃgha, she would bring it to trade [with them], yet the monks would not [accept it].
To dare to treat it lightly is therefore further prohibited and subject to exchange. For a bhikṣuṇī or a śikṣamāṇā who does so, it is equally a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika offense.
Kāḷodāyin made a robe for a bhikṣuṇī; he fashioned it with images of a man and woman engaged in sexual intercourse.
When the bhikṣuṇī came to collect it, he immediately folded the robe and gave it to her, saying: "This robe must not be opened or worn carelessly, nor should you show it to others.
When the time for the invitation to the meal arrives, you shall wear this robe and follow behind the bhikṣuṇīs. Thus spoke the bhikṣuṇī.
As instructed, when the laypeople saw this, they all mocked and laughed. The Buddha heard of it and therefore established a rule:

if one makes clothing for a bhikṣuṇī, whether cutting it to whatever size or using even a single needle or thread, it is a pāyattika offense. This applies equally to ironing, mending with thread, and so forth.
It is a *duṣkṛta*. Subsequently, the bhikṣus did not dare to make robes for their own relatives;
they informed the Buddha, who therefore added the words "if she is not a relative. For bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and others, whoever commits this offense incurs a *duṣkṛta* as well.
If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place with a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
One day, Kālodāyin went to the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā and sat together with her in a secluded spot outside the gate.
A householder saw them and censured them. The Buddha, knowing this, established the precept. "A secluded place" means...
If it is a concealed place where one may act privately, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If one is blind but not deaf, or deaf but not blind, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one stands while doing so, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and others, those who commit this offense all incur a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu travels along the same road with a bhikṣuṇī, even as far as the vicinity of a village, except at other times, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Other times" refers to when there is suspicion or fear regarding traveling together; these are called "other times."
The group of six bhikṣus traveled together with the group of six bhikṣuṇīs through the inhabited areas. When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and disparaged them.
The Buddha, knowing of this, established a precept: if they agree to travel together and reach the boundary of a village—according to the extent of that boundary—it is a pāyattika offense.
If there is no village and it is an open space, reaching ten *li* constitutes a pāyattika offense. If...
If one travels less than ten *li*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If multiple villages share the same boundary and one travels [through them], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one has agreed to go but does not go, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. For a *bhikṣuṇī*, a *śikṣamāṇā*, and others, committing this offense is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
Subsequently, there was a *bhikṣu* who did not dare to travel with a *bhikṣuṇī*; the *bhikṣuṇī* traveled behind him and was robbed by bandits.

Kāśyapa, the Buddha has thus opened up other occasions. These "other occasions" refer to places where one travels with a large group, or places where there is suspicion of bandits and thieves, or places where there is actual fear of bandits and thieves;
in all such cases, traveling together on the same path is permitted and does not constitute an offense.
Furthermore, traveling together without prior arrangement also does not constitute an offense.
If a bhikṣu travels upriver or downriver in the same boat as a bhikṣuṇī, except when crossing directly across, it is a pāyattika.
The group of six bhikṣus traveled upriver and downriver in the same boat with the group of six bhikṣuṇīs. They resided...
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and found it objectionable. The Buddha, knowing this, established the precept: if one enters a boat together [with a layman], it is a *pāyattika*;
if one foot is on the boat and one foot is on the ground, or if one intends to enter but has not yet entered, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one agrees to go together but does not go, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For *bhikṣuṇīs*, *śikṣamāṇās*, and others, those who commit these offenses are likewise guilty.
It is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), except for one who crosses directly across.
Later, because a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī both wished to cross the Gaṅgā River, and the bhikṣu refused to cross with the bhikṣuṇī, the bhikṣuṇī was unable to cross and was robbed on the riverbank.

For this reason, the Buddha made an exception for crossing directly across. If they board the same boat without prior agreement, there is no offense. If there are difficulties or obstacles, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu knowingly eats food obtained through the cause of being praised or exhorted by a bhikṣuṇī, except when the donor had a prior intention [to give], it is a pāyattika.
There was a householder who invited Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana for a meal; at that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā [was present].
A nun came to that house and asked, "Who have you invited? They replied, "We have invited Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana. The nun said, "These are all lowly men.
Had you told me first, I would have invited the Dragon among Dragons for you. The man asked, "Who is the Dragon among Dragons?
The nun then pointed to the group of six bhikṣus (the Ṣaḍvargika). Just then, Śāriputra and the others arrived, and the nun immediately—
When she said, "The dragon among dragons has arrived," the householder rebuked her, saying, "Why did you previously call him a person of low birth, and now say he is a 'dragon among dragons'?
From this day forth, he is not permitted to come to my home again. It turned out that this nun was actually one of the group of six who had been inciting people to offer alms.
When Śāriputra and the others returned, they informed the Buddha of these events, and thus [the rule] was established. Later, there were further [incidents].
Previously, there was an intention to offer a meal to Rāṣṭrapāla. When Rāṣṭrapāla arrived, a nun informed him [of the invitation], and the elder subsequently prepared a vegetarian feast (*śrāddha*).
Rāṣṭrapāla, having heard that this was informed by a nun, did not dare to eat and reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha granted an exemption for such cases:

if one knows that the nun was acting as an agent of persuasion (*parivartaka*), it is a *pāyattika* offense; if one suspects that the nun was acting as an agent of persuasion, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
Dust-offense (duṣkṛta). If one does not provide instruction while perceiving that one has provided it, it is a dust-offense.

If one does not provide instruction while suspecting that one has provided it, it is a dust-offense. If one provides instruction and receives items such as undergarments, lamps, or oil, it is a dust-offense.
For bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and others, whoever commits this offense incurs a dust-offense. If one does not know, or if the bhikṣuṇī provides the offerings herself...
If a donor instructs a bhikṣuṇī to manage [the provisions], neither commits an offense.
If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a woman to travel along the same road, even as far as a village, it is a pāyattika.
A woman from the kingdom of Vaiśālī was married to a man from Śrāvastī. One day, after quarreling with her mother-in-law, she fled back to her native country.
On the road, she encountered Aniruddha and requested to travel together; Aniruddha consented, and they proceeded together.
Later, her husband caught up with them and asked, "For what reason have you fled with my wife? He then struck Aniruddha nearly [to death].

Upon hearing of this death, the Buddha established a precept: if one makes a prior agreement to travel together with others, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense for every boundary segment traversed according to the number of people.
If there is no village and one travels through an uninhabited area, it is a *pāyattika* offense for every ten *li*; if it is less than ten *li*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one travels together with a village-dweller within the same boundary, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

For a *bhikṣuṇī*, a *śikṣamāṇā*, and others, the offense for such an act is likewise a *duṣkṛta*. However, there is no offense if there was no prior agreement, if it was necessary to go there for the sake of safety, or if one was constrained by force.
If there is a place where a monk is offered a single meal, a monk who is not ill should accept only one meal. If he exceeds this, it is an *pāyattika* offense.
If there is no monastic dwelling in a village, and laypeople construct a dwelling for the monks for those coming and going...
The Buddha had always permitted eating only one meal a day. When the group of six bhikṣus arrived at a place where food was being served, they accepted food repeatedly and did not leave.

The lay devotees criticized and disparaged them. Upon hearing this, the Buddha established a precept. Later, Śāriputra became ill; he forced himself to eat only one meal, and his illness consequently worsened.
The Buddha then made an exception for sick bhikṣus. However, if one who is not ill accepts more than one meal, it constitutes an offense for every swallow.
*Pāyattika*. If, after having finished eating, one further accepts undergarments, lamp oil, and so forth, it is an *dukkaṭa*.
The offense for a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this is the same. For *śikṣamāṇās* and others, it is likewise an *dukkaṭa*.
However, there is no offense if the donor retains the food, or if one receives food from that person on a subsequent day, or if there are obstructions on the road, or if one is held by force.
Offense:
If a bhikṣu eats in succession (at multiple locations), except at the remaining times, it is a pāyattika. The remaining times are: when one is ill, and when robes are being distributed;
these are called the remaining times.
The Buddha, accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty followers, was traveling through the country of Ānāpinḍada.
There was a śramaṇa brahmin who, with a cart laden with food and drink, followed behind the Buddha, intending to provide offerings on days when no other offerings were made.
As time passed, there was not a single day that he failed to provide an offering. Eventually, Ānanda saw him and asked about his original intention, saying, "Now, as for this offering..."

It was too late to set up [the offerings]. Having been away from home for a long time, he wished to place food and drink on the road in his cart so that the Buddha and the Sangha might step over them with their feet as an act of offering. Ānanda stopped him and informed the Buddha on his behalf.
The Buddha permitted that they prepare gruel at dawn to provide for the assembly to eat. Later, when it was time for the invitation, the Brahmin again offered ghee and oil.
The Buddha permitted the offering of cakes to the assembly. Later, when the lay devotees heard of this, each of them sent offerings of rice gruel and cakes.
There was a high minister who prepared a meal and invited the monks; however, the monks had already become full after eating the delicious gruel and arrived at the minister's house.
They were unable to eat much. The ministers took offense at this, and the Buddha established a rule: one must not attend an invitation after having already eaten thick gruel.
Furthermore, on a day of a major festival when a musician invited the monks for a meal, many people brought rice, parched grain flour, and dried cakes to the Jetavana to offer to the Sangha.
After the monks had finished eating and were satiated, they went to the musician’s house to accept his invitation; however, they were unable to eat much.
The musicians also complained about this. The Buddha then established a precept:

if one has been invited to a meal by the Sangha in order of seniority, or invited individually, and on that day happens to have invitations from two places, one should relinquish one to another bhikṣu and accept the meal at one place oneself.
If one does not relinquish [the first] and eats successively at both, it is a *pāyattika*. If one does not relinquish the prior invitation and accepts a subsequent invitation, it is a *pāyattika*.
*Pāyattika*. If one does not relinquish a later invitation but accepts a prior invitation, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Furthermore, there was a sick bhikṣu who could not eat his fill in a single meal; he feared that eating a second time would constitute the offense of "successive meals" (*paryāya-bhojana*).

Also, there was a lay devotee who wished to provide offerings and donate robes, yet on that day he already had a prior engagement. Both cases were reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha granted an exception for them. This is the [allowance for] giving.

Regarding the time for robes: after the Saṃgha has completed the *pravāraṇā*, there is a period of one month if the *kaṭhina* robe-privilege has not been spread, and five months if the *kaṭhina* robe-privilege has been spread.
A bhikṣuṇī who violates this incurs the same offense; for śikṣamāṇās and others, it is all a *duṣkṛta*.

The remainder of the ninety *pāyattika* rules:
If a bhikṣu eats separately from the community, except at other times, it is a *pāyattika*. "Other times" refers to the time of illness and the time when robes are being offered.
"When making robes, when traveling on a journey, when traveling by boat, when the great assembly gathers, and when śramaṇas are being given alms—these are called 'other times.
Devadatta instructed others to harm the Buddha and further incited King Ajātaśatru to kill his father; thus his evil reputation spread."

[The Buddha] distributed [the food]. Because the offerings of profit and honor were cut off, he went with his five followers—Trayodaśa, Khaṇḍadravya, Kauṇḍinya, and Kālodāyin—to beg for alms from house to house. When the Buddha heard of this, he established a rule:
to eat in a separate group of four or more constitutes an offense. For a bhikṣuṇī who commits this, it is a pāyattika. Śikṣamāṇā...
For Māṇava and the others, it was all a *duṣkṛta* offense. Later, there was a sick bhikṣu who, at a place where food was being offered, was unable to eat.
There was another bhikṣu who, after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony was concluded and while he was making robes, did not dare to eat when various laypeople provided him with food.
Furthermore, there was another layperson who provided food along with a gift of robes, yet the bhikṣu still did not dare to eat. There were also various laypeople who... [acted] together.

A group of bhikṣus were traveling together on a road. When a householder offered them food, they did not dare to eat it and instead entered a village to beg for alms, where they were robbed by bandits.
It was the same when they were traveling by boat. Once, a large assembly of bhikṣus was wandering and arrived at a small village.
A lay devotee prepared food, but the bhikṣus did not dare to eat it. There was a sister of King Bimbisāra who wished to become a śramaṇa of the non-Buddhist sect;
the king ordered her to enter Jetavana to provide a meal, yet the assembly did not dare to accept it. These preceding circumstances were all reported to the Buddha.
The Buddha granted exemptions for both cases. Regarding the term "śramaṇa," it refers here to non-Buddhist śramaṇas.

If there is a valid reason or circumstance, one should rise and inform the assembly before receiving food in accordance with the order of seniority. To enter and eat without having informed the assembly constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If there are four or five people, they should be divided into two groups; entering to eat in this manner is without offense.
If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson and is offered cakes, parched grain flour, or cooked rice, and the bhikṣu requires them, he may accept two or three bowls.
If a monk who is not ill takes more than two or three bowls of food, carries it into the monastery,
and does not share it with the other monks, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
A certain woman returned to her parents' home and was preparing food as alms for a begging bhikṣu.

While she was cooking, a messenger arrived from her husband's family to take her back. The woman said, "I will go with you once I have finished preparing this meal. As the begging bhikṣus continued to arrive one after another, the woman was unable to leave.
Her husband became angry and took another wife. Furthermore, there was a merchant who prepared food while traveling on the road.
When a mendicant bhikṣu arrived, he gave his own food to him. When another mendicant bhikṣu arrived, he gave away all that remained.
He then prepared food once more. His companion had departed earlier because of the delay; that merchant, traveling later, was plundered by bandits.
The Buddha heard of this and therefore established a rule: if one receives more than three bowls of food when not ill, and then exits that gate, it is a *pāyattika* offense.

If one steps with one foot across the threshold and then stops, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. Whenever encountering food, one must ask whether it is food for returning women or food for merchants on the road;
if it is such food, one may receive one, two, or three bowls and carry it back to share.
When other bhikṣus are eating, one must inform the other bhikṣus: "In such-and-such a place there is food from a woman returning home and food from merchants.
I have already taken back one bowl; you may go and take back two bowls. Or he may say:
"I have already taken back two bowls; you may go and take back one bowl. Or he may say: "I have already taken back three bowls; you..."
If one goes to that place to eat and it is not permissible to take food back, yet one asks for food to take home or for food for a merchant, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one does not share [the food] with other bhikṣus, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. For a bhikṣuṇī who commits this, it is a *pāyattika*.
For śikṣamāṇās and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*. If a sick bhikṣu receives more than is permitted, [it is not an offense].
If one personally delivers [the food] to the monastery, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu, having finished his meal or having accepted an invitation, eats while not performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (remaining-food) rite,
it is a *pāyattika*.

The Buddha was staying at Jetavana. He taught the practice of eating a single meal and praised this practice of eating a single meal. The bhikṣus, filled with faith and joy, adopted the practice of eating a single meal.
Some ate gruel, some ate rice, parched grain, cakes, and the like; others drank thin gruel or took medicine, yet they would eat only once.

Because they could not eat much and did not reach satiety, their bodies became emaciated and haggard. The Buddha then permitted them to eat until full while remaining seated in one posture. Once they were full...

After having eaten, if they encountered rice, parched grain, cakes, or the like, they did not dare eat further; their bodies thus became emaciated. The Buddha then permitted eating again after the single meal.
However, the sick bhikṣus were unable to eat their fill while remaining seated for one sitting. The Buddha then permitted eating at intervals.
They gave the remainder to those who attended to them, and the attendants also ate at intervals. Furthermore, there were other bhikṣus...

The Buddha returned from his almsround carrying the food he had received; he shared his portion with the bhikṣus. When the bhikṣus had finished eating their fill, they did not dare eat more and threw it away.
The Buddha, knowing this, taught them the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the practice of leftover food). As for the *khalupaścādbhakti*:
holding the food in one's hand, one says to a bhikṣu, "Venerable sir, I have already eaten my fill; know this and look upon this. That bhikṣu should...
Having taken a small amount of food, he said to the bhikṣu, "I have finished eating; you take this and eat it.
One who performs the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the ritual of leftover food) in this manner does not commit an offense.

Furthermore, there was a gluttonous bhikṣu who ate whenever he encountered food, neither knowing whether he had eaten enough or not, nor whether the food was considered leftover or not. The Buddha then established the precept regarding the non-performance of *khalupaścādbhakti*.

Regarding the rule for eating: each swallow constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. However, there are exceptions: if one prepares food for another; if one knows that another has already finished eating and yet prepares food for them;
if one holds the food with one's own hand; if one causes a *kappiyakāraka* (a pure person) to hold the food; if one prepares it in the presence of a *kappiyakāraka*;

or if one covers good food with inferior food while preparing it—in all these cases, it is a *dukkaṭa*. This also applies when a bhikṣu accepts the "remaining-food" (*atirittabhojana*) procedure from another.
If one takes it all away, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and others, those who commit this offense are likewise guilty of a *duṣkṛta*.
If a sick person does not perform the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual of leaving food), and eats the remains of that sick person's meal without having performed the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta*, there is no offense.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has already finished his meal, should, having been invited, persistently offer food to him without performing the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the formal rite for leftover food),
saying, "Venerable sir, please take this food," and does so for no other reason than with the desire to cause the other to commit an offense,
it is a *pāyattika*.
A certain bhikṣu was greedy for food and never satisfied. Another bhikṣu admonished him, and he harbored resentment in his heart.

Later, when they encountered food together, [the resentful bhikṣu] knew that the one who had previously admonished him had already finished his meal. Without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of declaring one has finished eating), he urged the other to eat.

When the one who had been admonished ate it, the first bhikṣu then turned around and reviled him, saying, "You are greedy for food. The other asked, "Did you know that I had already finished my meal when you made me eat?"
He replied, "I knew it. He was asked again, "Did you do this intentionally, knowing [it was improper]? He replied, "I knew it. The assembly all rebuked him.
When the Buddha heard of this, he established the rule: if one knows that another has already finished eating and yet encourages them to eat more, both parties commit a *pāyattika* offense.

If one gives food to someone who has not finished eating, or transfers it to another person, or if the recipient performs the ritual for leftover food (*khalupaṭiggahaṇa*) before eating, then the giver is at fault.
It is a *duṣkṛta*. If one does not know that the other has already finished eating, and gives [food] while perceiving them as not having finished eating, there is no offense.
For bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and others, an offense committed is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu eats food at an improper time, it is a pāyattika offense.
The two bhikṣus Nanda and Upananda entered the city to watch a festival with music and performances;
the laypeople there provided them with food and drink, and they did not return until dusk. Furthermore, Kālodāyin went out for alms late in the evening and encountered a pregnant woman.
He opened the door. It happened to be a day of thunder and lightning; he caught a brief glimpse of his face and, startled, thought it was a ghost, whereupon he suffered a miscarriage.

The Buddha heard of this and therefore established the rule. "At an improper time" refers to the period from after midday until the appearance of the morning light. If it is an improper time and one perceives it as such, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If it is an improper time but one suspects it is the proper time, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If it is an improper time but one perceives it as the proper time, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Duskṛta. If one perceives it as the improper time when it is actually the proper time, it is a duṣkṛta. If one suspects it is the improper time when it is actually the proper time, it is a duṣkṛta.

If one eats at the improper time, or consumes a seven-day medicine after the seven days have passed, it is a pāyattika. If one consumes a lifetime medicine without a cause or necessity, it is a duṣkṛta.

For a bhikṣuṇī who commits this offense, it is a pāyattika. Śikṣamāṇā... [offense].* *Note: The text appears to be an excerpt from a Vinaya code concerning the rules on eating at improper times (vikālabhojana) and the consumption of medicines.*

For Māṇavas and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta* offense. If a sick person requires gruel while taking emetic or purgative medicine and the sun has already passed its meridian, one should boil barley so that the husks are not broken;
drinking the strained broth in this manner constitutes no offense.
If a bhikṣu eats leftover food that has been stored overnight, it is a pāyattika offense.
When the Venerable Kāla was begging for alms, he thought to himself: "Why must I undergo the exhaustion and suffering of entering the city to beg for food every single day?
From now on, I shall set aside the remainder of what I have eaten to keep for tomorrow; and the remainder of tomorrow's meal, I shall set aside for the day after."

One day, while the various bhikṣus were at the time of the morning meal or the midday meal, they did not see Kāla. Upon inquiry, they learned of this. Having heard of it, the Buddha established this rule:
if one has stored food and perceives it as such, it is a *pāyattika* offense. If one has stored food but suspects it is not stored, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one has not stored food but perceives it as stored, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one has not stored food but suspects it is stored, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one has stored food but perceives it as not stored, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī commits this offense, it is a pāyattika; for śikṣamāṇās and others, it is equally a duṣkṛta.
If there is food remaining, she may give it to her parents, to those who have built a stūpa, or to those who have built a dwelling, and then [go out to] beg for alms as a bhikṣuṇī.
There is no offense in begging for food from that person.
If a bhikṣu, without having received it, places food or medicine in his mouth—except for water and tooth-sticks—he commits a pāyattika.

A certain bhikṣu made a vow to always practice alms-gathering. When he went into the city and saw householders performing sacrifices for the deceased, he did not accept food from others but took the leftover offerings himself and ate them.
When the community saw this, they criticized and disparaged him. The Buddha heard of this and therefore established a regulation.
In all cases of eating, one must receive food from another person; if one takes it oneself, it constitutes theft, and therefore this rule was established.
As for medicinal substances—such as clarified butter, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar—if a bhikṣuṇī violates this rule, it is a pāyattika offense. The same applies to śikṣamāṇās and others.
In both cases, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one takes water or a tooth-stick without receiving them from another person, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu, being free from illness, seeks out fine food for himself, it is a *pāyattika*.
Bhadanta, he once asked a merchant for fine food. The merchant asked, "Venerable sir, what illness do you have?
He replied, "I have no illness; I simply desire it. The merchant said, "We toil at our livelihood and yet find it difficult even to obtain this;
how much more so for one who has left the household life? At that time, a bhikṣu who was begging for alms heard of this and censured him with reproach. The Buddha [heard of this].
Knowing [the rule], one establishes it: if one seeks and obtains [the item], one commits a *pāyattika* offense; if one does not obtain it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

For a *bhikṣuṇī* or a *śikṣamāṇā* who commits this, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*. If one begs for the sake of illness, or begs for the sake of a sick person, or obtains it without begging, there is no offense.
"If a bhikṣu gives food with his own hand to male or female followers of external paths, it is a pāyattika offense.
While the Buddha was traveling with the bhikṣus on the road, people prepared an offering and obtained many cakes.

The Buddha instructed Ānanda to distribute them among the community of monks; when there were still some remaining, he further instructed him to distribute them to beggars. Among them was a naked ascetic...
The daughter of a certain man possessed a beautiful appearance. By chance, two cakes became stuck together; she gave them away without realizing it.

When the assembly learned that this woman alone had received two cakes, they began to mock Ānanda, suggesting he had feelings for her. Furthermore, a certain brahmin who was there obtaining food encountered a physiognomist on the road.
The brahmin asked him where he had come from, and the man replied, "I have come from the place of the shaven-headed householder. The physiognomist—
"You said you received food from him; why do you mock him? The brahmin explained the circumstances. Upon hearing this, the Buddha established the rule:
"To give with one's hand and eat [the food so given] constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. To give and not receive it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
To intend to give but not actually give it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. If a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, or others commit this, they all incur the same offense."
It is a *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense if one places it on the ground to give, or if one causes another to give, or if it is forcibly seized by power.

If a bhikṣu, having previously accepted an invitation, goes to another household for a meal before or after the [formal] meal without informing another bhikṣu—except at other times—it is a *pāyattika*.
"Other times" refers to: when one is ill, when making robes, or when robes are being distributed. This is what is meant.

On another occasion, a certain householder prepared a vegetarian feast for Baddhananda and invited the community of monks as well. The assembly of monks all arrived, but when the time came, no food was served.
When they inquired about this, he replied, "I must wait for Baddhananda to arrive. Baddhananda ate beforehand and only went there afterward.
Other families did not arrive until after midday had passed; although the assembly received food, they were not satiated.
Furthermore, a high minister sent an envoy with fresh fruit to distribute among the community of Bhaddanta. After Bhaddanta had finished eating it himself, he went to other families.

When he returned, the day had already passed midday, and the assembly could not eat. The Buddha, knowing the cause, established a rule: "After having accepted an invitation, [one must eat] before midday."
Regarding eating after the [proper] meal time: it was not permitted to visit other households. Later, when there was a great invitation for the community, no one dared to go.
The Buddha then granted permission to go only after entrusting the matter to another bhikṣu. Later, there was a sick bhikṣu who first entrusted his affairs to someone in the city.
When it came to preparing soup, rice, and so forth, [the monks] did not dare to go. The Buddha permitted them to go without having made an announcement.

When monks needed utensils for making robes and wished to enter the city to fetch them, they did not dare to go. During the time of robe-offerings, when monks had no robes and wished to enter the city to beg for them, they likewise did not dare to go.
The Buddha permitted both cases of going without an announcement. "Before the meal" is self-evident.

Regarding the "initial departure": this refers to the time from when one first leaves until the mealtime. Regarding the "one who eats later": this refers to the time from the mealtime until midday. As for "entrusting another bhikṣu":
one should inform that person of the destination one intends to go to so that the community may know; there is no need to wait for them before eating.

If, after entrusting someone, one returns midway and then wishes to go again, one must entrust another. If one had entrusted someone to go to a certain place, but subsequently goes elsewhere, [one must likewise entrust another].
In such a case, one should go after having given further instructions. If one goes without giving instructions, except during other [permitted] times, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one intends to leave but turns back before exiting the gate, it is a *dukkaṭa*. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this offense, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is likewise a *dukkaṭa*.
If a bhikṣu sits down forcefully in a household where there is treasure while they are eating, it is a pāyattika.
Kāḷudāyin, being mutually infatuated with a long-time acquaintance—a laywoman who was an upāsikā—went to her house one day and sat down.
When her husband asked, "What do you need? she replied, "I need food. Her husband then sent [her some].
The wife gave him food. He ate it and still did not leave. Although her husband repeatedly sent him away, he would not go.

The husband spoke in anger, saying, "I am leaving; you may stay behind and do whatever you wish. When the bhikṣu begging for alms heard this, he felt resentment and reproach. Upon returning, he reported the matter to the Buddha, who therefore established this precept:
"To eat" means that a man takes a woman as his food, and a woman takes a man as her food; it refers to the sexual union of men and women.
Each receives and enjoys it as food. "Jeweled finger" refers to female beauty, and also includes carnelian, agate, gold, silver, and so forth.
If one sits down forcibly and does not leave, it is a *pāyattika*. If one is blind but not deaf, or deaf but not blind, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one stands rather than sitting, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If a *bhikṣuṇī* commits this offense, it is a *pāyattika*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*. If there is treasure, one may sit provided that it is within arm’s reach or at the threshold.
If one has a companion in the same place, one may sit. Or, if one is held by force, or falls to the ground due to a medical ailment, in all such cases there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place within a household where there are valuables, it is a pāyattika offense.

Because the Buddha had permitted sitting within arm’s reach [of the door] or at the doorway, Kālodāyin sat behind the door-panel and conversed with a laywoman (upāsikā) who was observing the upoṣadha fast.
A bhikṣu seeking alms saw this and, feeling reproachful and suspicious, informed the Buddha.
Therefore, it is prescribed: if one sits in a secluded place, it is a *pāyattika*. If one is blind but not deaf, and so forth, it is as stated above.
For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this offense, it is a *pāyattika*; for a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one can reach the door by stretching out the hand and is not sitting in a secluded place, or if one has a companion sitting in the same spot, or if one is acting under duress, there is no offense.
If one is holding something, or if illness causes one to fall to the ground, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in an open space, it is a pāyattika. This also concerns Kālodāyin;
because of the previous Buddha’s prohibition against sitting in a secluded place, he subsequently sat alone with a laywoman (upāsikā) who was observing the poṣadha.
A man sat in the open air and conversed with a woman. A bhikṣu who was begging for alms saw this and criticized it. He reported the matter to the Buddha, who therefore established this rule:
To sit alone with a woman in the open air constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. This applies equally if she is blind but not deaf, and so forth.
If a bhikṣuṇī commits this, it is a *pāyattika*. For a śikṣamāṇā and others, it is an *dukkaṭa*. If there is a companion present, there is no offense.
There is no offense: if one is constrained by force, or falls to the ground due to the onset of illness, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu, "Venerable sir, come with me to the village;
I shall give you food," yet that bhikṣu ultimately does not instruct [the other] to give food to this bhikṣu, but instead says, "I will sit or talk with you in one place."
"I do not find pleasure [in that]. I alone find pleasure in sitting alone and speaking to myself; for this reason and no other. If one uses such means to dismiss another, it is a *pāyattika*.
Vaddhananda first quarreled with a certain bhikṣu and harbored a grudge in his heart; at a later time, he enticed that bhikṣu.
He said, "Follow me to the city and I shall give you food. The bhikṣu believed him, and so they went together into the city.
Upon reaching a place where there was no food, they walked around it once; as the day was drawing to a close, he said to that bhikṣu, "You are a most wicked person.
Because of you, I too have been unable to obtain food. You should leave at once. I—
"I find no pleasure sitting or speaking with you; I find pleasure sitting and speaking alone. That bhikṣu departed and went directly to a house where food was being served.
When that bhikṣu returned to Jeta’s Grove, the sun had already passed its meridian, and he did not obtain any food.
The Buddha heard of this and therefore established a rule: if one sends [a monk] away to a place where he is no longer within range of seeing or hearing, it is a *pāyattika*.

If one sends him from a place where he can hear to a place where he can see, or from a place where he can see to a place where he can hear, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this offense, it is a *pāyattika*.
For śikṣamāṇās and others, it is equally a duṣkṛta offense. However, there is no offense if one gives food and sends them away;

nor is there an offense if they are sent away due to illness and one brings the food to the monastery to give it to them. Furthermore, there is no offense if they have broken their precepts, their views, or their conduct;
or if they have been formally censured by the community, or have been expelled, or are subject to expulsion; or if they were previously denied food and one employs a skillful means to send them away.
[If one] commits [this offense], it is a *dukkaṭa*. If one has already previously consented to eat, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

If a monk receives medicine offered during a four-month invitation, he should accept it provided he is not ill; if he accepts it beyond that limit, except for a regular invitation, [he commits an offense].
Inviting [for a specific meal], inviting [for a portion], or inviting for as long as one lives constitutes a *pāyattika*.
Mahānāma of the Śākya clan invited the Saṃgha to receive medicine. Out of respect for the elders, he gave the best [medicines] to them;
he gave them to those who asked and also to those who did not ask. The group of six [monks] went to his house to seek medicine. The man...

"To say 'it exists' when it is given as a gift, and to say 'it does not exist' when it is bought and given," the group of six monks then criticized him for having a heart of attachment and for speaking falsely.

The man’s resolve to give was consequently broken, and he ceased providing medicine. When the Buddha heard of this, he established the rule. "Four months" refers to the four months of the summer retreat.
To receive [medicine] after the four months have passed constitutes receiving it late. Later, there were sick bhikṣus who did not dare to receive it late.

Because [the previous rule] concerned medicine, the phrase "free from illness" was added. Later, there was a lay devotee who, without limiting the number of months, constantly invited [monks] to receive medicine.
Mahānāman stopped this and subsequently invited others to give. Some brought medicine to the monastery to distribute it; others invited [monks] to receive medicine for as long as they lived.
In all cases, because the period exceeded four months, they did not dare to accept it and reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha [said]:
Each case is explained in detail: if a bhikṣuṇī commits this offense, it is a pāyattika; for śikṣamāṇās and others, it is equally a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣu goes to view an army formation, except on other occasions due to specific causes and conditions, it is a pāyattika.
King Prasenajit, due to a rebellion among his subjects, personally led an army on a campaign. The group of six bhikṣus went to observe him. When the King saw them, he was displeased;
he then sent a package of stone honey as an offering to the World-Honored One, entrusting it with the instruction:

"On my behalf, pay homage to the World-Honored One and inquire after his well-being. The World-Honored One, knowing the circumstances, established a precept: to see [such a person] constitutes a *pāyattika* offense, as does the preparation for such an act.
If one intends to go but has not yet gone, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one has gone but has not yet seen [the army], it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If, while on the road, one encounters a marching army and should avoid it but does not avoid it, it is a *duṣkṛta*. Later, there were two generals who wished to see the bhikṣu and sent someone to invite him;
the Buddha permitted him to go. Therefore, it is said: "except in cases of timely causes and conditions. As for a bhikṣuṇī who commits this offense: [it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*].
It is a *pāyattika*. For *śikṣamāṇās* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu has a legitimate reason, he is permitted to stay within an army for two or three nights; if he exceeds this, it is a *pāyattika*.
The group of six bhikṣus had a reason to stay overnight in an army camp. When a layperson saw them, he criticized and disparaged them.
Consequently, the Buddha established a rule: staying for more than three nights is not permitted. If one stays for three nights and the dawn appears, it is a *pāyattika* offense.

If one moves from a place where one can see [the army] to a place where one can only hear it, or from a place where one can hear it to a place where one can see it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. For a bhikṣuṇī who commits this, it is a *pāyattika*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*. If one is constrained by difficult circumstances, there is no offense.

If a bhikṣu stays among an army for two or three nights, or at any time observes military arrays and combat, or observes the strength and power of the marching troops' elephants and horses, it is a *pāyattika*.
The group of six bhikṣus had a reason to go among the army and stayed for three nights. While there, they watched the fighting. One man was wounded by an arrow;
he was wrapped in his robes and carried back. When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and disparaged them. The Buddha heard of this and established a rule:
to go and see [the fighting] constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; to go but not see it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; and to employ the means to go but not yet... [go].
In the past, it was a *duṣkṛta*; for a bhikṣuṇī who commits it, it is a *pāyattika*;
for śikṣamāṇās and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one is constrained by force.
If a bhikṣu drinks alcohol, it is a pāyattika offense.
The Venerable Sāgata frequently went to the house of a brahmin to stay overnight and subdued a venomous dragon within that dwelling.
On one occasion, the King of Kauśāmbī saw him and conceived great reverence for him. On another day, the king prepared a meal for the Venerable One. The Venerable One...
He received food and drank much black liquor; on his way back, he fell to the ground and vomited.

When the Buddha heard of this, he rebuked him, saying, "If you cannot now subdue a small dragon, how much less a great dragon? Thereupon, he established a precept: for any monk who drinks an intoxicant capable of causing intoxication, it is a *pāyattika*;
if he drinks that which is incapable of causing intoxication, it is a *dukkaṭa*. [The same applies to] bhikṣuṇīs.
One who commits this offense incurs a *pāyattika*. For a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*. If one uses alcohol to treat an illness, there is no offense.
If a *bhikṣu* plays and sports in water, it is a *pāyattika*.
The group of seventeen bhikṣus were bathing in the Ajiravatī River, sporting therein:
going with and against the current, surfacing and submerging, or splashing one another, and so forth. At that time, King Prasenajit and Queen Mallikā saw them from atop a terrace.
The King said, "Look at those for whom you serve. The Queen replied, "These are..."
Having left home at a young age, he had not long been in the Buddha-dharma;

therefore, he quickly dispatched a messenger to Jetavana to inquire after the World-Honored One and present a package of rock honey, reporting the preceding matter in detail. Upon hearing this, the Buddha established a rule:
"Whoever, while in the water, gives rein to their own desires and engages in any kind of play or sport, commits a *pāyattika* offense. This applies whether using curd-milk or..."
If one plays with sour wine, barley juice, or similar substances, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense for all. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, it is a *pāyattika*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*. If there is a valid reason for entering the water and it is not for the purpose of play, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu tickles another with his fingers, it is a pāyattika.
Among the group of six bhikṣus, one struck a member of the group of seventeen bhikṣus until he died.
Because the Buddha heard of this, he established the rule: whether using a finger or a toe to tickle, it is in all cases a pāyattika.
If one strikes or tickles another with a staff, a whisk handle, or similar objects, both parties commit a *duṣkṛta* offense. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if the contact causes the other to wake from sleep, or if the contact was accidental.
If a bhikṣu does not accept admonition, it is a pāyattika offense.
When the bhikṣu Chanda was about to commit an offense and did not comply with the admonitions of other bhikṣus, the Buddha heard of this and established the rule:
"If one knows for oneself that what one has done is wrong, yet does not comply with admonition, it is a pāyattika offense. [The rule continues: "If one does not know for oneself..."
To act contrary [to the admonition] and not follow the advice constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, it is a *pāyattika*.
For *śikṣamāṇās* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*. If an ignorant person comes to offer advice that is itself incorrect, one should reply:
"You should ask your preceptor (*upādhyāya*) to learn the method of advising; only then may you come to advise me. If...
If spoken in jest or laughter, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu causes another bhikṣu to feel fear, it is a pāyattika.
When the Venerable Kanaśvara was attending upon the Buddha, the Buddha went out from his room one night to practice walking meditation during the first watch of the night.
Having already invited the Buddha to return to his room, the Buddha remained silent. When the latter part of the night was nearly over, he invited the Buddha again to return to his room;
the Buddha remained silent once more. Nāpa thought to himself, "I shall terrify the Buddha so that he will return to his room.
He then turned his back, put on a hideous garment, and assumed the form of a non-human being. Uttering a terrifying voice, he said, "Śramaṇa, I am a ghost! The Buddha replied, "Know this..."
The mind of this foolish person is also evil; therefore, a precept is established.

Whenever one uses the six kinds of objects—form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena—to terrify another person, if the other person knows, sees, or hears it, it is an *pāyattika* offense.
If the other person does not know, see, or hear it, it is an *dukkaṭa* offense. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, it is an *pāyattika* offense.

For śikṣamāṇās and others, it is equally a duṣkṛta offense. However, if there is a reason for not reporting it, or if one lacks the intention to cause alarm to others, there is no offense in either case.

If a bhikṣu bathes once every half-month, it should be accepted by a bhikṣu who is not ill. If he bathes more frequently than that, except during the remaining times, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika).
The remaining times are: the hot season, the time of illness, the time of labor, the time of wind and rain, and the time of traveling on a journey; these are called the remaining times.
King Bimbisāra possessed a pond where he always permitted the bhikṣus to bathe. One night, after midnight, the group of six bhikṣus entered the pond to bathe.
At that time, the king, together with his court ladies, went to the pond; hearing voices from within, he asked, "Who is there?"
The attendants said, "This is a bhikṣu. The king ordered them not to be alarmed and let him go. The group of six bhikṣus bathed for a long time until the dawn light appeared;
the king had not yet finished his bath when they departed. When the Buddha heard of this, he established the precept:

"A bhikṣu may bathe once every half-month. If he exceeds one [bath], it is a pāyattika offense. If water is poured over half the body, it is also a pāyattika offense. If he makes an effort to leave..."
If one has not yet departed, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. Regarding "the hot season": this refers to the forty-five days of spring and the first month of summer;
in the land of this region, it corresponds to the first day of the third month until the fifteenth day of the fifth month. "One who is ill" may be understood accordingly.
"One who performs work" refers to one who engages in various tasks involving physical labor. "A traveler on the road" means even as far as half a *yojana*.
It was so. These bhikṣus were afraid and did not dare to bathe, so they informed the Buddha. The Buddha granted them an exemption.
For a bhikṣuṇī who commits this offense, it is a pāyattika; for śikṣamāṇās and others, it is equally a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣu, when not ill, lights a fire on open ground for the purpose of warming his body— whether lighting it himself or instructing another to light it—
except during other exceptional circumstances, it is a pāyattika offense.
The group of six bhikṣus wished to kindle a fire to warm their bodies. They said to one another, "In the presence of the elder, we cannot speak as we please.
They immediately went outside into the open air, gathered wild wood, and lit a fire to warm themselves.
Within a decaying tree nearby was a venomous snake; driven out by the smoke from the fire, it emerged. Seeing this, the assembly all fled.
He threw firebrands about, setting the lecture hall ablaze. The Buddha, knowing this, established the rule:

"Whoever, on open ground, burns grass, wood, cow dung, or any other fire to scorch their body, commits a *pāyattika* offense. If they are half-burnt by the fire, or if they throw themselves into the fire, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If they burn charcoal, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense. This applies unless one has first informed those nearby."
If a person knowingly looks at this [naked body], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If a *bhikṣuṇī* commits it, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
For *śikṣamāṇās* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*. This excludes cases involving special circumstances, such as when one is ill and naturally uses fire to warm the body.
Nor is there an offense if one instructs another to light it. There is no offense if there is a specific reason that necessitates lighting a fire.
If a bhikṣu conceals another bhikṣu’s robes, bowl, sitting mat, or needle case—whether he conceals them himself or instructs another to do so.
Down to those who do so in jest, it is a *pāyattika*.
The group of seventeen bhikṣus placed their robes, bowls, sitting mats, and needle-cases on one side and paced back and forth, waiting for the time of the meal to arrive.
The group of six bhikṣus, seeking to mock them, took the robes, bowls, and other items from behind and hid them. When the time arrived...

The group of seventeen bhikṣus took their robes, bowls, and other belongings, but were unable to obtain them. Other bhikṣus observed this and reported it to the Buddha, who consequently established the rule:
"To conceal [another's property] is a pāyattika offense. To employ means with the intent to conceal, yet fail to conceal it, is a duṣkṛta offense.
The same penalty applies to one who instructs another to do so. If a bhikṣuṇī commits this, it is a pāyattika offense; for śikṣamāṇās and others, it is likewise a duṣkṛta."
If one knows for certain that it belongs to such-and-such a person and takes it up out of a desire to protect it;

or if a bhikṣu, because of his habit of being conceited about his storage, takes it up and stores it as a disciplinary measure for that person; or if he lends his robe to someone and the other does not take care of it.
If one takes up an item for fear of losing it, or if there is danger because of such items as robes or alms bowls, and one takes them to hide away,
there is no offense in either case.
If a bhikṣu makes a formal gift (*śuddha-dāna*) of his robes to a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī.
If one subsequently wears [a robe] without asking the owner, it is a *pāyattika*.

Regarding the six groups of bhikṣus who, having given a robe to a bhikṣu with whom they were close and intimate, later took it back and wore it themselves without informing the original owner—the Buddha heard of this and established the rule.
There are two kinds of pure giving (*śuddha-dāna*): first, true pure giving; second, indirect pure giving (*parivartaka-śuddha*). True pure...

Regarding the donor: he says, "This is my extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*) which has not yet been purified; now, for the sake of purification, I give it to you, Venerable Sir. This is a true purification (*bhūta-visuddhi*).
Regarding the indirect purification by transfer (*paramparā-visuddhi*): he says, "This is my extra robe which has not yet been purified;
now, for the sake of purification, I give it to you, Venerable Sir. The recipient should speak as follows: "Listen, Venerable Sir. You, Venerable Sir, possess such..."
"This extra robe has not yet been purified. Now, for the sake of purifying it for me, I accept it. Having accepted it, one should ask:
"To whom do you wish to give it? He should reply: "To so-and-so. The other should speak as follows:
"Venerable sir, you have this extra robe which has not been purified. Now, for the sake of purifying it for me, I accept it; having accepted it, I give it to so-and-so."
"O Bhikṣu, this robe belongs to such-and-such a bhikṣu. You shall guard and maintain it for his sake;
you may use it as you wish. Regarding "purifying through transfer": whether one informs the owner or not, one may take and wear it at will without offense.
However, if it is a true purification by gift (*viśuddha-dāna*), and one takes and wears it without informing the owner, it is a *pāyattika*. For a bhikṣuṇī who commits this, it is a [pāyattika]."
For a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu obtains a new robe, he must dye it to spoil its color in one of three ways: blue, black, or madder-brown.
If one obtains a new robe and wears it without having dyed it into one of the three types of discolored hues, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
When the six groups of bhikṣus wore white robes, laypeople saw them and criticized them, saying they were like kings or royal ministers.
The Buddha heard of this and established the rule: "new robe" does not refer only to a robe first made, but includes any robe first obtained from another person.
This refers to "new clothing. Regardless of the color of the garment one obtains, it must all be dyed with three types of discoloring agents:
blue with copper sulfate (t'ung-ch'ing), black with mixed mud, and madder-brown (*mó-lán*) with tree bark. To wear it without having dyed it to discolor it is a *pāyattika* offense;
to keep it without having dyed it to discolor it is a *dukkaṭa* offense. Furthermore, if the garment has not been dyed and is kept in the house of a layperson, it is likewise [an offense].
It is a *duṣkṛta*. For a bhikṣuṇī who commits it, it is a *pāyattika*. For śikṣamāṇās and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
If one possesses small items such as bags for robes, bowls, or sandals, bags for thread, or hand towels, and does not dye them [the required color], [it is an offense].
There is no offense.
If a bhikṣu intentionally takes the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika.
Kāḷudāyin, who did not like seeing crows, made a bamboo bow and shot them; many died. [The matter was reported to] the householder.
People saw this and criticized it with disdain. When the Buddha heard of it, he established a rule:
whether one kills by one's own hand or instructs another to kill—whether using a blade or an arrow, a tile or a stone, a pitfall or poison—it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If one employs the means to kill but does not actually kill, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, it is a *pāyattika*; for a *śikṣamāṇā*, [it is likewise].
In all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If there was no intent to kill and the injury was accidental, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu knowingly drinks or uses water that contains insects, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
The group of six bhikṣus took and drank water containing various insects. Those who saw this criticized and disparaged them. Consequently, the Buddha established a precept:
if there are insects in the water and one perceives that there are insects, it is a *pāyattika* offense. If there are insects in the water but one suspects they are not, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one knows that fermented rice wine, clear curd-liquor, barley juice, or similar liquids contain insects and drinks or uses them, it is a *pāyattika* offense. [This applies to] bhikṣuṇīs as well.
One who violates this incurs a *pāyattika*. For a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
If one does not know there are insects, or if one uses water that has been strained, there is no offense. If there are large insects, one should touch them with the hand to make them leave.
If a bhikṣu intentionally harasses another bhikṣu so that he experiences even a moment of displeasure, it is a pāyattika.
The group of seventeen went to the place of the group of six and asked, "Venerable sirs, how do you enter the first dhyāna, up to and including arhatship?
The group of six replied, "You yourselves claim to have attained the state of a superior person; you have committed a pārājika offense."
The group of seventeen monks caused great disturbance and confusion. They went to ask the Elder, who said they had not committed an offense. When the Buddha heard of this, he established the rule:
"If one intentionally causes another to be disturbed and speaks with clarity, it is a *pāyattika*. If one speaks but without clarity, [it is a *dukkaṭa*]."
It is a *duṣkṛta*. For a bhikṣuṇī who commits it, it is a *pāyattika*. For śikṣamāṇās and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
If one does not act intentionally, or if the fact is indeed as it appears, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), conceals it, he commits a pāyattika.
Upananda was on intimate terms with a certain bhikṣu; although that bhikṣu repeatedly committed grave offenses, Upananda would not let him speak of them to others.
Later, Upananda quarreled with that bhikṣu, who then spoke to other people, saying: "Upananda has committed such and such an offense."
"I must not speak of this to others. Because the Buddha heard of this, he established the rule. "Gross offenses" (*sthūlātyaya*) refer to *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If a bhikṣu knows that another bhikṣu has committed a gross offense, and speaks of it after having known it during the morning meal, or speaks of it after having known it during the afternoon meal, or speaks of it after having known it during the middle watch of the night or the final watch of the night, in each case it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If he intends to speak but does not speak, and the time reaches the appearance of the dawn light, it is a [pāyattika].
*Pāyattika*. If one conceals other offenses, it is a *duṣkṛta*. To conceal one's own *sthūlātyaya* offense, it is an additional *duṣkṛta*.
With the exception of monks and nuns, to conceal the *sthūlātyaya* offenses of *śikṣamāṇās* and others is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a nun who commits [this], it is a *pāyattika*; for *śikṣamāṇās* and others, it is equally a *duṣkṛta*. If one did not previously know [of the offense], there is no offense.
Regarding a grave offense, if one perceives it as not being a grave offense; or if one wishes to speak of it to others but there is no one to whom it can be told;
or if, upon speaking, there might be danger to life or danger to the holy life such that one does not dare to speak—there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu confers the full ordination upon one who has reached twenty years of age, it is proper.

If a bhikṣu knows that one has not yet reached twenty years of age and nevertheless confers the full ordination upon them, this person does not obtain the precepts. Because the other bhikṣus may censure him for his folly, it is a pāyattika offense.
In the city of Rājagṛha, there was a group of seventeen youths who had been close friends since childhood;

the eldest was seventeen years old and the youngest twelve. Encouraging one another, they all sought to leave the household life. The bhikṣus ordained them, allowing them to go forth and receive full ordination.
Because the youths were so young, they could not endure eating only one meal a day; at midnight, suffering from hunger, they wept.
He wept and begged for food. The Buddha heard this and declared that one who has not yet reached twenty years of age should not receive the full precepts (*mahāśramaṇa-saṃvara*).

This is because those under twenty are unable to endure cold and heat, hunger and thirst, violent winds, mosquitoes, gadflies, venomous insects, harsh words, and the various physical sufferings of the body;
furthermore, they are incapable of upholding the precepts. One should know that [the candidate] must have reached twenty years of age.

Only when one is first able to endure this is the precept established. If a preceptor confers the full ordination upon someone known to be less than twenty years of age, at the conclusion of the third *karmavācanā*, the preceptor commits a *pāyattika* offense;
at the conclusion of the second *karmavācanā*, the preceptor commits three *dukkaṭa* offenses.
When the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is completed, the preceptor incurs two *duṣkṛta* offenses; when the motion (*jñapti*) is completed, the preceptor incurs one *duṣkṛta* offense;

while the motion has not yet been completed, the preceptor incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. This applies even if he has merely initiated the preparatory effort for the motion, such as intending to assemble the community and so forth.
In both cases, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) was unaware, there is no offense. If the community of monks (*saṃgha*) knew [of the transgression], it is a *duṣkṛta*;
if they were unaware, there is no offense. If a bhikṣuṇī commits this, it is a *pāyattika*.

If one was previously unaware and merely accepted the words of the person receiving the precepts, or if there is testimony from a bystander, or if one trusts the account given by the parents, there is no offense. If, after having received the precepts, one has doubts, the Buddha—
It should be said that one must calculate the months of the pregnancy, including intercalary months; if they are complete, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that a matter of dispute has been settled according to the Dharma, should later re-raise it, it is a pāyattika.
The group of six bhikṣus engaged in disputes with other bhikṣus. After the dispute had been settled according to the Dharma, they initiated it again, saying:
"You did not observe well; your observation was not accomplished. You did not understand well; your understanding was not accomplished.

You did not settle well; your settlement was not accomplished. When the Buddha heard of this, he established a precept: if a matter of dispute has already been settled and one raises it again, and speaks so as to make it clear, it is a *pāyattika*.
If it is not clearly understood, it is a *duṣkṛta*. Once this dispute has been settled, if one further engages in other disputes or verbal abuse, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*.
Except for [disputes with] monks and nuns, if one initiates a dispute again after having committed an offense together with others, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a nun commits this, it is a *pāyattika*. For *śikṣamāṇās* and others, [the same applies].

In both cases, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one did not previously know [the person] but, having observed them, formed the perception that they were not [a thief], and the fact is indeed so, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu knows someone to be a companion of thieves and agrees to travel together with them, even as far as a village, it is a *pāyattika*.
There were certain bhikṣus who went to the city of Vaiśālī. At that time, there was a merchant who wished to evade customs duties and requested the Saṃgha to accompany him as companions.
Upon crossing the frontier, they were apprehended by the customs officials and brought before King Prasenajit.
The king asked the merchants, "Why have you not paid the taxes? What business does this śramaṇa have? They replied, "He traveled as a companion with us.

The king said, "By law, he should be put to death. [The merchants] pleaded, "Since he is also a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākya, let us rebuke him and send him away. The Buddha, knowing the situation, established this rule:
if one intends to go to a city or a village, for every path traveled, it is a pāyattika offense. If one travels even a single path...
If one goes halfway, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one travels through a desolate place where there are no villages, and reaches ten *li*, it is a *pāyattika*;
if it is less than ten *li*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one sets out but does not actually go, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If a *bhikṣuṇī* commits this offense, it is a *pāyattika*.
For *śikṣamāṇās* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*. If one did not previously know that they were thieves...
[This applies to] those who did not intend to travel together, or those who were constrained by force; in such cases, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu speaks thus: "I know that the Dharma taught by the Buddha is such that engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path," [he commits an offense].
That bhikṣu should admonish this bhikṣu, saying: "Venerable sir, do not speak such words. Do not slander the Blessed One; it is unwholesome to slander the Blessed One.
The Blessed One does not say such a thing. By means of countless skillful methods, the Blessed One has declared that the practice of sexual intercourse is a dharma that obstructs the path.
When that bhikṣu admonishes this bhikṣu and he persists in his refusal to relinquish [his position], that bhikṣu...
He should be admonished three times. Up to the third admonition, if he relinquishes [the view], it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a *pāyattika*.
When the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa gave rise to an evil view, saying, "I understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One:

engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path," the bhikṣus admonished him, but he was unwilling to relinquish it. They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha performed the formal motion (*jñapti*) for him.
The fourfold *karmavācanā*: To admonish him through censure so that he will relinquish [his position], one makes this formal announcement (*jñapti*): "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
This bhikṣu Ārliṭa speaks thus: 'I know that what the Buddha has taught—that engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the Path—is indeed so.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its ear, let the Saṃgha now perform a censure against the bhikṣu Ārliṭa, so that he may relinquish this."
This is the formal motion. Ārīṭa, do not speak such words. Do not slander the Blessed One; it is unwholesome to slander the Blessed One.
The Blessed One does not speak such words. By means of countless skillful methods, the Blessed One has declared that sexual desire is a dharma that obstructs the path.
To commit sexual misconduct is indeed to obstruct the path. This is the proclamation. Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This Ārīṭa...
"O Āḷavaka bhikṣu, you have spoken these words: 'I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha; engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path.
The Saṃgha now issues this formal admonition to you so that you may relinquish this matter. Āḷavaka, do not speak such words! Do not slander the World-Honored One!
It is unwholesome to slander the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One does not say such things; the World-Honored One has said countless times..."
As a skillful means, it has been said that sexual desire is a dharma that obstructs the Path. If one commits sexual misconduct, it constitutes an obstruction to the Path.
Which elders among you consent to the Saṃgha’s formal admonition of the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa so that he may relinquish this matter?
Those who consent remain silent; those who do not consent speak. This is the first *karmavācanā*. The second and third are recited in the same manner.
The Saṃgha has already consented to complete the formal admonition against Ariṣṭa; because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

Having performed the *karmavācanā* in this manner, the Buddha further established a precept: for anyone who commits an offense and does not relinquish it after three admonitions, one should likewise perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
After the initial motion (*jñapti*) has been made, one should say: "I have finished the motion."
[The motion] is concluded. There remains the formal act (*karmavācanā*). You should relinquish this; do not incur further offense by being rebuked by the community.
If you relinquish it, it is well. If you do not relinquish it, the first formal act shall be performed. Having performed the first formal act, one should say:
"I have completed the first *karmavācanā*. Two *karmavācanās* remain. You should relinquish this;
do not commit further offenses so as to be censured by the community. It would be well if you relinquish it. If you do not relinquish it, I shall perform the second *karmavācanā* for you.
When the second *karmavācanā* is finished, I shall say: 'I have completed the second *karmavācanā*. The remainder..."
One *karmavācanā* remains. You should relinquish this; do not commit further offenses so as to be rebuked by the community. It is well if you relinquish it.
If you do not relinquish it, after the third *karmavācanā* is completed, it is a *pāyattika*. If one relinquishes it after the *jñapti* has been made, it is one *duṣkṛta*.
If one relinquishes it after the first *karmavācanā*, it is two *duṣkṛtas*. If one relinquishes it after the second *karmavācanā*, it is three *duṣkṛtas*.
If the formal announcement (*jñapti*) has not yet been completed, or if one abandons it before the announcement is finished, in both cases there is one *duṣkṛta* offense.
If other monks, nuns, or others obstruct another monk while he is exhorting him by saying, "Do not exhort him," all incur a *duṣkṛta* offense.
