For a nun who commits this, it is a *pāyattika*; for a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
It is a *duṣkṛta*. If one relinquishes [the view] at the time of the first admonition, there is no offense.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that such a person has not yet performed the formal act (*karman*) and does not relinquish such an evil view, provides them with what they require, performs formal acts together with them, stays overnight with them, or converses with them, it is a *pāyattika*.
Āḷavaka did not relinquish his evil view. The monks then performed the formal act of *kamma* for him regarding his refusal to relinquish that evil view.
The group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) nevertheless provided him with what he required, shared in the communal *kamma*, and stayed and conversed with him. The Buddha, knowing this, established a rule:
"Regarding those who speak thus"—meaning they speak as those who hold the aforementioned evil views—"if the formal act has not yet been performed, the Saṃgha shall [perform it] for them."
If one raises [a point] but does not resolve it, and has not yet repented to be cleared of the offense—such persons, once their nature is known, should not be associated with.
To provide them with their necessities and so forth is also a category of wrong view; it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
There are two kinds of requisites provided: those of the Dharma and those of material wealth. Regarding those who dwell together, it does not matter whether one entered the house first or later;
if they are aware [of the offense], both commit an offense. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If they were unaware, there is no offense. This also applies if one was constrained by force.
There is no offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that a śrāmaṇera has spoken thus: "I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha;
engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path," that bhikṣu should admonish this śrāmaṇera, saying: "Do not speak such words. Do not slander the World-Honored One."

"Venerable Sir, it is unwholesome to slander the World-Honored One; the World-Honored One does not speak such words. By means of countless skillful methods, the World-Honored One has taught that engaging in sexual desire is a dharma that obstructs the path.
When those bhikṣus have thus admonished this śrāmaṇera and he still obstinately persists and does not relinquish [his position], those bhikṣus should admonish him up to three times.
If he relinquishes it after being admonished up to three times, that is well. If he does not relinquish it, those bhikṣus should say to him:
This śrāmaṇera said: "From this day forward, you are no longer a disciple of the Buddha. You must not say, 'The Buddha is my World-Honored One.
You may not follow other bhikṣus. While other śrāmaṇeras are permitted to stay with bhikṣus for two or three nights, you now have no such right.
Depart! Be gone! You need not remain here. If a bhikṣu knows that this person has been thus expelled...
...Māriya. To entice and keep [a novice] as one who shares a lodging with oneself constitutes a *pāyattika*.
Baddhananda had two novices: one named Kanna and one named Mahuka.
They engaged in impure conduct together and said to each other, "I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha; practicing sexual desire is not an obstacle to the path. All...
When the bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked them, but they did not desist. They reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha performed the *karma* of admonition (*anuvāda-karman*) for them as described above.
The śrāmaṇeras still did not desist. The Buddha then performed the *karman* of expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*) for them.

He had the two śrāmaṇeras stand in a place where they could be seen but not heard, and made the following proclamation: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. These two śrāmaṇeras have been rebuked by the Saṃgha."
[The Sangha] reprimands them; therefore, they do not relinquish their evil views. If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha grant its consent and listen:
the Sangha now performs the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman* (banishment) for these two śrāmaṇeras on account of their failure to relinquish evil views.
From this day forward, these two śrāmaṇeras must not say, "The Buddha is my World-Honored One," nor may they follow after other bhikṣus, as is permitted for [other] śrāmaṇeras.
"Monks, you two have stayed for two or three nights; you may not remain. Depart, go away, and do not dwell here.
This is the formal announcement. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen: these two śrāmaṇeras, having been rebuked by the Saṃgha, still do not relinquish their evil views.
The Saṃgha now performs the *niḥsaraṇīya-karman* (act of banishment) against them for not relinquishing their evil views. From this day forward, these..."
"O two śrāmaṇeras, you must not say, 'The Buddha is my World-Honored One. You should not follow after other bhikṣus.
While other śrāmaṇeras are permitted to stay with bhikṣus for two or three nights, you are not permitted to do so now. Depart! Go away!
You should not remain here. Which elders among you approve of the Saṃgha’s action regarding these two śrāmaṇeras who hold evil views?"
Those who approve of the formal act of suspension for not relinquishing evil views remain silent; those who do not approve should speak. This has been stated three times.

The Saṃgha has approved and completed the formal act of suspension for these two śrāmaṇeras for not relinquishing evil views. Because the Saṃgha has approved by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, knowing that the Saṃgha had already suspended these two śrāmaṇeras, proceeded to entice them away and keep them as their followers.
They lived and stayed together. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha further established a precept:

whether one keeps [a child] for oneself, gives it to another, seduces it oneself, or teaches others to do so, and so forth—it is all a *pāyattika*. For a bhikṣuṇī who commits this, it is a *pāyattika*;
for śikṣamāṇās and others, it is all a *duṣkṛta*. If one did not know [the situation] beforehand, there is no offense. If by force...
There is no offense for one who is constrained by force.
If a bhikṣu, when other bhikṣus are admonishing him in accordance with the Dharma, speaks as follows: "I will not train in this precept now."
If one interrogates other bhikṣus who possess wisdom and uphold the Vinaya, it is a pāyattika offense. However, if it is for the purpose of seeking knowledge or study, one should interrogate them.
When the bhikṣus were admonishing the bhikṣu Chanda according to the Dharma because of his unlawful conduct, he then said: "Now I..."
If one does not study this precept, one should question other wise bhikṣus who uphold the Vinaya. Because the Buddha heard of this, he established the rule:
if one explains it clearly, it is a *pāyattika*; if one explains it unclearly, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī who commits this offense, it is a *pāyattika*; for śikṣamāṇās and others, it is equally a *duṣkṛta*. If a bhikṣu is deluded and...
Because it was understood. That bhikṣu should instruct him to ask his upādhyāya or ācārya; he may then further study, inquire, and recite the sūtras.
If the one who offered the admonition was indeed not in accordance with the Dharma, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu, when the precepts are being recited, speaks thus: "Venerable sirs, what is the use of reciting these minor and trivial rules?
When these rules are recited, they cause people distress, shame, and doubt," and because he thus disparages the precepts, it is a pāyattika offense.
"O monks, when they have gathered in one place to recite the Vinaya, the group of six will say among themselves:
'Those monks are proficient in reciting the Vinaya; they will surely repeatedly bring up our offenses. We must go and stop them from reciting.'"

He then spoke these words: "Elder, what is the use of reciting these miscellaneous minor precepts? If you wish to recite, you should recite only the four pārājika rules and the thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣa rules;
the rest should not be recited. Why is this? If one recites them, it causes people to harbor doubts and suffer from anxiety.
Because the Buddha heard of this, he established the rule: if one speaks [the other rules] clearly, it is a pāyattika offense; if not clearly, it is a dukkaṭa offense."
It is a *duṣkṛta*. If one disparages the Abhidharma or other sūtras, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For a bhikṣuṇī who commits this offense, it is a *pāyattika*.
For śikṣamāṇās and others, it is a *duṣkṛta* in all cases.

If a bhikṣu, when the precepts are being recited, speaks thus: "Venerable sirs, I have only now learned that this dharma is contained within the Prātimokṣa Sūtra and has come down through the recitation of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra every half-month.

If other bhikṣus know that this bhikṣu has sat through two or three such recitations of the precepts, let alone more, then that bhikṣu is ignorant and lacks understanding; if he commits an offense, [he must undergo the appropriate discipline].
He should be dealt with according to the Dharma. Furthermore, he incurs the offense of ignorance. One should say: "Venerable sir, it is not for your benefit; you have gained nothing good.
When the precepts were being recited, you did not attend with a single mind nor listen to the Dharma with focused ears. Because of that ignorance, it is a *pāyattika*.
Among the group of six bhikṣus, there was one who, at the time of the recitation of the precepts, realized he had committed an offense.
Fearing that a pure bhikṣu might expose him, he went ahead to inform them, saying: "I have only now learned of this rule as it is recorded in the Sūtra of the Precepts."
[The offense] arises from the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* every half-month. When the bhikṣus observed his intention, they informed the Buddha.

The Buddha therefore established the rule. When he says, "I only know this now," his underlying meaning is that because he was unaware prior to this, he committed an offense; thus he wishes to avoid punishment.
The pure assembly knows this after the second or third time he sits within the recitation of the precepts, let alone if it occurs many times.

"What do you mean by saying 'only now do I know'? This is ignorance. Therefore, in addition to being dealt with according to the Dharma for the offense committed, you shall further incur the offense of ignorance.
Regarding the phrase 'you have gained no benefit and not acquired it well,' this means that you have gained no benefit and have not properly acquired it.
One who properly acquires benefit should, at the time of the recitation of the precepts, maintain single-minded mindfulness and listen attentively."

Regarding the hearing of the Dharma: since this is no longer possible, although one hears the precepts, there is no understanding. Because of this lack of understanding, it is as in the case of a *pāyattika*.
If one does not grant [the opportunity], it is a *dukkaṭa*. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this offense, it is a *pāyattika*; for a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is equally a *dukkaṭa*.
If one has not previously heard the recitation of the precepts and only now hears them for the first time, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu, after a formal legal act (kamma) has been performed together with others, subsequently says,
"The bhikṣus have distributed the property of the Saṃgha according to their personal intimacy," it is a pāyattika offense.
The son of Dhama was occupied with monastic affairs and stūpa matters; when people outside held a gathering and offered alms, he was unable to attend.
His robes were worn out. At another time, someone offered expensive garments to the community of monks, and the monks deliberated together.
"This son of Taṃbapaṇṇi, because he was attending to the affairs of the Saṃgha and the stūpa, could not attend an assembly where outsiders were making offerings. His robes have been worn out;

it would be appropriate to give him these robes. At that time, the community of monks performed the formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the motion with one subsequent proclamation) and gave them to him.
The group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) likewise underwent the same *karman*. Later, they spoke thus: "The bhikṣus [acted] according to favoritism."
Thou! [The Buddha] gave the robe of the Saṃgha to him. Because the Buddha heard of this, he established the rule: if one speaks so as to be clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika*;
if one speaks but is not clearly understood, it is a *dukkaṭa*. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this offense, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is equally a *dukkaṭa*. If the matter is indeed as stated, but the person was not present in the *karmavācanā* assembly on that day, [the offense is not established].
Regarding what is stated therein: there is no offense.
However, if a bhikṣu, while the Saṃgha’s deliberation on a matter has not yet concluded, rises and departs without having granted his consent (*chanda*), it is a *pāyattika*.
On one occasion, when the assembly of monks had gathered to discuss monastic affairs, the group of six (the Ṣaḍvargikas) said to one another: "We wish to act for our own sake..."

Having performed the *karmavācanā*, he immediately rose and departed. The Buddha, knowing the reason, established this rule: if a monk leaves before the Sangha’s business is concluded, and goes outside the door, it is a *pāyattika*.
If he has one foot outside the door and intends to leave, but has not yet departed, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If a *bhikṣuṇī* commits this offense, it is a *pāyattika*. For *śikṣamāṇās* and others, it is likewise a *dukkaṭa*. If there is a [legitimate] matter...

There is no offense for one who departs after having given their consent (*chanda*). There is no offense for one who departs without giving consent if the *karmavācanā* (formal act) is contrary to the Dharma.
If a bhikṣu, having already given his consent, subsequently reviles [the assembly], it is a *pāyattika*.

Among the group of six, there was one who had committed an offense. Fearing that the assembly would bring it to his attention, the six of them followed one another without parting, mutually supporting and protecting him so that the community could not carry out the formal ritual (karmavācanā).
Later, while the group of six was making robes, the assembly summoned them for a formal ritual.
He said, "I cannot go because I am making robes. The one who summoned him said, "You should have one or two people take the *chanda* (consent) and go.
The group of six monks then sent one person to receive the *chanda*. The Sangha immediately performed a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) against this monk.
The group of six monks regretted their action and said, "That ritual they performed was not a valid ritual; the ritual was not accomplished. We [acted] on that matter..."

Regarding the granting of consent (*chandadāna*): if it is not for this specific purpose, yet the Buddha, knowing [the situation], has established the rule—then if one speaks so as to be clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika*;
if not clearly understood, it is a *dukkaṭa*. For a bhikṣuṇī who commits this offense, it is a *pāyattika*; for a śikṣamāṇā and others, it is likewise.
In both cases, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If the matter is such that the formal act (*kamma*) is not actually accomplished, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that other bhikṣus are quarreling, listens to these words and repeats them to those [others], it is a *pāyattika*.

The group of six monks listened to the disputes of other bhikṣus and reported them to those involved, causing disputes to arise where none existed before and preventing existing disputes from being settled.
Knowing this, the Buddha established a rule: if a bhikṣu goes to listen to the talk of others and hears it, it is a pāyattika offense;
if he does not hear it, it is a dukkaṭa offense. If he employs means to go but does not actually go, [it is also a dukkaṭa].
It is a *duṣkṛta*. If two people are together in a secluded place or speaking in private, one should snap one's fingers or clear one's throat to alert them;
failure to do so is a *duṣkṛta*. If two people are walking on a path and conversing ahead of one, one must likewise alert them;
failure to do so is a *duṣkṛta*. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this offense, it is a *pāyattika*. For a *śikṣamāṇā*, [it is a *sthūlātyaya*].
...and so forth; all are *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, strikes another bhikṣu, it is a *pāyattika*.
One of the group of six bhikṣus struck a bhikṣu from the group of seventeen out of anger; the one who was struck cried out in a loud voice, saying:
"Stop, stop! Do not strike me! The Buddha heard this and therefore established the rule: "If one strikes with the hand, a stone, or a staff, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one strikes with a light object, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If one strikes in jest, or strikes a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is likewise a *dukkaṭa*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this offense, it is a *pāyattika*. For *śikṣamāṇās* and others, it is likewise [a *dukkaṭa*]."
It is a *dukkaṭa*.
If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, strikes another bhikṣu with his hand, it is a *pāyattika*.
One member of the group of six, out of malice, struck a member of the group of seventeen with his hand; the Buddha heard of this.
The Regulation: "To strike" means either to ward off and push away, or to poke and touch. If one does so with the hand, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one uses the handle of a whisk or a light object, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense. If a bhikṣuṇī commits this, it is a *pāyattika* offense; the same applies to śikṣamāṇās and others."
In both cases, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, slanders another with a groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, it is a *pāyattika*.
When the group of six bhikṣus, out of anger, slandered the group of seventeen with a groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, those who heard it censured them in disgust.
The Buddha, knowing this, established the precept. "Without basis" means that among the thirteen matters, there is no offense based on seeing, hearing, or suspicion.
If one speaks clearly, it is a *pāyattika*; if not clearly, it is a *dukkaṭa*. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is a *dukkaṭa* in both cases.
If a bhikṣu enters the palace of a Kṣatriya king of the water-sprinkling lineage while the king has not yet emerged and the treasures have not yet been stored away,
and he crosses the threshold, it is a pāyattika.
Kālodāyin went into the palace of King Sreṇika. The king and Queen Māllikā had been sleeping together all day.
When the queen saw Kālodāyin arrive, she immediately rose, adjusted her robes, and prepared a seat for him to sit upon.
At that moment, the queen’s garment slipped from her body and fell to the ground; she crouched there, unable to stand up. Kālodāyin then departed and returned home.
He said to the bhikṣus, "I have now seen all the foremost treasures of King Prasenajit. Because the Buddha heard of this, he established the prohibition.
*Kṣatriya* means *kṣatrendriya*; here it means "royal lineage. As for "one whose head is sprinkled with water" (*abhiṣeka*):
one takes the waters of the four great oceans with a golden pitcher, takes [mud from] the right horn of a white ox, and fills [the vessel] with all kinds of seeds.
In the center, he was placed upon a golden palanquin, which was carried by various minor kings. The king and his first queen sat together upon the palanquin.
The great Brahmin poured water over the crown of the king’s head; having performed this, he was established as king.

They are collectively known as the Kṣatriya lineage of kings consecrated by the pouring of water (*abhiṣeka*). "The king has not yet emerged" means the king has not yet emerged from the [birth] canal. Not yet... [text ends].

Regarding "storing treasures": this refers not only to when female attendants have not yet returned to their original places, but also includes the case where gold, silver, and other valuables have not yet been stored away.
If one enters the palace and crosses the threshold, it is a *pāyattika* offense. If one foot has entered within and the other foot remains outside, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one enters the inner chambers of high ministers, elders, or others, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense. This is the comparison.
If a bhikṣuṇī or a śikṣamāṇā commits this offense, it is equally a duṣkṛta.
If the king summons her, or if there is a formal petition [to that effect], she must likewise conceal the treasure before entering; in such cases, there is no offense.

If a bhikṣu, whether it be a jewel or an ornament made of jewels, takes hold of it himself or causes another to take hold of it—except within a monastery or at a place where he is staying—he commits a pāyattika offense.

If, however, he is within a monastery or at a place where he is staying, and he takes hold of a jewel or an ornament made of jewels himself or causes another to take hold of it, he should form this intention: "Should there be an owner."
The wise should take it; such is the causal condition, and nothing else.
There was a non-Buddhist ascetic who came from the kingdom of Kosala, rested along the way, and left behind a bag of gold.

A great many bhikṣus later encountered it and picked it up, saying together, "We shall wait for the one who comes searching for it and return it to him. That non-Buddhist ascetic had long since departed.
As he was returning, the bhikṣu immediately returned the gold to him. The man, on the contrary, falsely claimed that the gold was short, and subsequently reported this to the king.

The king investigated the matter and found it to be true; thus, according to external law, the man’s conduct was deficient, and he was required to surrender the gold to the state. When the Buddha heard of this, he established a rule prohibiting the handling of precious objects or ornaments made of precious materials.
Later, on the occasion of a festival, the mother Viśākhā went to the assembly; on her way, she passed by Jetavana and entered it.

He paid homage to the Buddha and thought to himself, "It is not necessary to be formally adorned when paying homage to the Buddha. He therefore removed his ornaments and placed them under a tree before entering.
When he departed, he forgot to take them back. A bhikṣu saw them but did not dare to report it to the Buddha. The Buddha then permitted [the storage of items] within the saṃghārāma.
Furthermore, another bhikṣu stayed overnight at the house of a skilled craftsman. While the craftsman was away, there was gold in the room. The bhikṣu...
Having guarded [the property] throughout the night without sleeping, he informed the Buddha. The Buddha further permitted the establishment of lodging places.
Generally, when a bhikṣu sees anything lost within a saṃghārāma, he should pick it up.
He should clearly identify the fragments and portions of the lost object, as well as the characteristics of its wrapping or bag. If anyone comes to claim it, he should question them.
If [the owner] recognizes it, one should immediately return it. If they do not recognize it, one may say: "I did not see this object.
If a bhikṣu picks up a lost item without examining it closely or questioning [the owner], it is a duṣkṛta offense.

However, if it is an object for the purpose of making offerings to a stūpa or monastery, and one takes possession of it for the sake of preservation, there is no offense. This applies even if it is in another's house.
If one stays overnight with precious items, fearing they might be lost, one should collect and secure them.

If one sees a lost object outside the monastery, one may cover it with grass and leaves and wait for the owner to come and claim it. If no one claims it, one should take it back inside the monastery and keep it under private custody for seven or eight days.
If there is still no claimant, it should be deposited in the monastic storehouse. After five or six months, if there is still no claimant...
One should provide for the Saṃgha of those worthy of offerings and purchase sturdy vessels. If the original owner later comes to demand them back, one should encourage him to relinquish his claim;
if he does not relinquish it, one should return the original object without providing any interest. Even if the object is of high value and cannot be returned, one must by no means use it lightly.
If a bhikṣuṇī violates this rule, it is a pāyattika offense; for śikṣamāṇās and others, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu enters a village at an improper time without having informed another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika offense.
Once, when it was not the proper time, Upāli’s brother, Upananda, entered a village and played dice with a householder.

Because the bhikṣu won, the householder became stingy and jealous, saying, "For what purpose has this bhikṣu entered the village at an improper time? When the Buddha heard of this, he established the rule. Later, there was...
"O bhikṣus, for the sake of the Saṃgha, or for matters concerning the stūpas and temples, or for attending to the sick, one must not dare to enter a village at an improper time.

They reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha commanded that one should first entrust oneself to another bhikṣu before entering. "Proper time" refers to the period from the appearance of the morning light until midday.
"Improper time" refers to the period from after midday until the morning light has not yet appeared. "Entrusting oneself to another bhikṣu" means to entrust...

It may be the same room or an adjacent room; it is also permissible for those staying together. If one enters without having been informed, at the very first entry through the village gate, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one intends to leave but has not yet left, or intends to enter but has not yet entered, it is in both cases a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this offense, it is a *pāyattika*; for a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu makes a corded bed or a wooden bed, the legs should be no higher than eight fingers of the Tathāgata, excluding the portion inserted into the mortise holes and the top cut-off.
If they exceed this, it is a pāyattika.
Kāḷudāyin prepared a high bed. Seeing the Buddha approaching, he said to him, "World-Honored One, look at my bed.
The Buddha then established a precept: that [the height] should not exceed eight fingers of the Tathāgata. One finger of the Buddha is two *cun*; thus, it should be one foot and six inches high.
The *bèi* (梐) refers to the *xùntóu* (栒頭). If it exceeds eight fingers, whether one makes it oneself or instructs another to do so, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If it is a *pāyattika* offense, and it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one causes another to complete it, whether it is completed or not, it is in both cases a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this, it is a *pāyattika*. For a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is in all cases a *duṣkṛta*. If one makes it less than the prescribed measure, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu makes a rope bed, a wooden bed, bedding, or a sitting cushion stuffed with *tūla* cotton, it is a *pāyattika*.
When the group of six bhikṣus made bedding and sitting cushions stuffed with *tūla* cotton, the laypeople saw them and criticized them as follows: [text continues].
The King and his ministers heard of this, and consequently, the Buddha established a prohibition. "Tūla-wool" (兜羅綿) is translated here as "ice-cotton"; it is named after its color.
In the Western Regions there is the tūla tree, from which this wool grows; it is fragrant and pure white, and is thus called tūla.

This is a precious and expensive item. If one uses it as bedding or a cushion for sitting, it is an extreme display of luxury. Whether one makes it oneself or causes another to make it, if it is completed, it is a *pāyattika*;
if it is not completed, it is a *dukkaṭa*. This applies whether one does so for oneself or for another, regardless of whether it is completed or not.
In both cases, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For a *bhikṣuṇī* who commits this offense, it is a *pāyattika*. For a *śikṣamāṇā* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
If a *bhikṣu* uses bone, ivory, or horn to make a needle case, even if it is finished by scraping, it is a *pāyattika*.

There was a craftsman who possessed faith and devotion; for the sake of the bhikṣus, he exhausted his family’s resources making needle cases from bone, ivory, and horn until his food and clothing became scarce.
A householder remarked, "There is no merit in supporting śramaṇas; one only incurs misfortune. Knowing this, the Buddha established a prohibition.
Whether one accomplishes it oneself or instructs another to accomplish it, in both cases it is a *pāyattika*. If it is not accomplished, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

If one causes another to accomplish it, whether it is accomplished or not, in both cases it is a *dukkaṭa*. For a *bhikṣuṇī* or a *śikṣamāṇā* who commits this offense, in both cases it is a *dukkaṭa*.

If a bhikṣu makes a sitting mat (niṣīdana), he must make it according to the prescribed measurements. Regarding these measurements: the length shall be two spans of the Buddha’s hand, and the width one and a half spans;
it may be increased by an additional half span in both length and width. If it exceeds these dimensions when completed, it is a pāyattika offense.

One day, the World-Honored One did not go to a formal invitation but instead toured the various quarters. He saw that the monks' bedding had been spread out in the open air and was mostly defiled by impurities.
The Buddha then permitted the making of a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat).

When lying down, it should be spread over the bedding to serve as a barrier for the bedding, and also to serve as a barrier for the body against the undergarment. Thereupon, the group of six [monks]...
[The monks] made the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) wide and long. The Buddha, knowing [the cause], established a regulation.

Initially, he permitted it to be two spans (*vitasti*) in length and one and a half spans in width. Later, because Kālodāyin’s body was large, when he saw the Buddha approaching, he pulled the *niṣīdana* with his hand.
The Buddha asked why; he replied, "I pulled it only because I wished to make it wider and longer. Thereupon, the Buddha...
If one increases the length or width by more than half a *vitasti* (span), whether making it oneself or instructing another to do so, it is a *pāyattika*.
If it is not yet completed, it is a *dukkaṭa*. Whether the work is done for oneself or for another, if it exceeds the measure, it is a *dukkaṭa* in both cases.
For *bhikṣuṇīs*, *śikṣamāṇās*, and others who commit this offense, it is likewise a *dukkaṭa*. If one makes it less than the prescribed measure, it is not an offense.
[If one] commits [an offense]: if one obtains a pre-made garment from another, it must also be cut down to the proper measure. If one makes it double-layered by patching, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu makes a wound-covering robe, it must be made according to the proper measure. Regarding the measure herein: the length is four spans of the Buddha’s hand.
It shall be two spans wide. If it exceeds this and is completed, it is a *pāyattika*.
At that time, various monks suffered from diverse sores; pus and blood flowed out, defiling their bodies, their robes, and their bedding.

The Buddha then permitted the making of wound-covering robes (*vastrāpavāraka*). At that time, the monks’ wound-covering robes were coarse; when they placed them over their wounds, they suffered pain when lifting the robes.
The Buddha then allowed the making of fine, soft cloth. Subsequently, the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) made wound-covering robes that were excessively wide and long.
The Buddha, knowing this, established a regulation: if the length is within measure, the width must not exceed it; if the width is within measure, the length must not exceed it.

It must be of the prescribed measure. If it is either too long or too wide, such that it does not conform to the measure—whether made by oneself or caused to be made by another—if it is completed, it is a *pāyattika*;
if it is not completed, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If one makes it for another, whether it is completed or not, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and others, committing this offense is likewise a *dukkaṭa*. If one makes it smaller than the prescribed measure, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu makes a rain-bath robe, he must make it according to the prescribed measurements. Herein, the measurements are:
six spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and two and a half spans in width. If it exceeds these dimensions, it constitutes a pāyattika offense.
When the Mother Viśākhā prepared rain-bathing robes to offer to the Saṃgha, the group of six monks (ṣaḍvargika) immediately made many for themselves that were excessively large.
Because the Buddha heard of this, he established a regulation. Whether the length and width are according to measure or not, whether they are finished or not, and so forth, all are treated as above.
For bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and others, those who violate this rule commit a duṣkṛta offense. If [the robe] is less than the prescribed measure...
The author [of this rule] is not at fault.
If a bhikṣu makes a robe equal in measure to that of the Tathāgata, or makes it exceeding that measure, it is a pāyattika.
Herein, the measure is ten spans (vitasti) in length and six spans in width; this is called the measure of a robe for the Tathāgata.
Ānanda was four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha. One day, when the assembly saw him approaching from afar, they all thought it was the Buddha and rose to welcome him;
only upon his arrival did they realize it was Nanda. The assembly and Nanda were both filled with shame. The Buddha ordered that he wear black robes to distinguish him from the others.
The group of six monks did not make their robes according to the measurements of the Tathāgata, but instead made them oversized. The Buddha heard of this.

Therefore, this regulation was established. Regarding the length and breadth herein, whether they conform to the prescribed measurements or not, and whether they are properly completed or not, all are as stated above.
For bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and others, any violation constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅).
According to the Buddha’s own body measurement, which is one zhang and six chi, one *vitasti* (一磔手) corresponds to one chi and six cun. By this calculation, the length of the robe is one zhang.
The length is six chi and the width is nine chi and six cun; these are the measurements for a Buddha’s robe. Since people today are short and small of stature, it is difficult to follow and use them.
Furthermore, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "The great robe [saṃghāṭī] is four cun above the ankle; the seven-piece robe [uttarāsaṅga] is eight cun above the ankle;
the five-piece robe [antarvāsaka] is one chi and two cun above the ankle. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā* states: "The robe is five cubits in length and..."
Three *cubit* (*hasta*). The Master of the Southern Mountain says: "The *saṃghāṭī* and the *saptaka* are both five *cubit* in length and three *cubit* in width;

the *pañcaka* is four *cubit* in length and two *cubit* in width. Examining these three explanations in detail, one should simply use the current human hand span of ten *vitasti* for the length and six *vitasti* for the width;
for the *saṃghāṭī* and *antarvāsaka*, reduce this by four *cun*; for the *pañcaka*, reduce it by eight *cun*.
In both cases, there is no offense.
Venerable sirs, I have now recited the ninety *pāyattika* rules. I now ask the venerable sirs:
Are you pure in this regard? (Ask three times.)
Venerable sirs, we are pure in this matter, for we remain silent; thus it shall be held.
Venerable sirs, these four *pāṭidesanīya* dharmas are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
*Pratideśanīya*. This is translated as "confessing to another. It means that one who has committed this offense should confess it to another;
thus, the transgression shall be extinguished.
If a bhikṣu enters a village and, being free from illness, receives food with his own hands from a nun who is not a relative and eats it, that bhikṣu should confess to another bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir, I have committed a censurable offense, which ought not to have been done;
I now confess it to the Venerable sir. This is called the rule for confession (*deśanā-dharma*).
At that time, there was a famine and grain was expensive; the people lacked food, and those who died were beyond counting. It was difficult for bhikṣus to obtain almsfood.
When the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā entered the city to beg for food, she took whatever she obtained on her first day and gave it to a bhikṣu.
On the second and third days it was likewise. Later, while begging for alms, she encountered a chariot driven by an elder on the road.
The nun stepped aside to avoid it but fell into deep mud, lying face down upon the ground. When the elder saw her, he hurriedly ordered her to be helped up and asked the reason.
She replied, "I have been begging for food for three days and gave it all to the bhikṣus; now, because I am so hungry and exhausted, I have fallen to the ground."

The elder criticized and disparaged this. When the Buddha heard of it, he established a rule prohibiting the acceptance of food from a nun. Subsequently, the bhikṣus did not dare to accept food from nuns who were their relatives;
they informed the Buddha, who added the qualification "if she is not a relative. Furthermore, sick bhikṣus did not dare to accept food from nuns who were not their relatives;
they informed the Buddha, who added the qualification "if one is not ill. Regarding the phrase "accepting food with one's own hand":
It makes no difference whether one asks a relative or a non-relative; it is likewise impermissible whether one is ill or healthy.
For a bhikṣuṇī or a śikṣamāṇā and others, violating this rule constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one who is ill accepts food from a non-relative nun, or if one who is not ill accepts food from a relative nun, or if a nun places food on the ground to give, or causes another person to do so—[these are all prohibited].
If he gives [it] while in a monastery for monks or a convent for nuns, in neither case is there an offense.

If a bhikṣu is eating in the home of a layperson and a bhikṣuṇī is present there, directing that "Give such-and-such a bhikṣu soup" or "Give such-and-such a bhikṣu rice," the bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣuṇī: "Sister, please stop for a moment; wait until the..."
When the bhikṣus have finished eating, if there is not even one bhikṣu who speaks thus to the bhikṣuṇī, that bhikṣu should confess his transgression to another bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir, I have committed a censurable act which ought not to have been done; I now confess my transgression to you, Venerable sir.
This is called the procedure for confession (*pratideśanā-dharma*).
The community of monks and the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) were together receiving offerings at the home of a layperson. The group of six nuns requested soup and rice for the group of six monks;
consequently, they proceeded to serve them out of order. Among those present, some did not receive soup or rice. When the Buddha heard of this, he established a rule.
If a nun does not stop [the monks from being served out of order], it is a *pratideśanīya* offense. This applies to both nuns and *śikṣamāṇās*.

For śikṣamāṇās and others, those who violate this rule all commit a duṣkṛta offense. However, if a nun acts as her own patron, or if a layperson provides food and instructs the nun on how to distribute it, there is no offense.

There are families that are under training (*śaikṣa*). When the Saṃgha has performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) regarding these families as being under training, if a bhikṣu, knowing such a family to be under training, should—without having previously received an invitation and while not being ill—accept food with his own hands and eat it, that bhikṣu should confess to another bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir, I have committed a blameworthy act which ought not to have been done; I now confess this to you, venerable sir. This is called confession (*deśanā*).
Regarding past events:

there was a household of laypeople, husband and wife, who were faithful and devoted disciples of the Buddha. Whenever monks came to their home, they would always provide them with food and drink, never begrudging anything.
Later, they fell into poverty and lacked sufficient clothing and food. People then mocked them, saying: "The offerings..."

Having supported śramaṇas, they instead received the retribution of poverty. When the Buddha heard this, he performed the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for them as "householders under training" (*śikṣādattaka*).
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! In this city of Rājagṛha, there is a certain householder and his wife who have gained faith and become disciples of the Buddha;

their wealth and possessions have been completely exhausted. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent. The Saṃgha shall now designate them as householders under training."
The *karmavācanā*: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen. In this city of Rājagṛha, there is a certain householder and his wife who have gained faith and become disciples of the Buddha;
their wealth has been completely exhausted. The Saṃgha now performs the *śikṣādattaka-karman* (the formal act of declaring them a family under training) for them.
No bhikṣus shall receive food in their home. Thus it is announced. Venerable Saṃgha, please listen. [The rest of the formal motion follows. No bhikṣus shall receive food in their home.
"Receive and eat the food. O Venerable Ones, those who consent to the Saṃgha performing the *kula-śikṣāpada-karman* for the lay follower [Name] should remain silent;
whoever does not consent should speak. The Saṃgha has already consented to perform the *kula-śikṣāpada-karman* for the lay follower [Name].
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld. The Buddha further established a precept: "One shall receive food from a family under training (*śaikṣa-kula*)."
Regarding the *tishāni* (offenses requiring confession): if there are those who have previously accepted an invitation, one must not dare to attend the meal;

furthermore, if one is ill, one must not dare to accept the food. The Buddha permitted these exceptions in all cases. In this context, one should not eat if one has not accepted an invitation (the first case), nor should one eat if one is not ill (the second case);
how much more so when receiving food with one's own hands? Even if one has accepted an invitation or is ill, it remains improper to eat [if received by hand].

Regarding "families of practitioners": these are families who study the Path within secular life. For bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and others, to commit [an offense] against such a family constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for all.
If the family of practitioners becomes wealthy again and comes to request the lifting of the *karman*, the bhikṣu may accept food from them without committing an offense.
If a bhikṣu dwells in an araṇya, a remote place that is suspicious and fearful,

and has not previously informed the donor that he will not accept food outside the monastery grounds, yet— being free from illness— accepts food with his own hands and eats it inside the monastery grounds,
that bhikṣu should confess to another bhikṣu, saying: "Venerable sir, I have committed a blameworthy act which ought not to be done."
"I now repent before the Venerable One. This is called the method of repentance.
In the city of Rājagṛha, there was a woman who took food to the saṃghārāma; because it was remote and secluded, she was molested by a thief.
The Buddha then instructed the bhikṣus to tell the donors: "Do not go to the saṃghārāma on the road..."
Because there were robbers on the road, a further precept was established: it was not permitted to accept food from outside within the monastery.
Later, when people brought food even though they knew there were robbers, the bhikṣus—because the Buddha had prohibited accepting food from outside—dared not eat it.
Furthermore, those who were ill could not eat because they had not yet informed the *dānapati* (donor).

If one dares to eat [in these circumstances], the Buddha permits and accepts [the meal] for all. Within this context, there are three things one must not do while eating, provided one is not ill: first, one must not eat without having first spoken to the donor;
second, one must not eat food received directly with one's own hands; third, one must not eat food that constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense requiring confession).
For a bhikṣuṇī or a śikṣamāṇā and others who commit such acts, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) in all cases.
Venerable sirs, I have already recited the four *pāṭidesanīya* dharmas. Now I ask the venerable sirs:
Are you pure in this regard? (Ask three times.)
Venerable sirs, since there is silence, you are pure in this matter. Thus it shall be held.
