Composed by the monk Yuanyuan, a successor to the patriarchs at Mount Gu on Fuzhou, for the sake of the various virtuous ones.
These are the rules of training for the assembly; they are recited every half-month from within the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
Regarding the "rules for training" (*śikṣāpada*): in the Sanskrit language, this is called *śikṣā-karaṇī*, which here means "that which should be studied. These precepts are minor;
they are difficult to maintain and easy to violate, yet they are that which a bhikṣu ought to study.

They are also called *duṣkṛta*, which means "misdeed," referring to the fact that any loss of dignified decorum is an evil act. Furthermore, these precepts are divided into two categories. Those violations committed by the body are called...
It is an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*). To speak improperly with the mouth is called an offense of wrong speech (*dubbhāsita*).
One should train oneself to wear the *nivasana* (lower robe) properly and neatly.
Regarding this, the group of six bhikṣus wore the *nivasana* either hitched up high so that it reached the knees, or tied down low so that it hung below the navel. Or...

If one lets down a single corner like an elephant’s trunk, or lets down two front flaps like the leaves of a *tāla* tree, or makes pleats around the waist like those of kings or ministers, laypeople will criticize and find it offensive.
Because the Buddha heard of this, he established a rule: if one does so intentionally, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession;
this is a *duṣkṛta* offense for violating proper decorum. If one does not do so intentionally, there is no offense.
One commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession with self-reproach. If a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, or others commit this, they all likewise incur a *duṣkṛta*.
There may be cases where one has such an illness, or when performing labor, or while inside a saṃghārāma.
There is no offense when walking on a path outside a village.
One should train oneself to wear the three robes properly and neatly.

Because the group of six bhikṣus wore the three robes either too high or too low and so forth, the Buddha heard of this and established the rule. [This concerns] what constitutes an offense and what does not.
The same as above. One must not enter the house of a layperson with one’s robe tucked up behind; this is how one should train.

The group of six monks entered the house of a layperson walking with their robes tucked up behind, which caused the householders to criticize and disparage them. The Buddha heard of this and therefore established the rule against it. Tucking [the robe] up behind.
Regarding "draping the robe": one may drape it over either the left or the right shoulder, turning the robe back and placing it upon the shoulder. The offense is as described above.
One must not drape the robe back and sit in the house of a layperson; this is how one should train.
Based on the above, it is further regulated:
One must train oneself not to enter the houses of laypeople with a robe wrapped around the neck.

The group of six monks entered the houses of laypeople with their robes wrapped around their necks, which caused the householders to criticize and resent them. When the Buddha heard of this, he ruled that wrapping [the robe around the neck] was improper.
"Neck" means to grasp both corners of the robe together and place it over the left shoulder. The offense is as described above.
One must not enter the house of a layperson with the robe wrapped around the neck and sit there; this is how one should train.
Based on the above, a regulation was established:
"One must not enter the house of a layperson with one's head covered; this is how you should train.
The group of six monks entered the house of a layperson with their heads covered by their robes. A householder criticized them, saying they were like thieves. The Buddha heard of this.
Therefore, the rule is established: "Covering" refers to covering [the head] with cloth, tree leaves, or the like; the offenses are all as stated above.
If there is an illness of the head, covering it is not an offense. Or, if there is an emergency and one runs away while covering the head, it is not an offense.
One must train oneself not to enter the house of a layperson with one's head covered while seated.
This is further regulated by the preceding rule:
one must train oneself not to enter the house of a layperson by leaping. One must train oneself [in this].
The group of six monks entered the homes of laypeople by leaping about. Laypeople criticized them, saying they were like birds or small fowl. When the Buddha heard of this, he established a precept;
those who violate it are subject to the same penalty as before. However, there is no offense if one leaps while being struck by someone, or when fleeing from dangers such as thieves or wild beasts;
nor is there an offense if one leaps over thorns, or crosses a ditch, a pit, or mud by leaping.
One should train oneself not to skip rows when entering the house of a layperson to sit.
This was established as a precept together with the preceding rule.
One should train oneself not to squat while inside the house of a layperson. One should train oneself [in this].
The group of six monks went to a layperson’s house for a meal and squatted down. A bhikṣu touched them with his hand, whereupon they fell to the ground and their bodies were exposed.
The layperson criticized them, saying they were like naked heretics (*nirgrantha*). The Buddha heard of this and established a rule:

"Squatting" means either on a bed or on the ground, such that the buttocks do not touch the earth. The offense is as described above. However, if one has a disease in the area of the buttocks and is unable [to sit otherwise], there is no offense.
If one is seated, there is no offense.
One must train oneself not to enter the houses of laypeople with hands clasped behind the waist.
The group of six monks entered the houses of laypeople with hands clasped behind their waists, and the householders criticized them, saying they were like newlyweds enjoying their first intimacy.
Regarding this matter: because the Buddha heard of such conduct, he established a precept. One who violates it is subject to the same penalty as above.
One must not walk with hands clasped behind the waist or sit in the house of a layperson; this is how one should train.
This was established as a rule together with the preceding regulations.
One should train oneself: "I shall not enter the house of a layperson with my body swaying back and forth.
The group of six monks entered the houses of laypeople with their bodies swaying. When the householders saw this, they criticized them, saying they were like kings or ministers.
The Buddha heard of this and established the rule; the offense for one who violates it is as stated above.
One should train oneself: "I shall not enter the house of a layperson while swaying the body or sitting there.
This was established together with the preceding rule.
One should train oneself: "I shall not enter the house of a layperson while swinging my arms. One should train oneself.
The group of six monks entered the houses of laypeople with their arms swinging about. Laypeople criticized them, saying they were like kings or high ministers.
When the Buddha heard of this, he established a precept. "Swinging the arms" means walking with the arms hanging down, swaying them forward or backward.
The offense is as described above. There is no offense in cases where there is an urgent matter requiring escape, or when crossing a river, jumping over a pit, or traversing a moat.
There is no offense [if one is ill].
One must train oneself not to walk with arms swinging or to sit in the house of a layperson.
This was established as a regulation following the preceding rule.
"One should train oneself to enter the homes of laypeople well-covered.
The group of six monks did not cover themselves well; they remained exposed in various places, leading householders to criticize and despise them, saying they were like Brahmins and others.

The Buddha heard of this and established the rule. The offense for one who violates it is as stated above. This also applies if [the robe] is blown off the body by the wind or taken by another person.
One should train oneself to sit in the houses of laypeople with the body well-covered, without being bound [by improper conduct].
This was established as a regulation based on the preceding [incident].
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not walk into the house of a layperson while looking left and right.
The group of six monks walked into the house of a layperson looking left and right; the householders criticized them, saying they were like thieves stealing someone's property."

The Buddha heard of this and therefore established the precept. Those who violate it are subject to the same penalties as above. However, there is no offense if one seeks a means of escape due to danger, or if one is searching for something.
One must train oneself not to look left or right while walking into the house of a layperson or sitting there.
Based on the foregoing, it was established as a regulation:
"One should train oneself to enter the homes of laypeople in silence.
The group of six monks entered the homes of laypeople shouting and calling out loudly. The householders criticized them, saying they were like Brahmins. The Buddha [prohibited this].
It was established because of hearing. The offense for one who violates it is as stated above. There is no offense if one is deaf and does not hear sounds; or if someone is calling from a distance;
or if there is an emergency and one runs away at a loud voice.
One should train oneself: "I shall enter the house of a layperson in silence.
This was established together with the preceding rule:
One should train oneself: "I shall not enter the house of a layperson while laughing or joking."
The group of six monks entered the houses of laypeople while laughing and joking. Laypeople criticized them, saying they were like monkeys. When the Buddha heard of this, he established a precept;
those who violate it are subject to the same penalty as before. However, there is no offense for one who laughs out of joy while recollecting the Dharma.
One should train oneself: "I shall not enter the house of a layperson and sit there laughing or joking.
This was established as a regulation based on the preceding [incident].
One should train oneself: "I shall receive food with careful attention."
The group of six monks accepted food in the homes of laypeople while the layperson personally served them.

The group of six did not mindfully receive the food, spilling and wasting the soup and rice. The layperson criticized their greedy manner of eating, comparing it to times of famine when grain is scarce.

When the Buddha heard of this, he established a precept; those who violate it are subject to the same penalty as before. There is no offense if the bowl is small and some food is consequently left behind.
"One should train oneself to receive food with a level bowl.

The group of six monks went to a meal offering and received food until their bowls overflowed, causing them to spill the soup and rice. Laypeople criticized them, saying they were like starving people.
When the Buddha heard this, he established the rule. "With a level bowl" means that when receiving food, one must not fill the bowl to overflowing. The offense for violating this is as stated above.
If the bowl is small and thus becomes full, there is no offense.
One should train oneself to receive the soup level with the rim of the bowl.
When the group of six monks went to a meal, because they received so much rice in their bowls, they were unable to receive the soup. When the laypeople saw this, they also criticized them.
[The Buddha] disapproved. Having heard this, he established the rule. One who violates it is subject to the same penalty as above.
One should train oneself to eat both soup and rice together.
When the group of six monks went to a meal, the rice was finished before the soup arrived; when the soup arrived, the rice had already been consumed.

[The rule concerning] "finishing" (jìn): Laypeople also criticized and disapproved of this. Because the Buddha heard of it, he established the precept. "Eating both" means waiting until both the soup and the rice have arrived before eating.

The offense is as described above. There is no offense if one intends to pass [the meal], if there is some difficult circumstance, if at times one desires soup but not rice, or if at times one desires rice but not soup.
One should learn to eat in proper sequence.
When the group of six monks went to a meal, they did not eat in order from the bowl, but instead took food from here and there.

Laypeople criticized them, saying they were like dogs and pigs. The Buddha heard of this and established the rule; those who violate it are subject to the same penalty as before. Alternatively, if one suffers from heat, one may pick out cold food.
Eating while seated: no offense.
One must not pick at the center of the bowl while eating; this is how one should train.

The group of six monks, having received food, picked at the center of their bowls until it was empty. Laypeople criticized and disparaged them. The Buddha heard of this and established the rule. [Violation: an offense.
The above applies to these cases as well. If one suffers from a fever, it is not an offense to have the contents opened and cooled for the sake of the Saṃgha.
One who is not ill must not seek out soup or rice for oneself; this is how one should train.
The group of six monks, while at the home of a layperson, requested soup and rice for themselves. A householder criticized and disparaged them. Having heard of this, the Buddha established a rule;
those who violate it are subject to the same penalty as above. There is no offense if one requests on behalf of oneself when ill, or if one requests for the sake of a sick person.
"One must not cover the soup with rice while hoping to receive more; this is how one should train.
While the group of six monks was receiving food at the home of a layperson, the layperson gave them soup, whereupon they covered the soup with rice, hoping to receive more.
When the layperson asked, "Where is the soup? they remained silent. The layperson then expressed his reproach and censure, saying: [text continues].

Just as in the case of a hungry person, the Buddha established this rule upon hearing of it. The offense for one who violates it is the same as mentioned above. If, when invited to a meal, the soup soils one’s robes and so forth, it is appropriate to cover them with rice; in such a case, there is no offense.
"One must not look into the bowl of one's neighbor and give rise to a mind of resentment; this is how you should train.
While the group of six monks was receiving food at the home of a layperson, they saw that their own portions were small while the portions in the bowls of their neighbors were large.
They then remarked, "The layperson has favoritism and is unfair. The assembly all rebuked them, and the Buddha heard of it.

Regulation: The offense is as stated above. However, if one's neighbor is ill, or if their vision is impaired such that they cannot discern whether food has been received or not, nor whether it is pure or impure, there is no offense.
"One should eat while keeping one's bowl in mind; this is how you should train.
The group of six monks received their soup and looked around to the left and right. A neighbor sitting nearby took their soup and hid it without them noticing.

They then asked the neighbor, "Where is my soup? The assembly all reviled and disparaged them. The Buddha heard of this and established the rule; those who violate it shall be treated according to the same [offense].
[Upāli asked: "Venerable One, if one's neighbor in the seat is ill—such as having blurred vision so that they can or cannot receive food—and [one does not offer it], there is no offense.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not eat by making large mouthfuls of rice.'"
The group of six monks received offerings and ate large mouthfuls of rice. Householders criticized and disparaged this. When the Buddha heard of it, he established a rule;
those who violate it are subject to the same penalty as before. However, there is no offense if the day is nearly past midday, or if one wishes to eat quickly due to some difficult circumstance.
One must not open one’s mouth wide in anticipation of food; this is how one should train.

The group of six monks opened their mouths wide in anticipation of food before the morsels had even arrived. Laypeople criticized and disparaged them. When the Buddha heard of this, he established the rule.
Any who violate it incur the same offense as previously described.
One must not speak while food is held in the mouth; this is how one should train.
The group of six monks, while receiving food, spoke with rice held in their mouths. Householders criticized and disparaged them. Having heard of this, the Buddha established the rule.
One who violates it commits an offense as previously described. There is no offense in cases of urgent necessity.
One must not form a lump of rice and cast it into the mouth from a distance; this is how one should train.
The group of six monks, while receiving food, formed lumps of rice and cast them into their mouths from a distance. Laypeople criticized them, saying they were like illusionists.

The Buddha heard of this and established the rule. Any who violate it are subject to the same penalty as before. Furthermore, even when bound or restrained such that the hand cannot reach the mouth, one must not cast food from a distance to eat.
There is no offense [in this case]. One must train oneself not to let food fall or be scattered.
The group of six monks received food improperly; they took mouthfuls of rice with their hands and bit into it, causing much to be dropped. Householders criticized them.

This is like [the case of] birds and small fowl; because the Buddha heard of this, he established the rule. One who violates it commits an offense as described above. There is no offense if one has a hand ailment.
One must not eat with food hanging from the cheeks; this is how one should train.
The group of six monks ate with their mouths wide open, causing both cheeks to bulge like those of a monkey. Laypeople criticized and disparaged this behavior.

When the Buddha heard of it, he established a precept; the offense for violating it is as stated above. However, there is no offense if the day is nearly past midday, or if there are difficult circumstances, and one wishes to eat quickly.
One must not make noise while chewing food; this is how one should train.
When the group of six monks received food and made noise while chewing, householders criticized and disparaged them. Having heard of this, the Buddha established the rule.
The offense for violating it is as stated above. However, there is no offense if one chews dry cakes, scorched rice, fruits, melons, or the like.
One must not eat by taking large mouthfuls; this is how one should train.
When the group of six monks received offerings, they ate by taking large mouthfuls, which caused householders to criticize and resent them. The Buddha heard of this and established the rule.

To "take large mouthfuls" means to open the mouth wide and take a gulp from a distance. The offense for violating this is as stated above. However, if there is pain in the mouth, or if one is eating soup and the like, it is permissible.
There is no offense [in this case].
One must not lick food with the tongue; this is how one should train.

When the group of six monks accepted offerings, they extended their tongues to take the food. Laypeople criticized and disparaged them. The Buddha heard of this and established the rule. Any who violate it commit an offense.
As above. One should train oneself not to shake one’s hand while eating.

When the group of six monks went to a meal offering, they shook their hands as they ate, which caused the householders to criticize and resent them. The Buddha heard of this and established the rule. To "shake one's hand" means:
To shake the hand [while eating] is a transgression, the penalty for which is as stated above. There is no offense if one has such an illness.
One must not eat by grasping loose grains of rice with the hand; this is how one should train.
The group of six monks was eating at the house of a lay devotee, scattering the rice with their hands as they ate. The lay devotee criticized them, saying they were like chickens or birds.

When the Buddha heard of this, he established a rule. The offense for violating it is as stated above. There is no offense if there are insects in the food, or if one scatters it due to being stained by other substances.
"One must not grasp food vessels with defiled hands; this is how one should train.

The group of six monks grasped their vessels with unclean, greasy hands while drinking, which caused the householders to criticize and resent them. When the Buddha heard of this, he established the precept.
The offenses are as stated above. It is not an offense if one receives [food] upon grass or receives it upon leaves.
One must train oneself not to discard the water used for rinsing the bowl inside the dwellings of laypeople.

The group of six monks, while at the residence of a lay devotee, discarded the water used for washing their bowls on the ground after finishing their meal, leaving the remaining food in a state of disarray.
The lay devotee expressed his resentment and reproached them. When the Buddha heard of this, he established a rule; those who violate it are subject to the same penalty as before.
However, there is no offense if one uses a vessel to catch the water and discard it outside, or if one asks the host for a place where it may be discarded.
One must not void excrement, urinate, or spit upon living grass or vegetables, except when ill;
this is how one should train. The group of six monks voided excrement, urinated, and spat upon living grass and vegetables. Laypeople criticized and disparaged them.

The Buddha heard of this and established the rule, permitting it only for those who are ill. The offense for violating this is as stated above. If one voids excrement on ground where there is no grass or vegetables, and it flows onto grass...
[If one] voids excrement or urine, or spits, upon vegetables, there is no offense.
One must not void excrement or urine, or spit, into pure water, except in the case of illness; this is how one should train.
The group of six monks voided excrement or urine and spat into pure water. A householder saw this and criticized it with disdain. The Buddha heard of it.
Therefore, it is prescribed that it is contrary to principle for something impure to defile what is pure. This allowance is made because the sick person is unable to travel far;
the offense is as described above. However, if one is in impure water, there is no offense.
"One shall not stand while defecating or urinating, except when ill; this is how one should train.

The group of six monks stood while defecating or urinating and were censured by the householders. The Buddha heard of this and established the rule. It was permitted for those who are ill because they are unable to squat.
The offense is as described above. In this region, it is customary to stand while urinating; [in such cases], there is no offense.
One must not preach the Dharma to a person who has their robe draped over one shoulder in a disrespectful manner, except in the case of illness; this is how you should train.
The group of six monks preached the Dharma to people who had their robes draped over one shoulder and were being disrespectful. The assembly of bhikṣus criticized and disapproved of this.

When the Buddha heard of it, he established this rule, permitting it only for those who are ill. The offense is as described above. However, if the person is a king, a high minister, or the like, one may provide a brief explanation.
However, one should not speak extensively; the wise should know for themselves the proper time.
One must not preach the Dharma to someone with a cloth wrapped around their neck, except in the case of illness. This is how you should train.
One should train oneself not to preach the Dharma to a person whose head is covered, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself not to preach the Dharma to a person whose head is wrapped, except in the case of illness.
One should not preach the Dharma to a person who has their hands placed on their hips, except in the case of illness; this is a training to be observed.
One should not preach the Dharma to a person wearing leather sandals, except in the case of illness; this is a training to be observed.
One should train oneself thus: one must not preach the Dharma to a person wearing wooden clogs, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself thus: one must not preach the Dharma to a person riding a mount, except in the case of illness.
The above seven articles are all established based on the preceding regulations. Whether an offense is committed or not is in all cases the same as stated above.
One must not stay overnight within a Buddhist stūpa, except for the purpose of guarding it. This is how one should train.
The group of six monks stayed overnight inside a Buddhist stūpa. The community of bhikṣus censured them, and when the Buddha heard of this, he established a prohibition.

Later, because the bhikṣus did not dare to guard the stūpas, he granted permission [to stay]. Those who violate this are subject to the same rules as above. However, there is no offense for one who is constrained by external power.
Today, Buddhist halls, scripture towers, and the like are treated according to the same principles as the stūpa.
One must not store wealth or goods within a Buddha-stūpa, except for the purpose of securing them; this is how one should train.
The group of six monks stored wealth within a Buddha-stūpa, and the bhikṣus censured them. When the Buddha heard of this, he established the rule.

Later, when there was wealth among the Saṃgha that required secure storage, they did not dare to store it. They informed the Buddha, who granted permission. Those who violate this are guilty of the same offense.
[If one is] under the influence of superior power, there is no offense.
One must not wear leather sandals when entering a Buddhist stūpa; this is how one should train.

When the group of six monks wore leather sandals while entering a Buddhist stūpa, the assembly saw it and censured them with resentment. The Buddha heard of this and established the rule. Those who violate it commit an offense identical [to the preceding].
Furthermore, one day when the Buddha arose from meditative concentration and was walking in the open air, the bhikṣus followed him wearing leather sandals.
The Buddha looked back at them and said, "Even the disciples of external paths do not wear leather sandals when following their teachers out of respect for them;
how much more so should this be for the Tathāgata? From now on, [this shall apply] before the Buddha and before one's upādhyāya."
In the presence of the Ācārya, one must not wear [leather sandals] at all; to do so constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
One must not enter a Buddhist stūpa holding leather sandals in one's hand; this is how one should train.
One should train oneself not to walk around a stūpa wearing leather sandals.
One should train oneself not to enter a stūpa wearing *puṭa* (leather footwear).
One should train oneself not to carry *puṭa* while entering a stūpa.
The above four articles are all established based on the preceding regulations. *Pura* is a Sanskrit term; its correct pronunciation is *phulla*, which here means "short-heeled boots.
Whether an offense is committed or not is the same as in the cases above.
"One must not sit and eat beneath a stūpa, leaving grass or food to defile the ground; this is how one should train.

The group of six monks sat and ate beneath a stūpa, and after eating, they left grass and food to defile the ground and departed without sweeping it up. The bhikṣus expressed their disapproval and rebuked them.
The Buddha heard of this and established the rule. The offense for violating it is as stated above. However, if there is leftover food or grass, the Buddha permits [their removal].
If one places [the corpse] at the edge of one's feet and carries it out to discard it, there is no offense.
One must not carry a corpse past the base of a stūpa; this is how one should train.
The group of six monks carried a corpse past the base of a stūpa, and its foul odor defiled the stūpa, causing the guardian deity of the stūpa to become angry. The bhikṣus...

[The Buddha] censured [this behavior]. Because the Buddha knew [the situation], he established this precept. Those who violate it are subject to the same [penalties] as above. There is no offense if the path must necessarily be traversed, or if one is compelled by forceful power.
One must not bury corpses beneath a stūpa; this is how one should train.
One should train oneself: "I shall not burn a corpse beneath a stūpa.
One should train oneself: "I shall not burn a corpse in front of a stūpa.
One should train oneself: "I shall not burn a corpse around the four sides of a stūpa so that its foul odor enters [the sacred precinct]."
These four rules are all established based on the preceding regulations. There is no offense if the corpse is being cremated at a great distance such that its odor does not enter [the vicinity].
One must not pass beneath a stūpa carrying the clothes or the bed of a deceased person, except when they have been washed, dyed, or perfumed; this is how one should train.
The group of six monks passed beneath the stupa carrying a corpse’s shroud and a bed; the foul odor offended the stupa, and the deity who protects the stupa became angry.

The Buddha, knowing this, established the prohibition. Those who violate it are subject to the same penalty as before. However, there is no offense if the garment has been washed, dyed, or perfumed with incense.
One should train oneself: "I shall not defecate or urinate beneath a Buddha-stūpa.
One should train oneself: "I shall not defecate or urinate facing a Buddha-stūpa.
One should train oneself: "I shall not defecate or urinate while circumambulating the four sides of a Buddha-stūpa, causing foul odors to enter [the sacred precinct]."
One must not carry an image of the Buddha to places for defecation or urination; this should be studied.
These four preceding rules were all established because [the body] is touched by the foul odors of excrement and urine, which is equivalent to being touched by the clothes of a dead person.
An image of the Buddha must not be carried to places for defecation or urination, even if one must pass through them on the way.
If one is constrained by force, there is no offense.
One should train oneself: "I shall not chew a tooth-stick beneath a Buddha stūpa.
One should train oneself: "I shall not chew a tooth-stick while facing a Buddha stūpa."
One must not chew a tooth-stick while circumambulating the four sides of a Buddha stūpa; this is how one should train.
[The preceding] three items all concern the improper act of polluting those who are most venerable with the foul breath of one's mouth;

therefore, they are collectively prohibited. The offense for violating these rules is as stated above. Furthermore, the Vinaya states that there are two forms of defilement due to which one must not prostrate to the Buddha.
As well as one's preceptor and ācārya: first, one must wash clean after defecating; second, one must rinse the mouth after eating;
and one must not spit or sneeze beneath a Buddha stūpa. These are the rules you should train in.
One should train oneself not to spit or discharge nasal mucus toward a Buddhist stūpa.
One should train oneself not to spit or discharge nasal mucus while circumambulating the four sides of a Buddhist stūpa.
[The preceding] three items all concern defiling pure ground with the impurity of spittle; how much more so when one is near that which is revered? To spit...
Spitting. What could be more disrespectful than this? Therefore, the Buddha established each rule because of the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*). Those who violate them are dealt with as above.
If there was an intervening obstruction such that [the person] did not see it, there is no offense.
"One must not sit with legs extended toward a Buddha-stūpa; this is how one should train.
The group of six monks sat with their legs extended toward a Buddha-stūpa. The other bhikṣus censured them, and the Buddha established this precept.
The offense for those who violate it is as stated above. There is no offense if there is a partition between them, nor is there an offense for one sitting in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka).
One must not reside in an upper room while placing a Buddha-stūpa in a lower room; this is how one should train.
The group of six monks placed a Buddha-stūpa in a lower room and resided in an upper room. The other bhikṣus censured them, and the Buddha consequently established this precept.
The offense is as described above. However, if there are circumstances such as defilement or impurity in the upper room, one may move it to a lower room.
There is no offense.
One must not preach the Dharma while standing to a person who is seated, except in the case of illness; this is how one should train.

Regarding the transgression of the six groups of monks that insulted the Dharma, the Buddha, knowing [the situation], established this rule. If one preaches the Dharma for the sake of a sick person, there is no offense.
Listen. An offense is as described above. If one is taken away by a king or a high minister, there is no offense.
One who is lying down must not have the Dharma preached to them while one is sitting, except in the case of illness. This is how you should train.
One should train oneself: if another person is seated on a seat while one is not seated on a seat, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: if another person is on a high seat while one is on a low seat, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
If another person is walking ahead and one is walking behind, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness; this is how one should train.
If another person is on a high walkway and one is on a lower walkway, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness;
this is how one should train.
If a person is on the path while oneself is not on the path, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness; this is how one should train.
These six rules above were established one by one together with their prohibitions out of respect for the Dharma. Whether an offense has been committed or not is the same as described above.
"One must not walk along a road holding hands; this is how one should train.
The group of six bhikṣus walked along the road holding hands, obstructing men and women. When householders saw this, they criticized and disparaged them.

The Buddha, knowing [the circumstances], established this rule. One who violates it is subject to the same penalty as above. If one’s vision is impaired, or if one has an illness requiring assistance while walking, there is no offense in either case.
One must not climb a tree higher than the height of a person, except when there is a specific reason; this is how one should train.
There was a bhikṣu who was observing the summer retreat atop a large tree. When he voided excrement and urine, the tree deity became angry and intended to take his life.
The Buddha, knowing this, established a rule. Later, another bhikṣu encountered a fierce beast on the road;

he climbed a tree to avoid it but did not dare go higher, and was consequently injured by the beast. The Buddha then permitted [climbing trees] except under specific circumstances; otherwise, one commits an offense.

The above applies as before. The Buddha further prescribed: one must not defecate or urinate while walking around a tree; whoever violates this also commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. One must train oneself thus:
one must not carry a bowl placed in a net-sack suspended from the end of a staff on one’s shoulder while walking. This is how one should study.
Bhadanta, [it happened that] he placed his bowl in a netted bag, threaded it onto the tip of a staff, and carried it on his shoulder as he walked.
A lay devotee saw him from afar but did not know who he was, so he moved aside to a hidden spot on the lower path. Later, seeing that it was indeed Bhadanta, he began to criticize and disparage him.
When the Buddha heard of this, he established a precept; those who violate it are subject to the same penalty as before.
"One should not preach the Dharma to a person holding a staff, except in the case of illness; this is how one should train.

While the Buddha was preaching the Dharma to the assembly, King Prasenajit came to listen. Among his retinue were those carrying staffs, so the group of six monks preached the Dharma to them separately.
The Buddha, knowing this, established the rule. The offense for violating it is as stated above. This also applies if [one preaches] for a king or a high minister.
[In such cases,] there is no offense.
One should train oneself: "If a person is holding a sword, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: "If a person is holding a spear, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness."
One should not preach the Dharma to a person holding a sword, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule that should be observed.
One should not preach the Dharma to a person holding a parasol, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule that should be observed.
These four items above were all prohibited by the Buddha one by one because King Bimbisāra possessed them along with the multitude—specifically swords, spears, knives, and parasols.
Whether an offense is committed or not is as explained above.
Venerable sirs, I have now recited the rules of training for the community. Now I ask the venerable sirs: Are you pure in this matter? (This is asked three times.
Venerable sirs, since there is silence, you are pure in this matter. Thus shall it be held.
Venerable sirs, these seven principles for the settlement of disputes are recited every half-month from within the Sūtra of the Precepts.
Whenever a dispute arises among the bhikṣus, it should be settled immediately.

There are four types of legal disputes (*adhikaraṇa*): first, disputes concerning speech (*vāda-adhikaraṇa*); second, disputes concerning accusations (*anuvāda-adhikaraṇa*); third, disputes concerning offenses (*āpatti-adhikaraṇa*); and fourth, disputes concerning matters (*vinaya-adhikaraṇa*). Regarding disputes concerning speech:

this refers to deliberations that are discordant, such as [debates over] whether something is Dharma or non-Dharma, Vinaya or non-Vinaya, a grave offense or not a grave offense, and so forth, up to whether it was spoken by the Buddha or not spoken by the Buddha, or whether it was established by the Buddha or not established by the Buddha, and so on. It is because of these characteristics...
"Quarreling out of anger" refers to this. "Quarreling for the sake of finding fault" refers to when a bhikṣu asks another bhikṣu, "Do you remember committing such-and-such an offense?
and that bhikṣu is displeased and does not accept [the inquiry].

"Quarreling over an offense" refers to when a bhikṣu commits an offense ranging from a *pārājika* down to a *durbhāṣita*, and the community’s deliberations are in turmoil. "Quarreling over a matter" refers to within the Saṃgha...
This refers to all *karmas* (formal ecclesiastical acts) and all matters concerning the Saṃgha that are not in accord with the Dharma.
Should a dispute arise, it must be immediately eliminated. There are seven methods for such elimination, which are detailed below in the text.
"One should grant the *saṃmukha-vinaya*; one ought to grant the *saṃmukha-vinaya*.
The former phrase refers to the method for assessing what is appropriate; the latter phrase refers to settling the dispute through the Dharma. Hereafter, all cases shall follow this pattern.
*Vinaya* is here translated as "skillful governance" (*śubha-vinaya*) or "extinguishing evil" (*doṣa-nirodha*); it is the code of discipline (*śīla*). *Saṃmukha* means "present before [the eyes]."
The Vinaya universally extinguishes all disputes. There are five types of "presence" (*sammukhībhāva*): first, presence of the Dharma; second, presence of the Vinaya;
third, presence of the person; fourth, presence of the Saṃgha; and fifth, presence of the boundary (*sīmā*). What is meant by "presence of the Dharma"?
It refers to the actual application of the methods for settling disputes. What is meant by "presence of the Vinaya"? It refers to the actual application of the Vinaya rules for settling disputes.
This refers to the *bhikṣuṇī*. What is meant by "the person being present"? It is when the individuals involved in the dispute are present.
What is meant by "the Saṃgha being present"? It is when the Saṃgha has assembled in harmony. What is meant by "the boundary (*sīmā*) being present"?

It is when the formal act of establishing a restriction (*sīmā-bandha-karman*) is performed within the boundary. By means of these five types of presence, one treats the dispute; through repentance in accordance with the Dharma, the dispute is resolved.
The matter has been settled. If it is raised again, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
One should grant the *smṛtivinaya*; indeed, one must grant the *smṛtivinaya*.
This *vinaya* correctly extinguishes disputes arising from searching for faults. For example, when a bhikṣu is accused by another bhikṣu of a groundless offense.

If one has been slandered, yet knows for certain that one has not committed an offense, and others continue to speak of it within the Saṃgha without ceasing, one should request the *smṛtivinaya* (the discipline of mindfulness) from the Saṃgha.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu has committed an offense and has already confessed it according to the Dharma, yet others within the Saṃgha continue to speak of it without ceasing, he should likewise request the *smṛtivinaya* from the Saṃgha. Moreover, as in another case...

A bhikṣu has not yet committed this offense, though he is certain to do so in the future. When others within the Saṃgha declare that he has committed an offense and question him persistently, he should request the *smṛtivinaya* (the discipline of mindfulness) from the Saṃgha.
Whenever there is such a petitioner, the Saṃgha should examine his conduct regarding the precepts;
if it is found to be pure, they should grant it, which would be in accordance with the Dharma. If his conduct lacks integrity and they grant it falsely, it is improper.
This is contrary to the Dharma. Regarding *smṛtivinaya* (the legal procedure of recollection): because the monk himself does not recall having committed an offense, one causes him to recollect it.
If he has committed an offense, he shall receive punishment; if he is without offense, he shall be encouraged [to strive for purity].

To grant the *smṛtivinaya* dharma, that bhikṣu should go before the Saṃgha, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, prostrate at the feet of the Saṃgha, and kneel with his right knee on the ground to make his formal request.
I, Bhikṣu [Name], state: A certain Bhikṣu has come to me three times and asked me, "Do you remember committing such-and-such an offense?
To which I have answered three times, "I do not remember. Now I beg the Saṃgha for the *paṭiññātakara-vinaya* (the disciplinary procedure based on acknowledgment).
May the Saṃgha grant me the *paṭiññātakara-vinaya*, so that he shall no longer question me repeatedly. Out of compassion...

Out of compassion. Having thus requested three times, the Saṃgha should deliberate. If it is deemed appropriate to grant [the request], it should be granted through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal motion followed by three proclamations).
One bhikṣu should announce: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣu so-and-so has made a request before the Saṃgha, saying:
'That bhikṣu so-and-so... [and so on, as above, up to] "...no longer asks me repeatedly. [The rest follows.]
[The proponent] says: "The Saṃgha now grants the *smṛtivinaya* (the discipline of mindfulness) to [this monk], so that this bhikṣu shall no longer be questioned repeatedly regarding his offense.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience. This is the motion (*jñapti*). Furthermore, he proclaims: 'Venerable Saṃgha, listen...
[repeated as above] ...until the point where it says he shall no longer be questioned regarding his offense. Below this, he further says: 'Which elders who consent remain silent?'"
"Whoever does not consent, let them speak. Having spoken thus three times, he says: "The Saṃgha has granted the *smṛtivinaya* to the bhikṣu so-and-so;
the Saṃgha consents, as it is silent. This matter is thus upheld. Thus it is settled.
If he should commit it again, he commits a *pāyattika* offense.
He should be granted the *amūḷhavinaya*; indeed, the *amūḷhavinaya* should be granted.
This *vinaya* also extinguishes disputes arising from searching (*mṛgavya-vivāda*). For example, when a bhikṣu, being insane or having lost his mind, commits various offenses.
[If] later [it is discovered that he was] not insane, the bhikṣus ask him: "Do you remember committing such-and-such an offense? He replies, "I do not remember.

Even after being asked three times, he does not admit it. This person should beg from the Saṃgha for the *amūḍhavinaya* (the discipline for one who was not insane). The procedure for begging and the granting of this discipline is as follows.
The *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of) is the same, with the sole modification that "recollection" (*sati*) is changed to "non-delusion" (*amūḷha*).
One should grant the *pātimokkha-thapanā* (suspension of the Pātimokkha); one must grant the *pātimokkha-thapanā*.
This method rightly extinguishes disputes arising from offenses. Regarding "one's own statement": there is a bhikṣu who has committed a *pārājika* offense, up to...

This is called "confessing a bad report. When one comes forward and says, "I have committed such-and-such an offense," or when the Saṃgha raises the matter and asks, "Do you remember committing such-and-such an offense?
and that person says of themselves, "I have committed such-and-such an offense," the Saṃgha should further examine the details within the assembly.

If it is indeed found that they committed such-and-such an offense, then they shall be disciplined according to their own confession. Alternatively, there may be those who commit an offense but claim they did not, or there may be...

If one who has committed a grave offense claims it is light, or one who has not committed an offense claims they have, or one who has committed a light offense claims it is grave—in all such cases, [the penalty] should not be granted, for it is contrary to the Dharma.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu who has committed an offense does not confess it himself, yet one hastily grants him punishment, this too is contrary to the Dharma; for the offenses of the five categories are all based upon self-acknowledgment.
This refers to the *yebhuyyasika* (majority decision). One should apply the *tassapāpiyasikā* (procedure for the one deserving censure); indeed, one must apply the *tassapāpiyasikā*.
This method is also known as *mūla-yebhuyyasika*. It extinguishes disputes regarding offenses and disputes regarding transgressions. This is because of the person who has committed an offense.
Their statements are inconsistent; one cannot be disciplined based solely on their own words. One must investigate the characteristics of the offense committed and then discipline accordingly.
For example, suppose a bhikṣu is formally questioned by the Saṃgha and asked, "Do you recall committing such-and-such an offense?
He replies, "I did not commit it. When asked again, he replies, "I did commit it. Immediately thereafter, he says, "In truth, I did not commit it; I was merely joking. As in this case...
This bhikṣu should truly investigate the characteristics of his offense and be disciplined according to his original statement. A *karmavācanā* for the place of the offense shall be performed.
He should be granted the formal procedure for searching for many characteristics of the offense; he must be granted the formal procedure for searching for many characteristics of the offense.
This Dharma correctly extinguishes disputes over speech, as well as disputes over matters and disputes over offenses.

Because the substance of these matters is difficult to determine as right or wrong and difficult to adjudicate as light or heavy, the aforementioned methods were unable to extinguish them; therefore, one frequently seeks out the characteristics of the offense to bring about their cessation.
There are four kinds of "extensive seeking": first, extensive wisdom; second, many people who know the Dharma; third, extensively seeking causes and conditions;

and fourth, extensively seeking cessation in various places. Regarding "extensive wisdom," this refers to being broadly learned and well-informed, being thoroughly proficient in the Vinaya-piṭaka, being skillfully adept at discerning what is permitted and what is prohibited, and having a mind free from partiality or favoritism.
Regarding "many people who know the Dharma," this refers to reaching those many people who know the Dharma...

"Place" refers to the act of deciding by means of counting voting sticks (*śalākā*). "Seeking many causes and conditions" means extensively searching through the Tripiṭaka and citing numerous causes and conditions as evidence.
"Seeking a decision in many places" means traveling everywhere to various lands to seek a resolution for the matter at hand.
One should grant the *tṛṇaprastāraka* (covering with grass); one shall grant the *tṛṇaprastāraka*.

This method rightly extinguishes disputes arising from transgressions, while simultaneously extinguishing disputes of speech, disputes of seeking, and disputes of legal matters, which arise from the mutual hostility of two factions.

When the four types of disputes arise together, they cannot be investigated to their conclusion, nor can they be extinguished. The Buddha then taught the practice of repentance known as "covering the ground with grass.
As for "covering the ground with grass," both parties must each sincerely vow to cease their dispute and proceed together to the midst of the Saṃgha.
They should bare their right shoulders, remove their leather sandals, and kneel on their right knees, declaring: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen to us..."
They have engaged in mutual strife and committed many offenses, which they have not been able to expiate. Now they beg the Saṃgha for the *tṛṇaprastāraka* (grass-covering) confession.
Having thus spoken three times, they all stretch out their hands and feet and prostrate themselves on the ground before the *karmācārya*.
Listen with one mind to this *karmavācanā*. The *karmadāna* proclaims: "May the venerable Saṃgha listen.

These bhikṣus have quarreled and contended among themselves, committing many offenses that could not otherwise be extinguished. They now petition the Saṃgha for the *tṛṇaprastāraka* (covering with grass) confession.
The Saṃgha now grants them the *tṛṇaprastāraka* confession. If it is the time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent."
The motion is thus stated. Again, it is proclaimed: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

These bhikṣus have been quarreling with one another and have committed many offenses that cannot otherwise be extinguished. They now request from the Saṃgha the *tṛṇaprastāraka* (covering-over-with-grass) confession.
The Saṃgha now grants these bhikṣus the *tṛṇaprastāraka* confession. Which elders who approve of this remain silent?"
"Whoever does not approve, let them speak. The Sangha has granted the *tṛṇaprastāra* (grass-covering) confession to these bhikṣus.
Because the Sangha approves by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld. This is called the *tṛṇaprastāra* method of confession.
'Grass-covering' signifies the outward manifestation of accepting one's guilt. In this confession, neither the origin of the offense nor the name of the offense is mentioned. The Sangha...
Nor shall one further inquire into the specific characteristics of the offense before accepting the confession.
Venerable sirs, I have now recited the seven rules for settling disputes. I now ask the venerable sirs: Are you pure in this matter?
(Ask three times.)
Venerable sirs, because you are silent, you are pure in this matter; thus do I hold it to be so.
Venerable sirs, I have recited the introduction to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra; I have recited the four pārājika rules;
I have recited the thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣa rules; I have recited the two aniyata rules; I have recited the thirty naiḥsargika-pāyattika rules...
The *Pāyattika* Dharmas: The ninety *pāyattika* dharmas have been recited; the four *pratideśanīya* dharmas have been recited; the *saiksa* dharmas have been recited;
the seven *adhikaraṇa-śamatha* dharmas have been recited. This is the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* spoken by the Buddha, which is recited every half-month from within the *Sūtra*.
Whatever other teachings of the Buddha there may be, all are to be harmonized and integrated therein.
"One should train accordingly.
This concludes the preceding section. Regarding "there are further other Buddha-dharmas": while the precepts number only two hundred and fifty, the actual phenomena are inexhaustible.
There are a great many things that were neither prohibited by the Buddha nor explicitly permitted by him.
If one can thoroughly investigate the underlying intent within these precepts, then there will be nothing that does not harmonize; this is what should be studied by all.
Formerly, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "There may be occasions when there is a matter regarding which I have neither prohibited nor permitted from the past."
However, regarding this matter, if something contradicts what is impure and accords with what is pure, it should be practiced;
if it contradicts what is pure and accords with what is impure, it should not be practiced. Now, observing this instruction of the Buddha, it is precisely what is meant by:
"In these matters, one should train by being in full harmony with others."
Patience is the foremost path; the Buddha taught that non-action is supreme. One who leaves home to cause affliction to others is not called a śramaṇa.
The characteristics of the five categories of precepts have already been explained in detail above. What follows is the summary teaching spoken by the seven Buddhas. Understand this well.
If one acts with this intention, though one may not hit the mark exactly, one will not be far from it; therefore, I shall set each point forth in detail.
Those who aspire to the Way of the Sage must take patience (*kṣānti*) as the foremost. Why is patience the foremost?

Because the Way of the Buddha is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and one must enter it through patience. When one is able to practice patience, one gradually reaches the state of forgetting insult. [This applies to] self and others...
Their characteristics may be empty, so that one may hope to reach the realm of non-action (*wuwei*). The Fundamental Verse says: "Patience is the king among diligences;
it can attain the state of *nirvāṇa*. If one cannot endure humiliation, one will inevitably cause distress to others; how could this be the Dharma of a *śramaṇa*?
*Śramaṇa* is translated here as "diligent cessation," meaning to diligently cultivate precepts, concentration, and wisdom, and to cease and extinguish greed and anger.
Because of delusion, one is called a śramaṇa. Now, if you proceed to vex others, then the mountains of self and other will rise high and strife will arise daily;
what then can be said of your diligent pursuit of tranquility?
This is the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra* spoken by Vipaśyin Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Regarding "Vipaśyin," one alternative is "Vaiśvī"; this translates as "Victorious Vision.

The Sanskrit term *Tathāgata* is translated here as "Thus-Come One" (*Rúlái*), meaning that he has come by way of the path of reality to manifest birth among humans and to transform and guide sentient beings. [Sanskrit]...
"Arahan" is translated as "one who is unattached" (*wu suo zhu*) and also as "one worthy of offerings" (*ying gong*).

This means that regarding both mundane and supramundane phenomena, one is entirely without attachment and is thus fit to receive the offerings of the noble ones and ordinary beings throughout the nine realms.

"Samyaksambuddha" in Sanskrit is translated as "Equal and Perfectly Awakened One" (*deng zheng jue*) and also as "Right and Universal Knower" (*zheng bian zhi*). This means that there is nothing he does not know...
It is also correct that there is nothing it does not pervade, for it is entirely identical to the *dharmadhātu*. This refers to three of the ten titles of the Buddha.
When this Buddha appeared in the world, he first preached these precepts because sentient beings have not yet eliminated the notion of a self (*ātman-grāha*);
they will inevitably give rise to strife and contention. Among all things that obstruct the Path, none is more severe than this; therefore, he guarded against it from the very beginning.
Just as a person with clear vision can avoid dangerous and evil paths, so too there are wise people in this world who can distance themselves from all evils;
this metaphor clarifies that in studying the Way, possessing wisdom is paramount. As for those without wisdom, they crave immediate gain and place their trust [in worldly things].
Those who follow false teachings will inevitably enter the three miserable realms; even if they should attain birth as humans or devas, they will ultimately fall back into decline.

They are like travelers who, though possessing feet, lack the light of wisdom and are certain to fall into perilous places. Those with true intelligence can distinguish between the false and the correct, and are not deluded by minor gains;
thus, they attain the peaceful and secure bliss of *nirvāṇa*. They are like travelers who possess both feet and [wisdom].
"Eye! You must remain far from danger.
This is the precept scripture spoken by Śikhin Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Śikhin—alternatively called Śikhi—is translated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* as "Fire-Dependent. When this Buddha appeared in the world, it was at the very beginning.

This precept is taught because people lack far-reaching insight; they frequently accept the teachings of non-Buddhists and crave the pleasures of humans and devas, remaining unaware of their underlying afflictions.
Therefore, this is taught to warn them against their delusions.
Do not slander, nor be envious; you should practice the precepts. Know moderation in food and drink, and always delight in solitude.
With a concentrated mind, take joy in diligence—this is called the teaching of all Buddhas.
Not slandering restrains the karma of speech; not being envious restrains the karma of mind. When one practices the precepts, then the three karmas are all restrained.
It is forbidden. However, if the mind craves food and drink, one cannot uphold the precepts; if the mind is attached to the clamor of the world, one cannot uphold the precepts;
if the mind delights in indolence, one cannot uphold the precepts. Therefore, each of these is specifically addressed.

If one can act in this way, then the precepts may be purified, meditative concentration may be attained, and wisdom may be developed. Furthermore, the teaching of the Buddhas has further [instructions] beyond this.
This is it. This is the *Pratimokṣa Sūtra* spoken by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin.
"Vipaśyin" is also called Viśvabhū; this translates as "Pervasive Sovereignty over All. This Buddha appeared [in the world].
In this world, these precepts were taught first because the disciples were fond of speaking of others' faults while being themselves indolent in their spiritual cultivation;
thus, they were unable to attain the fruits of the śramaṇa. Therefore, these remedial methods were demonstrated.
Just as a bee gathers from a flower, Neither destroying its color nor its fragrance, But taking only its nectar to depart—
So should a bhikṣu enter a village, Not interfering with others' affairs,
But observing only his own conduct, Whether it be right or wrong.
The first verse consists of three lines as a simile and one line as the application of the Dharma.
Just as a bee gathering from flowers takes only its nectar lightly, without harming either the color or the fragrance, so too should a bhikṣu entering a village act like a bee;
though he may beg for various things, he should take only enough to satisfy his hunger and stop, rather than seeking excessively before withdrawing.
This refers to that mind of respectful faith. Regarding the next verse: the first two lines admonish one regarding others, while the latter two lines concern observing oneself.
This means that one must not oppose others in their affairs by disparaging them.
Not only must one not oppose them, but one should also not observe whether their actions are successful or not; rather, one should simply observe oneself.
Regarding one's own conduct—whether it be right or wrong—if it is right, one should exert oneself further; if it is wrong, one should strive to correct it.
This is the Discourse on the Precepts spoken by the Tathāgata Krakucchanda, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Krakucchanda—alternatively transcribed as Krakutsanda—means "that which is to be severed" or "functional activity.
This Buddha appeared in the world and first proclaimed these precepts because his disciples were largely seeking after gain and offerings.
Not knowing contentment, fond of speaking of the faults of others, and indolent in pure cultivation—for these reasons, one is cautioned:
"Let not the mind be heedless; diligently study the Noble Dharma. Thus, free from sorrow, the mind will enter Nirvāṇa."
In practicing the noble Dharma, one most fears negligence; for through negligence, nothing whatsoever is accomplished.
Therefore, he warns against it and exhorts diligent study. Once one is able to study diligently, afflictions can be severed; hence it is said, "There is no sorrow."
When there are no afflictions, the mind can become concentrated; when the mind is concentrated, one may enter the noble fruit of non-arising.
This is the precept scripture spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Kanakamuni.
Kanakamuni— also called Kanakamuni, or alternatively Kanakamuni,
which translates as "Golden Silence" (Jinjì) or "Golden Immortal" (Jinxian)— was the Buddha who first preached these precepts upon his appearance in the world.

This was taught in order to exhort and encourage the assembly of śrāvakas who, being addicted to the savor of minor meditative concentrations, had become self-indulgent and were unable to advance in their practice.
Commit no evil; Practice all that is good; And purify your own mind.
"This is what the Buddhas have taught:

'Commit not any evil. This refers to both natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and proscribed transgressions (*prajñapti-sāvadya*), as well as all immeasurable unwholesome dharmas, which are all forbidden and must be severed.
One should practice all that is good,' which refers to the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), the myriad practices (*sahasra-caryā*), and so forth."
The Dharma-gate of the Purification of the Means of Cognition (*pramāṇa*) is intended to exhort all to practice with diligence and progress. Regarding the phrase "purifying one's own will":
this means that although evil may have ceased, the underlying intention may still arise sporadically; and although good may be practiced, the thoughts may not yet be consistently pure.

Thus, these floating emotions and deluded imaginings must necessarily be purified. This is especially true when, despite having ceased evil, the very thought of ceasing evil has not yet been forgotten, and despite practicing...
It is good. Yet, the mind that performs good deeds has not yet been transformed. Within a pure mind, such matters do not exist;
nor, however, can it be anything other than pure. When these three qualities are fully possessed, then all the teachings of the Buddhas do not transcend them.
Therefore, it is said: "This is the teaching of all the Buddhas."
This is the precept scripture spoken by the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Kāśyapa" is also called "Kāśyapa"; it translates as "Drinking Light. When this Buddha appeared in the world, he first spoke these precepts.
These constitute the great framework of all precepts and the correct path for universal practice; they were not established for the sake of a single individual alone.
It was spoken at one time.
Guard well your speech; purify your own intentions; let no evil be done by the body.
When these three paths of action are pure, one who is able to practice in this way follows the path of the Great Sages.
The karma of the world does not depart from the three avenues of speech, mind, and body.

Karma of speech refers to false speech, frivolous speech, harsh speech, and double-tongued speech, as well as all forms of improper discourse. Karma of the mind refers to greed, anger, and delusion, as well as all forms of deluded thought.
Karma of the body refers to killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, as well as everything perceived by the eyes and heard by the ears.
This refers to what the ear hears, what the nose smells, what the tongue tastes, and what the body touches; it is from these that various transgressions arise.
If one can guard these three so as not to commit offenses, then there will be no precept that is not pure.
This is called the Way of the Great Awakened Golden Immortal. Now, practicing the precepts may only lead to rebirth in heaven; it is not the Holy Path. Nevertheless...
Without precepts, none of the noble paths can be accomplished. Therefore, those who seek great nirvana must obtain these as their foundation;
for what else could they be but the noble path?

This is the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra* spoken by the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, for the sake of the Saṃgha of non-active monks during the twelve years [following his enlightenment]. From this time forward, it shall be explained in detail.
All bhikṣus who delight in the Dharma, who delight in being śramaṇas, and who possess a sense of shame and dread of blame while desiring to train in the precepts, should train themselves therein.
Śākyamuni. This is translated as "The Benevolent Sage of Silent Stillness. "Silent Stillness" refers to the internal realization of the ultimate truth; it is the wisdom for one's own benefit.
"The Benevolent Sage" refers to the outward manifestation of benevolent transformation; it is the compassion for the benefit of others.

This auspicious title was established because compassion and wisdom are practiced in tandem. Regarding the passage following "for twelve years," it means that at that time the monastic community was pure and free from [faults].

The precepts can be maintained, and the signless (animitta) can be regulated; therefore, it is called the "Monastic Community of No Affairs" (wu-shi seng). For this reason, names and characteristics are not established, but the general meaning is briefly indicated.
This is what is known as the *Lüjie jing* (Brief Precept Sūtra). After twelve years had passed, there gradually arose instances of violation.

Therefore, the World-Honored One established prohibitions according to specific circumstances and extensively explained the characteristics of the precepts, so that they might recognize these characteristics, maintain them, and guard against all outflows (*āsrava*).
From the words "All bhikṣus" onwards, he concludes by exhorting them to practice and study. This means:

if a bhikṣu is thus fond of the True Dharma, delights in being a śramaṇa, feels shame regarding what is contrary to the Dharma, and takes pleasure in studying the pure precepts, he should [apply himself] to this gāthā.
This is the intermediate [explanation]. Furthermore, in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, this is called the "Gāthā Poṣadha.
When the Buddha was residing in Rājagṛha, there were ninety-six kinds of renunciants who all performed the poṣadha, yet the Buddha alone did not do so.
The people of the world resented this and said, "Why is it that the Śākya son alone does not perform the poṣadha? The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "It is indeed right that one should be censured by the world. From this day forward, you should perform the *poṣadha*. Therefore, he spoke this verse:
'A person of wisdom who can guard the precepts Shall obtain three kinds of happiness: Renown and material gain.'"
Upon death, one will be born in the heavens; one should contemplate such a state.
The wise who diligently guard the precepts—whose precepts are pure and who possess wisdom—shall attain the supreme path.
This clarifies the benefits of guarding the precepts. The first four lines clarify worldly benefits, meaning that for the wise...
A person who discerns the heterodox from the orthodox and understands benefit and harm is thus able to strictly guard this precept. Such a person will certainly attain three kinds of happiness.
As for these three kinds of happiness: first, one gains a good reputation, meaning that those who observe the precepts are praised by the multitude;
second, one gains material offerings, meaning that those who observe the precepts are delighted to provide support; third, one attains rebirth in heaven, meaning that those who observe...

For one who observes the precepts, the ten wholesome paths of action are fully perfected; because they shall obtain celestial blessings upon death, the final four lines clarify the supramundane benefits.
One should contemplate that the attainment of such happiness through guarding the precepts is thus. A person of wisdom should therefore be even more diligent in guarding the pure precepts.
When the precepts are pure, concentration can arise; because of concentration, wisdom can be developed. Once wisdom has been developed, then...
One shall attain the supreme path of unsurpassed bodhi; how could it be merely the attainment of the three kinds of worldly happiness?
As with the Buddhas of the past, those of the future, and the World-Honored Ones of the present—
One who can overcome all sorrow and is revered by all for their observance of the precepts—this is the Dharma of all Buddhas.
If there are those who act for their own sake and seek the path of the Buddha, they should revere the True Dharma;
this is the teaching of all Buddhas.
The first six phrases state that the Buddhas of the three periods of time all honor and teach this precept. Regarding "surpassing all sorrows":
the six classes of ordinary beings have the sorrow of segmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*), while those of the Three Vehicles have the sorrow of transformation (*pariṇāmi-bhava*).

Only a Buddha has exhausted the five stages of dwelling and forever eliminated the two types of death; therefore, he is able to surpass them. The Buddhas of the three periods of time have already attained the unsurpassed fruit.
Why, then, do we collectively revere this precept? It is because this precept is the true Dharma of all Buddhas.
As for the passage beginning with "If there are," it means that if sentient beings wish to seek the Buddha-way, they should especially revere this precept;
for this is the teaching the Buddha has bequeathed to posterity, intended for people to rely upon and practice.
The Seven Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, who have extinguished all fetters and defilements, have preached this Sūtra of the Seven Precepts;
through it, all bonds are liberated, and they have entered Nirvāṇa. All worldly play has forever ceased.
One should follow what the Great Sage has taught. The precepts praised by the noble sages are that which the disciples practice.
Following the entry into parinirvāṇa of the seven Buddhas, this section again cites the cultivation and realization of those Buddhas to manifest the supreme merit of upholding the precepts.
The seven Buddhas, in order to eliminate all fetters (*saṃyojana*), preached these Seven Precept Sūtras; these precepts are precisely what the seven Buddhas themselves cultivated.
By means of this Dharma, all fetters are liberated, and one enters nirvana; thus, all worldly dharmas of conceptual proliferation are forever extinguished without remainder.
As for the "fetters" (*saṃyojana*), there are nine: namely, attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, views, grasping, doubt, envy, and avarice.
As for the "proclivities" (*anuśaya*), these are the delusions of view; there are eighty-eight proclivities, and so forth.

The ninety-eight *anuśayas* (latent tendencies) are categorized as those abandoned through seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*) and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). There are four types of bonds (*bandhana*), namely:

greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), attachment to precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). "To practice" means to respectfully uphold; it refers to the disciple’s respectful practice of the precepts taught by the former sages.
This is what has been universally extolled by the sages and worthies, and it is precisely that which the disciples practice to enter the path to nirvana.
Since the Buddha realized enlightenment through this very means, how could his disciples not rely upon it in their conduct?
When the World-Honored One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he gave rise to a heart of great compassion;
he gathered the assembly of bhikṣus and gave them this instruction: "Do not say that because I have entered parinirvāṇa there is no one to protect the pure conduct.
I have now spoken the Sūtra of Precepts and have also well explained the Vinaya. Although I have entered parinirvāṇa..."
One should regard it as the World-Honored One; this sutra shall long abide in the world.
Through this, the Buddha-dharma will flourish, and because of this flourishing, one may enter Nirvana.
This concludes the Buddha’s final exhortation, intended to cause people to revere the precepts. At the Śāla Grove, the Buddha was about to enter [Nirvana].
At the time of my parinirvāṇa, out of great compassion, I have gathered this assembly of the Dharma and said to you:
"Do not think that now that I enter extinction there is no one to protect you. This *Prātimokṣa Sūtra* which I have now spoken is no different from my remaining in the world.
You should regard it as the World-Honored One, honoring and practicing it with reverence. If you honor it, then this sutra will endure."
If you remain long in the world, the Buddha-dharma will flourish; because the Buddha-dharma flourishes, all people will practice it, and thus they shall all enter nirvana.
If one does not uphold these precepts as they should be observed during the poṣadha,
it is like the world being perpetually shrouded in darkness when the sun has set; therefore, one should guard and uphold these precepts,
sitting together in harmony like a yak cherishing its tail, just as the Buddha has taught.
If it is not recited, based on the preceding text, the fault of failing to uphold it is revealed by way of contrast:
namely, if one does not uphold this precept, one will be unable to perform the *poṣadha* according to the Dharma every half-month.

Since the light of the day of precepts would then be absent, the realm of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-dhātu*) would be entirely shrouded in darkness, and all sentient beings would sink into the perilous and evil paths. *Poṣadha*.
In Sanskrit, it is called *pratideśanā* (or *pratideśanīya*), which translates as "confessing to one another. This refers to speaking of one's transgressions face-to-face.
Regarding the phrase "one should guard [the precepts] below," it means that one should protect the precepts with the same intensity as a yak cherishes its tail.
The yak is a beast of the southern barbarians; its form resembles that of an ox, yet its tail possesses five colors. When it moves...
"One must look back. Even when pursued by others, one still looks back and does not abandon [the tail]. Because one looks back at the tail, one is captured by others.
This is a metaphor for one who guards the precepts: even when there are circumstances that could cause the loss of life, they are able to remain without losing [the precepts].
"To harmonize and assemble in one place," etc., means that one should gather together every half-month to recite the *Prātimokṣa* (Poṣadha), as taught by the Buddha.
I have recited the Prātimokṣa Sūtra; the Saṃgha has completed the Poṣadha ceremony.
May the merit of this sūtra that I have now recited be bestowed upon all sentient beings, so that together they may attain the Way of the Buddha.
This verse consists of fifty-six lines. It represents the essential meaning established by the Vinaya Master Dharmaguptaka, and its intent is fully revealed herein.
Exalting the virtue of the precepts, one universally exhorts others to practice and uphold them. These first two lines summarize the preceding text;
the latter four lines constitute the vow of dedication. If all merits are not dedicated to sentient beings, they remain limited to self-benefit;
if they are not dedicated to the Buddha-way, they will stop halfway. Now, it is said that [merit] is bestowed upon sentient beings so that [all may] together...
Attaining the path of Buddhahood—this is the first vast dedication.
